\newpage

# HOW TO USE THIS PACK

1. **The pack is in two parts.** Part A holds the twenty-three question papers. Part B holds the answer key, marking scheme, curriculum blueprint, cognitive-level distribution, quality-control summary and examiner notes for each paper. **Photocopy Part A for the candidates only.**
2. **Each paper stands alone.** A paper may be used as an end-of-topic test as soon as its sub-strand has been taught, or several papers may be combined into a terminal mock.
3. **Edit page one of a paper before printing.** The school name, the academic year and the examination title are meant to be changed to suit your school.
4. **Timing.** Each paper is set for 2 hours: about 40 minutes for Section A and 80 minutes for Section B. Candidates who are new to the format should be given the full time.
5. **Figures.** Every figure is drawn in pencil style and prints clearly in black and white. Check the photocopies before the examination; a figure that has printed faintly should be redrawn on the chalkboard.
6. **Marking.** Section B answers are marked against the points listed in the marking scheme. The italic *Marking note* under each part states what is compulsory for the mark, what alternatives are acceptable, and the common errors. Accept any other correct and relevant answer.
7. **Recording.** Use the mark-sheet grids in this pack to record the papers written by each candidate, and the Section A answer sheet for the objective test.
8. **Difficulty.** Every paper is built to approximately 30% easy, 50% moderate and 20% challenging items, weighted by marks. A class average of 50-60% on a paper is normal at the first attempt.

\newpage

# INSTRUCTIONS TO THE INVIGILATOR

1. Seat the candidates so that no candidate can see another's work. Collect all notes, textbooks and mobile telephones before the papers are given out.
2. Give out the question paper and the answer booklet together. Candidates may use a pencil, a ruler and an eraser; calculators are not required for any paper in this pack.
3. Read out the instructions on page one of the paper and announce the starting time and the finishing time on the chalkboard.
4. Remind the candidates that **Section A carries 40 marks and Section B carries 60 marks**, and that all questions in both sections must be answered.
5. Allow no talking, no lending of instruments and no leaving of the room in the first and the last fifteen minutes.
6. Announce the time remaining thirty minutes and ten minutes before the end.
7. At the end, collect the answer sheets first and then the answer booklets, counting them against the number of candidates before anyone leaves.
8. Report any irregularity in writing to the head teacher on the same day.

## 2. The curriculum areas in full

*The wording of every content standard and indicator below is taken from the NaCCA Common Core Programme Science Curriculum (B7/JHS1 - B9/JHS3), 2021 edition. The curriculum areas (topics) are the teaching headings used in the blueprint of each paper to group the items under an indicator.*

### STRAND 1: Diversity of Matter

#### Sub-Strand 1: Materials — Paper 1, 2

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.1.1.1** — Demonstrate knowledge of types of mixtures, and understanding of the processes of scientific ways of separating the components of mixtures.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.1.1.1.1* — Identify types of mixtures by name and characteristics.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.1.1.1.2* — Design and perform processes for separating kinds of mixtures.
- **Content standard B8/JHS2.1.1.2** — Demonstrate understanding of atoms and the atomic structure of elements in the periodic table.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.1.1.2.1* — Describe atoms as composed of sub-atomic particles.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.1.1.2.2* — Explain the arrangement of elements in terms of the number of protons in the nuclei of atoms of each element.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 1.1 Mixtures: Definition and Classification; 1.2 Solutions, Colloids and Suspensions; 1.3 Light Scattering in Mixtures (Tyndall Effect); 1.4 Separation Methods: Filtration, Decantation, Sieving and Magnetism; 1.5 Separation Methods: Evaporation, Distillation and Sublimation; 1.6 Choosing and Performing Separation Methods; 2.1 The Atom and the Sub-Atomic Particles; 2.2 Atomic Number and Mass Number; 2.3 Electron Configuration, Shells and Valence Electrons; 2.4 Ions and How They Are Formed; 2.5 Molecules, Chemical Formulae and Bonding.

#### Sub-Strand 2: Living Cells — Paper 3

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.1.2.1** — Demonstrate an understanding of the types of cells and their structure in relation to different organisms.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.1.2.1.1* — Examine and describe the structure of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.1.2.1.2* — Classify organisms (plants or animals) as prokaryotic or eukaryotic based on the type of cells they are made of.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 3.1 The Cell, Its Parts and Their Functions; 3.2 Plant Cells and Animal Cells; 3.3 Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cells; 3.4 Classifying Organisms by Cell Type; 3.5 Micro-Organisms, Health and Safety Measures.

### STRAND 2: Cycles

#### Sub-Strand 1: Earth Science — Paper 4

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.2.1.1** — Demonstrate understanding of the process of the carbon cycle as an example of a repeated pattern of change in nature and how it relates to the environment.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.2.1.1.1* — Explain the process of the carbon cycle.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.2.1.1.2* — Describe the role of the carbon cycle to the environment.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 5.1 The Carbon Cycle as a Repeated Pattern of Change; 5.2 Photosynthesis as a Stage of the Carbon Cycle; 5.3 Respiration as a Stage of the Carbon Cycle; 5.4 Burning and Fossil Fuels; 5.5 Decay and the Work of Decomposers; 5.6 The Carbon Cycle and the Environment.

#### Sub-Strand 2: Life Cycle of Organisms — Paper 5

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.2.2.1** — Demonstrate an activity to show the life cycle of the Anopheles mosquito and show how the effects of the mosquito on humans can be managed.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.2.2.1.2* — Discuss the impact of the Anopheles mosquito on humans and how it can be controlled.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.2.2.1.1* — Describe the life cycle and economic importance of the Anopheles mosquito.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 6.1 The Anopheles Mosquito and Malaria; 6.2 The Life Cycle of the Anopheles Mosquito; 6.3 The Adult Mosquito: Parts and Feeding; 6.4 Economic Importance of the Mosquito; 6.5 Impact of the Mosquito on Humans; 6.6 Management and Control of the Mosquito.

#### Sub-Strand 3: Crop Production — Paper 6

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.2.3.1** — Demonstrate knowledge and skills in planting crops on different seed beds.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.2.3.1.1* — Explore the different seed beds for planting crops in your community.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.2.3.1.2* — Plant different types of crops on different seed beds.
- **Content standard B8/JHS2.2.3.2** — Demonstrate understanding of the differences in height, size, and flowering of crops grown in different seed beds.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.2.3.2.1* — Compare and contrast the differences in height, size, and flowering of crops grown in different seed beds.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 7.1 Types of Seed Beds; 7.2 Land Preparation and Planting Practices; 7.3 Planting Materials and Transplanting; 7.4 Comparing Crop Growth on Different Seed Beds; 7.5 Measuring, Recording and Presenting Results.

#### Sub-Strand 4: Animal Production — Paper 7

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.2.4.1** — Recognise the different types of feed for different types of animals.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.2.4.1.1* — Compare and contrast the different types of feed for different types of animals.
- **Content standard B8/JHS2.2.4.2** — Demonstrate understanding of the importance of water and animal feed to the growth of animals.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.2.4.2.1* — Explain the importance of water and animal feed to the growth of animals.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 8.1 Types of Animal Feed and the Animals that Need Them; 8.2 Nutrients in Animal Feed and their Sources; 8.3 Reading and Using Feed Labels; 8.4 Importance of Water to the Growth of Animals; 8.5 Feeding, Watering and Management of Farm Animals.

### STRAND 3: Systems

#### Sub-Strand 1: The Human Body System — Paper 8

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.3.1.1** — Demonstrate knowledge of parts of the mammalian tooth and the functions of the different types of teeth in relation to feeding in man.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.3.1.1.1* — Identify parts of a mammalian tooth.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.3.1.1.2* — Discuss the functions of the different types of teeth such as incisors, canines, premolars, and molars.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.3.1.1.3* — Explain the causes and prevention of tooth and gum decay.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 9.1 Regions of a Mammalian Tooth; 9.2 Internal Structure of a Tooth and the Functions of its Parts; 9.3 Types of Teeth and their Functions in Feeding; 9.4 Causes of Tooth Decay and Gum Disease; 9.5 Prevention of Tooth Decay and Care of the Teeth.

#### Sub-Strand 2: The Solar System — Paper 9

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.3.2.1** — Demonstrate knowledge of the outer planets of the solar system.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.3.2.1.1* — Identify the outer planets of the solar system and describe their properties.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 10.1 Composition of the Solar System; 10.2 Identifying the Outer Planets; 10.3 Properties Peculiar to Each Outer Planet; 10.4 Why There is No Life on the Outer Planets; 10.5 Modelling and Studying the Outer Solar System.

#### Sub-Strand 3: Ecosystem — Paper 10

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.3.3.1** — Demonstrate an understanding of the interdependence of organisms in an ecosystem and their interaction.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.3.3.1.1* — Explore the feeding relationships within an ecosystem.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 11.1 The Ecosystem and its Parts; 11.2 Producers, Consumers and Feeding Terms; 11.3 Food Chains and Food Webs; 11.4 Energy Transfer and the Role of the Sun; 11.5 Interdependence and the Balance of an Ecosystem.

#### Sub-Strand 4: Farming Systems — Paper 11

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.3.4.1** — Demonstrate understanding of the different crop, animal and land combinations under various farming systems.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.3.4.1.1* — Identify and describe the types of crops, animals and land combinations for the different farming systems.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.3.4.1.2* — Discuss the usefulness of the different crops and animals involved in the different farming systems.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 12.1 Types of Farming Systems; 12.2 Crop, Animal and Land Combinations; 12.3 Advantages and Disadvantages of Farming Systems; 12.4 Usefulness of the Crops and Animals; 12.5 Contribution to Sustainability and Soil Care.

### STRAND 4: Forces and Energy

#### Sub-Strand 1: Energy — Paper 12, 13

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.4.1.1** — Demonstrate the skill to evaluate the conversion of energy from one form to another.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.1.1.1* — Describe energy conversion.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.1.1.2* — Discuss the importance of conversion of energy.
- **Content standard B8/JHS2.4.1.2** — Show an understanding of the sources of renewable energy and how to manage these sources in a sustainable manner.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.1.2.1* — Describe renewable and non-renewable forms of energy.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.1.2.2* — Demonstrate how to manage sources of renewable energy sustainably.
- **Content standard B8/JHS2.4.1.3** — Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between heat and temperature.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.1.3.1* — Discuss the differences and the relationship between heat and temperature in the environment.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 13.1 Forms of Energy; 13.2 Energy Conversion in Everyday Devices; 13.3 Producing Electricity from a Dammed River; 13.4 Harnessing Natural Forms of Energy; 13.5 Importance of Energy Conversion and Energy Losses; 14.1 Renewable and Non-Renewable Sources of Energy; 14.2 Producing Energy from a Renewable Source; 14.3 Managing Renewable Energy Sources Sustainably; 14.4 Differences between Heat and Temperature; 14.5 The Relationship between Heat and Temperature.

#### Sub-Strand 2: Electricity and Electronics — Paper 14

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.4.2.1** — Demonstrate knowledge of electricity transmission.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.2.1.1* — Explain how electricity transmission occurs.
- **Content standard B8/JHS2.4.2.2** — Demonstrate understanding of the functions of capacitors in relation to LEDs, diodes and resistors in electronic circuits.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.2.2.1* — Demonstrate the charging and discharging action of a capacitor in a DC electronic circuit.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 15.1 Stages of Electricity Transmission; 15.2 Transformers and High-Voltage Transmission; 15.3 Distribution, Use and Electrical Safety; 15.4 Resistors, Diodes and LEDs in Circuits; 15.5 Charging and Discharging of a Capacitor.

#### Sub-Strand 3: Conversion and Conservation of Energy — Paper 15

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.4.3.1** — Evaluate the impact of conversion of energy and energy conservation on the environment.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.3.1.1* — Explain the importance of conversion of energy and energy conservation in daily life.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 16.1 Conservation of Energy and the Meaning of Energy Conservation; 16.2 Importance of Energy Conversion in Daily Life; 16.3 Energy Waste, Efficiency and Household Energy Use; 16.4 Impact of Energy Conversion on the Environment; 16.5 Conserving Energy at Home, in School and in the Community.

#### Sub-Strand 4: Force and Motion — Paper 16

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.4.4.1** — Demonstrate the production of magnet, domestic and industrial application of magnetic force and its relationship with Newton's Second Law of motion and in everyday life.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.4.1.1* — Demonstrate simple ways of making magnets and show how magnetic force can be applied in domestic and industrial activities.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.4.1.2* — Explain the relationship between magnetic force and Newton's Second Law of motion; and show the law's application to life.
- **Content standard B8/JHS2.4.4.2** — Demonstrate understanding of complex machines and how they work.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.4.2.1* — Identify complex machines and describe their functions in life.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 17.1 Magnets, Magnetic Materials and Simple Ways of Making Magnets; 17.2 Magnetic Force in Domestic and Industrial Activities; 17.3 Magnetic Force and Newton's Second Law of Motion; 17.4 Simple Machines Recalled; 17.5 Complex Machines and the Quality of Life.

#### Sub-Strand 5: Agricultural Tools — Paper 17

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.4.5.1** — Demonstrate knowledge and skills in the use of basic and simple agricultural tools for basic on-farm activities.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.5.1.1* — Show and discuss the use of basic and simple agricultural tools for basic on-farm activities.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.4.5.1.2* — Engage in the use of basic and simple agricultural tools for basic farm activities.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 18.1 Types and Names of Agricultural Tools; 18.2 Matching Tools with On-Farm Activities; 18.3 Correct Use of Tools on the Farm or in the School Garden; 18.4 Selecting the Appropriate Tool for a Task; 18.5 Care, Maintenance and Safe Use of Agricultural Tools.

### STRAND 5: Humans and the Environment

#### Sub-Strand 1: Waste Management — Paper 18

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.5.1.1** — Demonstrate knowledge of waste management systems and apply it in an environment.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.5.1.1.1* — Explain sustainable waste management practices.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.5.1.1.2* — Apply knowledge of waste management practices to manage waste in a community.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 19.1 Waste and the Types of Waste; 19.2 Sustainable Approaches to Waste Management; 19.3 Effects of Poor Waste Management on Health and the Environment; 19.4 Surveying and Reporting on a Community's Waste Management Practices; 19.5 Managing and Evaluating Waste Management in the School and Community.

#### Sub-Strand 2: Human Health — Paper 19, 20

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.5.2.1** — Demonstrate knowledge of common communicable diseases, such as hepatitis, of humans, causes, symptoms, effects and their prevention.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.5.2.1.1* — Explain the symptoms, effects and prevention of common communicable diseases.
- **Content standard B8/JHS2.5.2.2** — Demonstrate knowledge of the nature of selected bacterial diseases of humans, their causes, symptoms, effects and prevention.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.5.2.2.1* — Explain the nature of bacterial diseases with special emphasis on food poisoning, gonorrhoea and meningitis, their causes, symptoms, effects on humans and prevention.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 20.1 Communicable Diseases and How They Spread; 20.2 Hepatitis B: Cause, Symptoms, Effects and Prevention; 20.3 HIV and AIDS; 20.4 Measles and Other Common Communicable Diseases; 20.5 Health Data and Planning to Minimise Disease; 21.1 The Nature of Bacteria and Bacterial Diseases; 21.2 Food Poisoning; 21.3 Gonorrhoea; 21.4 Meningitis; 21.5 Managing Bacterial Diseases: the Individual, the Community and Government.

#### Sub-Strand 3: Science and Industry — Paper 21

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.5.3.1** — Demonstrate an understanding of connections among science, technology, innovation, society and the environment.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.5.3.1.1* — Examine the relationship among science, technology, innovation and society.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 22.1 Science, Technology and Innovation and How They Are Linked; 22.2 Technology at Work in Ghanaian Life; 22.3 Technological Advancement and the Ghanaian Environment; 22.4 Innovation, Responsible Use and Judging Information.

#### Sub-Strand 4: Climate Change and Green Economy — Paper 22

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.5.4.1** — Demonstrate an understanding of the effects of climate change in the world and greening of other tropical countries including Ghana.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.5.4.1.1* — Explain the concept of climate change and its effect on the environment.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.5.4.1.2* — Describe climate change and green economy actions.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 23.1 Climate Change and Its Signs; 23.2 Causes of Climate Change; 23.3 Effects of Climate Change on the Environment and on Ghana; 23.4 Adapting to Climate Change; 23.5 Mitigation and the Green Economy.

#### Sub-Strand 5: Understanding the Environment — Paper 23

- **Content standard B8/JHS2.5.5.1** — Demonstrate understanding of the differences among soils, plant roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits of plants in the different environments.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.5.5.1.1* — Discuss physical properties of soils.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.5.5.1.2* — Analyse the physical properties of soils and soil water content and demonstrate their importance in crop production.
- **Content standard B8/JHS2.5.6.1** — Recognise the different types of rocks as origin of different types of soils.
  - *Indicator B8/JHS2.5.6.1.1* — Observe and describe different types of rocks as origins of soils.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 24.1 Soil and Its Physical Properties; 24.2 Soil Types, Water Retention and the Support of Roots; 24.3 Soil Water, Osmosis and Crop Production; 24.4 Rocks and Their Visible Characteristics; 24.5 Weathering: How Rocks Become Soil.

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** A mixture is best described as

A. a single pure substance made of one kind of particle.
B. two or more substances that are combined without joining chemically.
C. a substance that can only be separated by chemical means.
D. a substance that always looks the same throughout.

**2.** Which statement about the particles of a mixture is correct?

A. The particles of a mixture keep their own properties.
B. The particles of a mixture are chemically joined together.
C. The particles of a mixture lose all their properties.
D. The particles of a mixture can only be seen under a microscope.

**3.** Which of the following is a **homogeneous** mixture?

A. Sand and water
B. Milk
C. Sugar solution
D. Seawater with floating seaweed

**4.** Which of the following is a **heterogeneous** mixture?

A. Salt solution
B. Palm wine
C. Kerosene and water
D. Fresh orange juice with pulp

**5.** A mixture in which the solute particles are too large to pass through filter paper is called

A. a solution.
B. a colloid.
C. a suspension.
D. an alloy.

**6.** Which of the following mixtures is a colloid?

A. Milk
B. Kerosene
C. Sugar solution
D. Muddy water

**7.** In a salt solution, salt is the

A. solvent and water is the solute.
B. solute and water is the solvent.
C. solute and water is also a solute.
D. solvent and water is also a solvent.

**8.** A pupil dissolves two spoons of sugar in a glass of water. The mixture formed is

A. a suspension.
B. a colloid.
C. an emulsion.
D. a solution.

**9.** The path of light from a torch is clearly visible when it is shone through milk because milk

A. is a clear solution.
B. is a suspension of large stones.
C. scatters the light.
D. absorbs all the light.

**10.** Which of the following is **NOT** a property of a suspension?

A. It is always clear and transparent.
B. Its particles settle on standing.
C. It scatters a beam of light.
D. Its particles can be separated by filtration.

**11.** Which of the following mixtures is **homogeneous**?

A. Fufu and soup
B. Salt solution
C. A mixture of rice and stones
D. Sand and water

**12.** Which of these substances will **not** dissolve in water?

A. Sugar
B. Common salt
C. Glucose
D. Chalk powder

**13.** A technique used to separate a solid that does not dissolve in a liquid from the liquid is

A. distillation.
B. decantation.
C. filtration.
D. sublimation.

**14.** In filtration, the solid collected on the filter paper is called the

A. filtrate.
B. residue.
C. solvent.
D. solution.

**15.** In filtration, the liquid that passes through the filter paper into the conical flask is called the

A. filtrate.
B. residue.
C. solute.
D. distillate.

**16.** The method that quickly separates a mixture of fine sand and water into two separate layers is

A. evaporation.
B. distillation.
C. sublimation.
D. decantation.

**17.** Which of the following mixtures can be separated by **magnetic separation**?

A. A mixture of iron filings and sulfur powder
B. A mixture of salt and sugar
C. A mixture of chalk powder and water
D. A mixture of kerosene and water

**18.** The sieving of gari to remove fine cassava flour and larger particles works mainly because the two substances

A. have different colours.
B. have different particle sizes.
C. have different melting points.
D. are both solids.

**19.** Which of the following **is not** used as a method of separating mixtures?

A. Evaporation
B. Filtration
C. Decantation
D. Fermentation

**20.** Substances that can undergo sublimation change from

A. liquid to solid directly.
B. vapour to liquid directly.
C. solid to vapour directly.
D. liquid to vapour directly.

**21.** One difference between evaporation and distillation is that during evaporation

A. water is recovered as a liquid.
B. the salt inside the water is dissolved.
C. the water escapes into the air as a vapour.
D. the mixture is heated until it boils.

**22.** In distillation, the liquid obtained after condensation is called the

A. distillate.
B. solvent.
C. residue.
D. solute.

**23.** The method most suitable for obtaining pure drinking water from seawater is

A. filtration.
B. sieving.
C. sedimentation.
D. distillation.

**24.** A mixture of two liquids that do not mix is called

A. a solution.
B. an immiscible mixture.
C. a homogeneous mixture.
D. a colloidal mixture.

**25.** Separating cream from milk at the factory uses

A. a centrifuge.
B. a sieve.
C. filter paper.
D. sublimation.

**26.** The conversion of a liquid into vapour by heating, followed by cooling the vapour back into a liquid, is called

A. melting.
B. evaporation.
C. condensation.
D. distillation.

**27.** Which of the following statements about a mixture is **true**?

A. A mixture has a fixed boiling point.
B. A mixture can be separated by physical means.
C. The parts of a mixture are joined in fixed ratios.
D. A mixture is always a solid.

**28.** A student is given a beaker containing salt solution and asked to obtain dry, pure salt. Which combination of methods should the student use?

A. Filtration followed by decantation
B. Evaporation followed by filtration
C. Evaporation, then drying the residue
D. Distillation followed by sedimentation

**29.** A beam of light is shone through four mixtures: muddy water, milk, kerosene and palm oil. In how many of them will the path of the light be clearly seen?

A. One
B. Two
C. Three
D. Four

**30.** Equal volumes of sand, salt, iron filings and water are mixed together. Which of the following correctly shows the first two steps needed to obtain dry sand, dry salt and the iron filings separately?

A. Magnetic separation, then filtration
B. Evaporation, then filtration
C. Filtration, then sieving
D. Sieving, then distillation

**31.** A pupil adds sugar to a glass of water. After stirring for a long time, some sugar remains undissolved at the bottom of the glass. The best way to dissolve the remaining sugar is to

A. add more sugar.
B. pour the mixture into another glass.
C. warm the mixture and stir it.
D. filter the mixture.

**32.** Amoako wants to obtain clean water from muddy water at home. He performs the following steps: (i) he allows the water to stand, (ii) he pours the clear water on top into another container, (iii) he pours the water through a clean white cloth. Which method has Amoako used in step (ii)?

A. Filtration
B. Distillation
C. Evaporation
D. Decantation

**33.** Osman dissolves a spoon of salt in a cup of water and a spoon of sugar in another cup of water. Both solids dissolve, but the sugar solution tastes sweet while the salt solution tastes salty. This shows that

A. the solids have dissolved completely and disappeared.
B. the solids are still present and have kept their own properties.
C. the water has changed the nature of the solids.
D. the two mixtures are now pure substances.

**34.** Akosua and Yaw were given a clear liquid. Akosua said it was pure water; Yaw said it was a salt solution. Which of the following is the best test to settle the argument?

A. Filtering the liquid
B. Shining a torch through the liquid
C. Smelling the liquid
D. Boiling the liquid to dryness

**35.** Which of the following pairs of apparatus are used together during filtration?

A. Filter paper and funnel
B. Evaporating dish and tripod
C. Liebig condenser and round-bottom flask
D. Magnet and sieve

**36.** Filtration can be used to separate

A. salt from a salt solution.
B. ethanol from water.
C. chalk powder from a chalk–water mixture.
D. iron filings from sulfur powder.

**37.** Which of the following mixtures is a suspension?

A. A mixture of petrol and water shaken together
B. A mixture of salt and water
C. A mixture of vinegar and water
D. A mixture of milk and water

**38.** A cook adds oil to boiling water in a pot. After the pot is left to stand, the oil floats on top of the water. This is because the oil

A. dissolves in the water.
B. is less dense than water.
C. is denser than water.
D. changes into a solid.

**39.** The difference between a solution and a colloid is that

A. the particles of a solution are larger than those of a colloid.
B. a colloid settles on standing, while a solution does not.
C. the particles of a colloid are large enough to scatter light, while those of a solution are not.
D. a solution can be filtered, while a colloid cannot.

**40.** Which sequence of processes correctly describes the changes of state during distillation?

A. Liquid → solid → liquid
B. Liquid → vapour → solid
C. Solid → liquid → vapour
D. Liquid → vapour → liquid

## SECTION B: THEORY (60 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Write your answers in your answer booklet. The marks for each question are shown in brackets.*

### Question 1  [12 marks]

Pupils of a Basic 8 class were asked to study the different kinds of mixtures found in their homes and in the school.

**(a)** Define a mixture.  **[2 marks]**

**(b)** State **two** differences between a mixture and a compound.  **[2 marks]**

**(c)** Classify each of the following mixtures as **homogeneous** or **heterogeneous**:
(i) air
(ii) sand and water
(iii) salt solution
(iv) a bowl of groundnut and rice mixture  **[4 marks]**

**(d)** For each of the mixtures in (c), state **one** method that can be used to separate it.  **[4 marks]**

---

### Question 2  [14 marks]

Mixtures can be grouped as solutions, colloids and suspensions, and the three groups behave differently.

**(a)** Copy and complete the table below on solutions, colloids and suspensions. Write only the letters (i) to (vi) and your answers.

| Property | Solution | Colloid | Suspension |
|---|---|---|---|
| Particle size | Very small (about 1 nm) | (i) ………………… | Large (more than 1000 nm) |
| Settling on standing | (ii) ………………… | (iii) ………………… | (iv) ………………… |
| Ability to scatter a beam of light | (v) ………………… | (vi) ………………… | Scatters light |
  **[6 marks]**

**(b)** Give the particle size range of particles in a solution.  **[1 mark]**

**(c)** Give **two** examples each of:
(i) a solution
(ii) a colloid
(iii) a suspension  **[3 marks]**

**(d)** The table below shows the mass of sugar that dissolves completely in 100 cm³ of water at different temperatures.

| Temperature of water (°C) | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mass of sugar that dissolved in 100 cm³ of water (g) | 20 | 24 | 29 | 36 |

(i) What mass of sugar dissolves in 100 cm³ of water at 60 °C? **[1 mark]**
(ii) Describe how the mass of sugar that dissolves changes as the temperature of the water rises. **[1 mark]**
(iii) At 80 °C, a pupil added 40 g of sugar to 100 cm³ of water. State, with a reason, whether all the sugar will dissolve. **[2 marks]**

---

### Question 3  [10 marks]

Fig. 1 shows a beam of light from a torch being shone through **three different mixtures** A, B and C.

![Fig. 1: A beam of light from a torch passing through a salt solution (A), milk (B) and muddy water (C).](/home/user/figures/pencil_fig1_mixtures.png)

*Fig. 1: A beam of light from a torch passing through a salt solution (A), milk (B) and muddy water (C).*

**(a)** State what will be observed about the beam of light in each of A, B and C.  **[3 marks]**

**(b)** Explain the observation made in **B**.  **[2 marks]**

**(c)** Classify **each** of A, B and C as a solution, a colloid or a suspension.  **[3 marks]**

**(d)** Give the general name of the effect that is observed when a beam of light is scattered by the particles of a mixture.  **[1 mark]**

**(e)** State **one** example, other than milk, of a mixture that shows this effect.  **[1 mark]**

### Question 4  [12 marks]

Fig. 2 shows an apparatus set up to separate a mixture of **ethanol and water**.

![Fig. 2: Apparatus for separating a mixture of ethanol and water by distillation.](/home/user/figures/pencil_fig2_distillation.png)

*Fig. 2: Apparatus for separating a mixture of ethanol and water by distillation.*

**(a)** Name the parts labelled **I, II, III** and **IV**.  **[4 marks]**

**(b)** State the function of each of the parts labelled **I** and **III**.  **[2 marks]**

**(c)** Name the process by which the liquid in **II** changes into a vapour on heating.  **[1 mark]**

**(d)** Which of the two liquids, ethanol or water, will be collected first in **IV**? Give a reason for your answer.  **[2 marks]**

**(e)** Give **one** reason why water is passed through the part labelled **III**.  **[1 mark]**

**(f)** State **one** difference between the mixture in the apparatus and the liquid collected in **IV**.  **[1 mark]**

**(g)** Why is it **not** correct to use this apparatus to obtain salt from a salt solution?  **[1 mark]**

### Question 5  [12 marks]

A class was asked to choose the most suitable method for separating different mixtures found in the home and in the community.

**(a)** For **each** of the following mixtures, state the **most suitable** method of separation. You may choose from the list below.

*List: Filtration · Evaporation · Magnetic separation · Sieving · Decantation · Distillation*

(i) A mixture of iron filings and sand
(ii) A mixture of ground pepper and groundnut soup
(iii) A mixture of salt and water
(iv) A mixture of salt, sand and water  **[4 marks]**

**(b)** Choose **two** of the mixtures in (a) and explain why the method you chose is suitable for each of them.  **[4 marks]**

**(c)** You are given a mixture of salt, sand and water in a beaker. Describe, step by step, how you would obtain dry salt and dry sand from the mixture.  **[2 marks]**

**(d)** A juice seller at Kaneshie market wants to show customers that a bottled drink is a true solution and not a suspension. Describe a simple test she can perform.  **[2 marks]**

**1.** The smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction is called

A. a molecule.
B. a compound.
C. an atom.
D. an electron.

D. cholera

A. telescope.

D. Chloroplast

A. dry.

A. a cell wall while an animal cell has no cell wall.

C. water
D. nucleus

A. prokaryotic organisms.
B. non-living things.

D. eukaryotic organisms.

A. Bacteria have no cytoplasm.
B. Bacteria are always harmful to humans.

D. Bacteria are multicellular organisms.

**27.** Blue-green algae are grouped as prokaryotic organisms because they

A. have no enclosed nucleus.
B. are blue in colour.
C. live only in water.
D. are very small.

**28.** The process by which green plants make their own food, using light energy trapped by chlorophyll, is called

A. photosynthesis.
B. respiration.
C. digestion.
D. excretion.

**29.** Which of the following is a raw material that green plants use during photosynthesis?

A. oxygen
B. carbon dioxide
C. protein
D. food from the soil

A. a human cheek.
B. a bacterium.
C. a goat's liver.
D. a mango leaf.

A. mitochondria
B. cell membrane
C. cytoplasm
D. cell wall

A. have no cell membrane.
B. are made up of only one cell.

**33.** A cell that has a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane, and membrane-bound organelles, is described as

A. eukaryotic.
B. prokaryotic.
C. bacterial.
D. a virus.

**34.** Which of the following is an example of a prokaryotic organism?

A. Plasmodium
B. yeast
C. Escherichia coli
D. Mucor

A. malaria
B. measles
C. guinea worm disease
D. cholera

A. Boiling the water before drinking it.
B. Adding sugar to the water.
C. Pouring the water from a height.
D. Keeping the water in an open bucket.

**37.** Which statement best explains why a bacterium is classified as a prokaryotic organism?

A. It is too small to be seen with the naked eye.
B. It is made up of only one cell.
C. It has a cell membrane.
D. Its genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus.

**38.** Which of the following pairs of organisms is made up of cells that have a **cell wall**, a **nucleus** and **cytoplasm**?

**38.** Which of the following best explains why a food web gives a better picture of feeding relationships than a single food chain?

B. copy a food chain from another country's textbook

D. collect all the organisms and keep them in one jar

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** A farming system is best described as

A. the type of soil found on a piece of farmland
B. the number of workers employed on a farm
C. the way a farmer combines crops, animals and land in the production of food
D. the market where a farmer sells the farm produce

**2.** The growing of only one kind of crop on the same piece of land season after season is called

A. crop rotation
B. mixed farming
C. mixed cropping
D. mono-cropping

**3.** Growing two or more different crops together on the same piece of land at the same time is known as

A. shifting cultivation
B. mono-cropping
C. mixed cropping
D. crop rotation

**4.** The keeping of crops and animals together on the same farm is called

A. mono-cropping
B. mixed cropping
C. mixed farming
D. pastoral farming

**5.** Growing different crops one after the other on the same piece of land in a planned order is called

A. sole cropping
B. mixed cropping
C. shifting cultivation
D. crop rotation

**6.** A farmer who clears a piece of forest, crops it for three years and then moves to a new piece of land is practising

A. irrigation farming
B. crop rotation
C. shifting cultivation
D. mixed farming

**7.** In bush fallowing, the farmer

A. moves his house to a new village every few years
B. burns the land after every harvest and plants at once
C. plants the same crop on the land every year
D. leaves the land to rest under bush for some years before cropping it again

**8.** A farming system in which farmers move with their herds from place to place in search of pasture and water is called

A. nomadic pastoralism
B. plantation farming
C. arable farming
D. mixed farming

**9.** A farmer who produces mainly to feed his own family, with little left to sell, is practising

A. nomadic farming
B. plantation farming
C. subsistence farming
D. commercial farming

**10.** The main aim of commercial farming is to

A. leave the land to rest for several years
B. produce on a large scale for sale and for profit
C. keep a few animals as pets around the house
D. produce only enough food for the farmer's household

**11.** Which of the following is an example of arable farming?

A. Catching fish from a river
B. Rearing cattle on open grassland
C. Cutting timber from a forest
D. Growing maize and cassava on cleared land

**12.** The growing of a single tree crop such as oil palm or rubber on a large estate is called

A. bush fallowing
B. plantation farming
C. subsistence farming
D. mixed cropping

**13.** A farming system in which trees and food crops are grown together on the same land is known as

A. agro-forestry
B. nomadic pastoralism
C. crop rotation
D. mono-cropping

**14.** Which of the following crops is best described as a legume in a crop-rotation plan?

A. Cassava
B. Groundnut
C. Tomato
D. Maize

**15.** Legumes such as cowpea and groundnut are useful in crop rotation because they

A. kill all the micro-organisms in the soil
B. prevent rainfall from reaching the soil
C. take all the nitrogen out of the soil
D. add nitrogen to the soil through the nodules on their roots

**16.** One advantage of mixed cropping is that

A. pests spread faster from one plant to another
B. the farmer can use large machines easily on the farm
C. the farmer harvests more than one kind of produce from the same piece of land
D. the crops are all harvested on exactly the same day

**17.** A disadvantage of mono-cropping is that

A. it always gives the farmer a very small harvest in the first year
B. it cannot be practised on a large farm
C. it exhausts particular soil nutrients and encourages the build-up of pests
D. it makes the use of machinery impossible

**18.** In mixed farming, the animals help the crops mainly by

A. providing shade for the young seedlings
B. providing manure that improves the fertility of the soil
C. eating the growing crops in the field
D. chasing away all the farm workers

**19.** In mixed farming, the crops help the animals mainly by

A. providing water for the animals to drink
B. providing feed such as grain, stalks and husks
C. providing manure for the animals to eat
D. protecting the animals from diseases

**20.** Which of the following is a disadvantage of shifting cultivation today?

A. It requires expensive machinery
B. It makes the soil too rich for crops to grow
C. It needs a large area of land, which is no longer available in many communities
D. It can only be used for rearing cattle

**21.** Leaving a piece of farmland fallow for some years helps mainly to

A. allow the soil to recover its fertility naturally
B. increase the number of weeds the farmer must buy
C. make the land unsuitable for farming for ever
D. kill all the earthworms in the soil

**22.** An advantage of commercial poultry farming over keeping a few fowls at home is that

A. the birds never suffer from any disease
B. a much larger quantity of eggs and meat is produced for the market
C. no feed or medicine is needed at all
D. it requires no capital to begin

**23.** Which farming system is most likely to be practised in the dry northern grasslands of Ghana?

A. Oil palm estate farming
B. Large-scale rubber plantation farming
C. Cocoa farming under forest shade
D. Rearing of cattle, sheep and goats on open pasture

**24.** Which of the following pairs is a crop and an animal commonly combined on the same holding in Ghana?

A. Maize and poultry
B. Wheat and reindeer
C. Rubber and camel
D. Cocoa and tilapia

**25.** A farmer who grows cocoa on his land and also keeps bees among the trees benefits because the bees

A. eat the insect pests on the cocoa pods
B. loosen the soil around the roots of the trees
C. pollinate the flowers and also give him honey to sell
D. provide manure for the cocoa trees

**26.** The main reason why a farmer rotates his crops instead of planting maize every year is to

A. keep the soil fertile and reduce pests and diseases
B. make sure the farm looks beautiful
C. make the land easier to sell
D. avoid the need to weed the farm at all

**27.** Which of the following best explains sustainability in a farming system?

A. Keeping only animals and no crops at all
B. Farming in a way that keeps the land productive for future generations
C. Harvesting the largest possible crop in one season whatever the cost
D. Using the land until it is completely worn out and then abandoning it

**28.** Continuous cropping of the same land without adding manure or fertiliser leads to

A. a fall in soil fertility and lower yields
B. a steady increase in yield every year
C. complete control of all weeds
D. an increase in the depth of the topsoil

**29.** Which of the following practices is LEAST likely to protect the soil in a farming system?

A. Planting cover crops between the rows
B. Applying compost and animal manure
C. Leaving part of the land to fallow
D. Burning the bush on sloping land before every planting season

**30.** A mixed farmer sells eggs and tomatoes every week while waiting for his maize to mature. This shows that mixed farming

A. gives the farmer a steady income throughout the year
B. makes the maize ripen more quickly
C. stops pests from attacking the farm
D. removes the need for the farmer to work

**31.** One disadvantage of mixed farming is that

A. it requires more skill, labour and capital than keeping crops alone
B. manure from the animals cannot be used on the land
C. the farmer can obtain only one product from the farm
D. the soil loses all its nutrients within one season

**32.** In the taungya system practised in Ghana, farmers

A. grow only vegetables under irrigation
B. keep cattle inside the forest reserve all year
C. cut down forest trees and sell them as timber
D. grow food crops among young forest trees and care for the trees as they grow

**33.** Which of the following is an advantage of keeping animals in a zero-grazing (housed) system rather than letting them roam?

A. They grow without being given any water
B. Their droppings can be collected easily and used as manure
C. They need no feed from the farmer
D. They can never fall sick in the house

**34.** Irrigation is most useful to a farming system because it

A. prevents animals from entering the farm
B. allows crops to be grown during the dry season
C. makes the soil permanently fertile
D. removes all the weeds from the farm

**35.** Which of the following is a social benefit of farming systems to a Ghanaian community?

A. They provide employment and income for many families
B. They reduce the amount of food available in the markets
C. They stop children from going to school
D. They make the land unsuitable for building

**36.** A farmer in Techiman plants maize in the first year, groundnut in the second and cassava in the third on the same land. The main benefit of planting the groundnut is that it

A. shades the land so that no weeds grow for ever
B. removes all the pests from the soil
C. restores nitrogen to the soil for the crops that follow
D. makes the land ready for building

**37.** A farmer keeps 12 cattle and grows 2 hectares of maize, feeding the stalks to the cattle and spreading the manure on the field. The best description of this arrangement is that the two components are

A. in competition for the same food
B. harmful to each other
C. independent of each other
D. interdependent, each supplying a need of the other

**38.** Two farmers have the same size of land. Kofi grows only cassava while Yaa grows cassava with cowpea between the rows. Yaa is likely to harvest more in the long run because

A. the cowpea enriches the soil and gives her a second harvest from the same land
B. cassava grows faster when it is crowded
C. cowpea kills all the soil organisms
D. two crops always need less water than one

**39.** Which of the following would be the MOST suitable way for a village to keep its farmland productive?

A. Clearing the river banks for more farms
B. Cropping every piece of land every year without rest
C. Burning the grass on all the land each dry season
D. Practising crop rotation and adding compost and animal manure

**40.** A development officer advises a community to add a few goats and a vegetable plot to their maize farms. The strongest reason for this advice is that it would

A. make the maize grow twice as tall
B. spread the farmers' risk and make better use of the land and farm wastes
C. do away with the need for weeding
D. guarantee that no animal ever falls sick

A. turbine

**1.** A renewable source of energy is one that

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** The law of conservation of energy states that energy

A. can be stored only in fuels and in food
B. can be created whenever a machine is switched on
C. can neither be created nor destroyed, but only changed from one form to another
D. is destroyed each time it is used by a machine

**2.** Energy conservation, as used in daily life, means

A. using energy carefully so that none of it is wasted
B. creating new energy for the home
C. using as much energy as possible every day
D. changing energy from one form into another

**3.** Which of the following is an example of energy conversion?

A. Switching off a lamp that is not in use
B. Buying a cheaper electricity meter
C. Closing the windows of a room
D. A gas stove burning to cook rice

**4.** Which of the following is an example of energy conservation?

A. Plugging a kettle into the socket to boil water
B. Switching off the fan when leaving the classroom
C. Burning charcoal in a coal pot
D. Using a dynamo to light a bicycle lamp

**5.** In every energy conversion, the total energy after the change is

A. equal to the total energy before the change
B. less than the total energy before the change
C. greater than the total energy before the change
D. equal to zero

**6.** The useful energy given out by an electric fan is

A. sound energy from the blades
B. chemical energy in the wires
C. heat energy in the motor
D. kinetic energy of the moving air

**7.** A machine is said to be efficient when it

A. converts a large part of the energy supplied into the useful form
B. works without being supplied with any energy
C. produces a great deal of heat and sound
D. uses a very large amount of energy each time

**8.** A lamp is supplied with 100 J of energy and gives out 20 J as light. The energy wasted is

A. 120 J
B. 20 J
C. 100 J
D. 80 J

**9.** Which of the following household appliances usually uses the MOST electricity in a month?

A. A radio used for one hour a day
B. An air conditioner used every night
C. A torch with two dry cells
D. A mobile-phone charger

**10.** Replacing filament bulbs with LED bulbs in a school helps mainly because LED bulbs

A. give out far more heat than filament bulbs
B. make the classroom cooler by producing cold
C. give the same light while using much less electricity
D. need no electricity at all to work

**11.** Drying clothes in the sun instead of using an electric dryer is an example of

A. converting heat energy into chemical energy
B. wasting energy that could be stored
C. conserving energy by using a free natural source
D. creating new energy for the home

**12.** Which of the following habits wastes electricity in a home?

A. Covering a pot while cooking
B. Switching off the lights before travelling
C. Using daylight for reading in the afternoon
D. Leaving the television on when nobody is watching

**13.** Covering a cooking pot with a lid saves energy because it

A. keeps the heat in the pot, so the food cooks faster
B. adds extra heat energy to the food
C. prevents the pot from becoming hot at all
D. changes the heat energy into light energy

**14.** A refrigerator should not be opened too often mainly because

A. opening it adds heat energy to the electricity supply
B. warm air enters and the refrigerator uses more electricity to cool again
C. the food inside changes into energy
D. the cold inside escapes and is destroyed

**15.** Which of the following is the BEST reason for a school to conserve energy?

A. It reduces the school's bills and protects the environment
B. It makes the classrooms darker and quieter
C. It stops the school from needing any electricity
D. It increases the amount of fuel burnt at the power station

**16.** Burning fossil fuels to generate electricity harms the environment mainly because it

A. produces large amounts of clean water
B. releases carbon dioxide and other harmful gases into the air
C. makes the rivers flow faster than normal
D. removes all the oxygen from the soil

**17.** The gas produced in the greatest amount when petrol or charcoal is burnt is

A. oxygen
B. hydrogen
C. carbon dioxide
D. nitrogen

**18.** A build-up of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere leads mainly to

A. the complete loss of the atmosphere
B. an increase in the oxygen of the air

D. a fall in the temperature of the Earth

**19.** Cutting many trees to make charcoal for cooking leads to

A. deforestation, soil erosion and loss of habitats
B. more oxygen being produced by the land
C. cooler rivers and more rainfall every year
D. an increase in the number of forests

**20.** Which of the following energy sources causes the LEAST air pollution?

B. Coal

D. Charcoal

**21.** Smoke from a wood fire inside a kitchen is harmful mainly because it

A. cools the food that is being prepared
B. causes coughing and chest diseases in the people who breathe it

D. prevents the fire from burning properly

**22.** Which of the following shows energy being wasted?

A. A fan switched on in a room full of pupils
B. A lamp lit in a dark classroom at night
C. A solar panel charging a battery during the day
D. An electric iron left switched on with nobody using it

**23.** A family changes from a petrol generating set to a solar home system. The main benefit to the environment is that

A. the family can use more electricity than before
B. the solar panel produces energy without any conversion
C. the home becomes cooler during the day
D. no fuel is burnt, so no smoke or harmful gases are produced

**24.** Which of the following is the best example of using energy efficiently in a school kitchen?

A. Cooking for the whole school at one time in covered pots
B. Cooking small quantities many times a day
C. Leaving the gas burner on between meals
D. Boiling a full pot of water for one cup of tea

**25.** A pupil says, “Energy saved today is energy available tomorrow.” This statement supports the idea that

A. energy can be created by saving it
B. energy conservation makes resources last longer for future use
C. energy stops being used when it is saved
D. saving energy destroys part of the energy

**26.** Which of the following is NOT a way of conserving energy?

A. Servicing appliances so that they work efficiently
B. Leaving the security lights on throughout the day
C. Using natural daylight in the classroom
D. Switching off the computer when it is not in use

**27.** The main reason why a country encourages the use of energy-saving bulbs is to

A. increase the heat produced in homes
B. make people use more electricity at night
C. make electricity more expensive for everybody
D. reduce the total demand for electricity and the fuel burnt to produce it

**28.** The energy used to run a refrigerator is finally given out to the surroundings mainly as

A. heat
B. sound
C. chemical energy
D. light

A. GH¢450.00

D. GH¢45.00

**30.** In a hydroelectric station, the energy that does not become electricity is lost mainly as

A. chemical energy stored in the water
B. nuclear energy in the dam wall
C. heat and sound in the turbines and generators
D. light from the surface of the lake

**31.** Which of the following best explains why no machine can be 100% efficient?

A. Machines create new energy as they work
B. Some of the energy supplied is always changed into forms that are not useful, such as heat
C. The energy supplied disappears into the air
D. Some of the energy supplied is destroyed inside the machine

**32.** A school fits solar panels and also teaches pupils to switch off fans. This programme shows

A. the conversion of energy only

**33.** Two families use the same number of appliances, but one pays a much smaller electricity bill. The MOST likely reason is that the family

A. make the streets brighter than daylight

**35.** The energy from the Sun that falls on a school roof is best described as

A. a free and renewable supply that can be converted into electricity

D. a form of chemical energy stored in the roof

**36.** A poster on energy conservation in a school should contain mainly

A. advertisements for expensive appliances

**37.** Before using information from the internet for a project on energy, a pupil should FIRST

A. print every page that mentions energy

**38.** A community uses firewood for cooking. Which measure would BOTH save energy and protect the environment?

**39.** A factory manager claims that his machine produces more energy than it uses. A pupil should conclude that the claim is

A. true, because the machine is very modern

**40.** Which of the following actions would reduce a school's energy use the MOST over a whole term?

C. it is done once and never repeated

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** A communicable disease is a disease that

A. can be passed from one person to another
B. cannot be treated by any drug
C. is caused by a shortage of food nutrients
D. is inherited from one's parents only

**2.** Which of the following is a communicable disease?

A. Measles
B. Night blindness
C. Diabetes
D. Sickle-cell disease

**3.** Which of the following is NOT a communicable disease?

A. Hepatitis B
B. Tuberculosis
C. Hypertension (high blood pressure)
D. Cholera

**4.** Communicable diseases are caused by

A. the hardening of the walls of the arteries
B. a shortage of vitamins in the diet
C. the inheritance of faulty genes
D. germs such as viruses, bacteria, fungi and protozoa

**5.** Cholera and typhoid fever are spread mainly through

A. food and water contaminated with human faeces
B. the bite of a tsetse fly
C. the sharing of school desks
D. breathing the air in a cold room

**6.** Measles and tuberculosis are spread mainly through

A. drinking water from a covered pot
B. walking barefoot on wet grass
C. eating food that has been well cooked
D. droplets released when an infected person coughs or sneezes

**7.** Malaria is spread from one person to another by

A. sharing a cup with a patient
B. breathing the same air as a patient
C. the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito
D. shaking hands with a patient

**8.** Hepatitis B is caused by

A. a worm
B. a virus
C. a bacterium
D. a fungus

**9.** The organ of the body chiefly attacked by the hepatitis B virus is the

A. heart
B. liver
C. kidneys
D. lungs

**10.** Which of the following is a common symptom of hepatitis B?

A. Bowing of the legs
B. Loss of hearing
C. Yellowing of the eyes and the skin
D. Swelling of the gums only

**11.** The yellowing of the eyes and the skin seen in a hepatitis patient is known as

A. dehydration
B. jaundice
C. inflammation of the throat
D. anaemia

**12.** Apart from the yellowing of the eyes, another symptom of hepatitis B is

A. dark urine with tiredness and loss of appetite
B. a sudden increase in body weight
C. an itching rash on the palms only
D. the growth of extra teeth

**13.** Hepatitis B is commonly spread through

A. eating fruits that have not been washed
B. sitting beside an infected person in class
C. contact with the blood or body fluids of an infected person
D. breathing the air in a crowded market

**14.** Which of the following practices can spread hepatitis B?

A. Playing football with an infected friend
B. Sharing razor blades, needles and toothbrushes
C. Eating from a clean bowl with a friend
D. Sharing a textbook in class

**15.** A mother infected with the hepatitis B virus can pass it on to her baby

A. during pregnancy or at birth
B. by talking to the baby every day
C. by carrying the baby on her back
D. only when the child is ten years old

**16.** A serious long-term effect of hepatitis B on a patient is

A. damage to the liver, which may lead to liver cancer
B. the breaking of the bones of the legs
C. the complete loss of all the teeth
D. permanent loss of the sense of smell

**17.** The most effective way of protecting a child against hepatitis B is

A. drinking plenty of palm wine
B. eating only roasted foods
C. bathing twice every day
D. immunisation with the hepatitis B vaccine

**18.** A barber can prevent the spread of hepatitis B in his shop by

A. washing the floor of the shop once a week
B. sterilising the clippers and using a new blade for each customer
C. charging a higher price for a haircut
D. giving each customer a cold drink

**19.** Blood collected for transfusion is screened before it is used in order to

A. increase the amount of blood collected
B. make the blood thicker
C. change the blood group of the donor
D. make sure that it does not carry hepatitis B, HIV and other germs

**20.** The letters HIV stand for

A. harmful internal virus
B. human immunodeficiency virus
C. human infectious viral anaemia
D. high internal viral fever

**21.** AIDS is best described as

A. a disease that is inherited from the parents
B. the condition that develops when HIV has weakened the body's defence system
C. a disease of the bones caused by poor diet
D. an allergy to certain kinds of food

**22.** HIV weakens the body because it attacks the

A. enamel of the teeth
B. bones, which support the body
C. white blood cells, which defend the body against disease
D. red blood cells, which carry oxygen

**23.** Which of the following can spread HIV?

A. Being bitten by a housefly
B. Sharing a seat with an infected person
C. Transfusion with unscreened infected blood
D. Eating food prepared by an infected person

**24.** HIV is NOT spread by

A. an infected mother breastfeeding her baby
B. unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected person
C. sharing needles and other skin-piercing instruments
D. hugging or shaking hands with an infected person

**25.** A person living with HIV should be

A. blamed for the illness in public
B. sent away from the community
C. kept away from all school activities
D. treated with care and respect, and supported to take the prescribed medicines

**26.** Measles is caused by

A. a virus
B. a bacterium
C. a protozoan
D. a mineral deficiency

**27.** A common sign of measles in a child is

A. a deep cut on the skin
B. a sudden loss of all the hair
C. the swelling of one leg only
D. fever with a rash over the body and red watery eyes

**28.** A serious effect of measles in young children is that it can lead to

A. the growth of stronger bones
B. an increase in height
C. blindness, pneumonia and even death
D. a permanent change of eye colour

**29.** Measles can best be prevented by

A. immunising children with the measles vaccine
B. giving children a daily dose of salt
C. keeping children indoors all day
D. feeding children on only one kind of food

**30.** A child suffering from measles should be kept away from other children in order to

A. make the child recover more slowly
B. punish the child for falling sick
C. allow the rash to grow larger
D. prevent the disease from spreading to them

**31.** A patient with cholera loses a lot of water from the body through severe diarrhoea and vomiting. The first aid given is to

A. give oral rehydration salt solution and send the patient to hospital at once
B. ask the patient to sleep until the next day
C. give the patient a bottle of soft drink and wait
D. give the patient a cold bath only

**32.** Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium and mainly attacks the

A. liver
B. skin
C. lungs
D. kidneys

**33.** Which of the following best prevents the spread of communicable diseases in a school?

A. Sharing drinking cups in the classroom
B. Washing the hands with soap under running water at the right times
C. Sweeping the classroom once a term
D. Keeping all the windows closed during lessons

**34.** Immunisation protects a person from a disease because it

A. replaces the blood of the person with new blood
B. makes the person too strong to fall sick at all
C. causes the body to produce antibodies against the germ before the person meets it
D. kills every germ that enters the body for life

**35.** In a community where many people fall sick with typhoid fever, the most likely source of the infection is

A. the sharing of school books
B. the noise from a nearby factory
C. a contaminated well or water supply
D. the hot weather in the afternoon

**36.** Pupils compiling data on communicable diseases from a health centre should obtain the figures

A. from the records of the centre, with the permission of the staff in charge
B. by copying the figures from another district
C. by guessing from the number of people they see outside
D. by asking patients to show their prescriptions to the class

**37.** When pupils report the data they have collected on patients, they must

A. change the figures so that the report looks better
B. publish the names of all the patients on the notice board
C. tell their friends which families are affected
D. keep the names of the patients confidential

**38.** In one year a health centre recorded 40 hepatitis B cases out of 100 cases of communicable diseases. The percentage of the cases that were hepatitis B is

A. 4%
B. 40%
C. 140%
D. 60%

**39.** A record showing that more males than females suffer from hepatitis B in a community is most useful because it

A. means that the males should be sent out of the community
B. shows that the disease is not serious at all
C. proves that females can never catch the disease
D. helps the health workers to direct their education and screening to the group at greater risk

**40.** The best plan for a school that wants to reduce hepatitis B among its pupils is to

A. stop all sporting activities in the school
B. organise health education, encourage vaccination and stop the sharing of blades and needles
C. serve all meals in the classroom instead of the canteen
D. ask every sick pupil to stay at home for the whole year

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

**1.** Bacteria are best described as

A. tiny grains of sand found in dirty water
B. very small living things, each made of a single cell
C. poisonous chemicals released by rotting food
D. the smallest animals with a backbone

**2.** Bacteria can be seen only with the aid of a

A. pair of spectacles
B. hand lens held close to the eye
C. telescope
D. microscope

**3.** Which of the following diseases is caused by bacteria?

A. Measles
B. Hepatitis B
C. Ringworm
D. Meningitis

**4.** Which of the following diseases is NOT caused by bacteria?

A. Gonorrhoea
B. Cholera
C. HIV and AIDS
D. Tuberculosis

**5.** A disease caused by bacteria is usually treated with

A. antibiotics prescribed by a health worker
B. a drug used against malaria parasites
C. vitamin tablets alone
D. any painkiller bought from a hawker

**6.** Not all bacteria are harmful. Some bacteria are useful because they

A. make the soil hard so that it holds water
B. change a virus into a vitamin
C. destroy all the nutrients in food before it is eaten
D. help to decay dead matter and are used in making foods such as yoghurt

**7.** Bacteria multiply fastest when they are in a place that is

A. boiled and then covered
B. exposed to strong sunlight all day
C. cold, dry and salty
D. warm, moist and has food

**8.** The best reason why a wound should be washed and covered is that

A. the skin will grow a new layer of hair
B. bacteria from dirt can enter the body through the broken skin
C. the blood will change from red to white
D. the bone under the wound will become weak

**9.** Food poisoning is an illness that a person gets after eating food that

A. contains harmful bacteria or the poison they produce
B. contains a large amount of vitamin C
C. has been cooked with too much salt
D. has been eaten while it is still hot

**10.** Which of the following bacteria is a common cause of food poisoning?

A. Amoeba
B. Plasmodium
C. Salmonella
D. Anopheles

**11.** A common symptom of food poisoning is

A. the loss of hearing in one ear
B. a yellow colour in the whites of the eyes
C. vomiting, stomach pains and diarrhoea a few hours after eating
D. a stiff neck with a dislike of bright light

**12.** The greatest danger to a child who is vomiting and passing watery stools after food poisoning is

A. dehydration, the loss of too much water and salts from the body
B. the loss of the sense of smell
C. the sudden growth of extra teeth
D. a permanent change in the colour of the skin

**13.** The first help that should be given at home to a person suffering from food poisoning is to

A. give oral rehydration salts solution and send the person to a health facility
B. give the person more of the same food to eat
C. ask the person to sleep until the pain goes away
D. give the person a strong antibiotic kept in the house

**14.** Cooked rice that is left uncovered on a table from morning till evening is unsafe to eat because

A. the rice loses all its colour
B. the rice becomes too hard for the teeth
C. bacteria have had warmth, moisture and time to multiply in it
D. the starch in the rice changes into a vitamin

**15.** Which practice by a food vendor is MOST likely to cause food poisoning?

A. Handling money and then serving food without washing the hands
B. Covering the food with a clean net
C. Keeping the food hot over a fire
D. Serving the food with a clean ladle

**16.** Which of the following is the BEST way to prevent food poisoning in a school canteen?

A. Wash the plates in a bucket of water used all week
B. Keep the left-over stew in the open until the next day
C. Cook food thoroughly, keep it covered and serve it while it is still hot
D. Prepare all the food a day before it is needed

**17.** Before a food vendor is allowed to sell food in a market, the Environmental Health Unit of the assembly requires the vendor to

A. undergo a medical examination and obtain a health certificate
B. pay a fine to the chief of the town
C. buy all the food items from one shop
D. prepare the food inside the market office

**18.** Gonorrhoea is a disease that is spread mainly through

A. eating food prepared by an infected person
B. unprotected sexual contact with an infected person
C. the bite of an infected mosquito
D. sharing a desk with an infected person

**19.** Gonorrhoea is caused by

A. a roundworm
B. a virus
C. a bacterium
D. a fungus

**20.** A disease such as gonorrhoea, which is passed on during sexual contact, is called a

A. hereditary disease
B. deficiency disease
C. vector-borne disease
D. sexually transmitted infection

**21.** A common symptom of gonorrhoea is

A. a yellow colour of the whites of the eyes
B. white patches on the tongue only
C. a sudden swelling of the knee joints
D. pain or a burning feeling when passing urine, with a discharge

**22.** Gonorrhoea is often not noticed early in many women because

A. the bacteria cannot live in the body of a woman
B. the disease changes into malaria in women
C. a woman may have mild symptoms or none at all while still carrying the bacteria
D. women are treated with antibiotics every month

**23.** If gonorrhoea is not treated, a serious effect on a young person later in life may be

A. a permanent change in the colour of the hair
B. difficulty in having children
C. the loss of the sense of balance
D. the inability to digest fat

**24.** A baby born to a mother who has untreated gonorrhoea may suffer from

A. an extra finger on each hand
B. a shortage of red blood cells only
C. a serious infection of the eyes, which can lead to blindness
D. the loss of all its milk teeth

**25.** Apart from abstaining from sex, which of the following helps to prevent the spread of gonorrhoea?

A. Washing the body with hot water after sexual contact
B. Early reporting to a health facility so that the patient and the partner are both treated
C. Keeping the infection a secret from the health worker
D. Buying antibiotics from a hawker and taking half of them

**26.** Meningitis is an inflammation of the

A. covering of the brain and the spinal cord
B. wall of the heart
C. air sacs of the lungs
D. lining of the stomach

**27.** Meningitis is spread from one person to another mainly through

A. droplets from the nose and the throat during coughing, sneezing and close talking
B. sharing a reading book
C. walking barefoot on a dusty road
D. drinking water from a borehole

**28.** Which of the following is a well-known symptom of meningitis?

A. A painless swelling of the big toe
B. A slow loss of weight over two years
C. A rash on the palms only
D. A sudden high fever with a severe headache and a stiff neck

**29.** A patient with meningitis often turns away from a window because the patient

A. has lost the use of both legs
B. cannot bear bright light
C. is afraid of the people outside
D. needs more fresh air than other patients

**30.** A person who recovers from meningitis that was treated late may be left with

A. a permanent yellow colour of the skin
B. deafness or damage to the brain
C. an inability to grow adult teeth
D. a longer arm on one side

**31.** Outbreaks of meningitis are common in the northern parts of Ghana during the Harmattan because

A. mosquitoes breed faster in the dry season
B. the food sold in the markets is cheaper at that time
C. the air is hot, dry and dusty, which injures the lining of the nose and throat and helps the bacteria to enter
D. the people drink more water in the dry season

**32.** Sleeping in a crowded, poorly aired room increases the risk of meningitis because

A. crowded rooms have more food for the bacteria
B. the bacteria are carried by the mosquitoes in the room
C. the floor of such a room is always wet
D. droplets from an infected person are easily breathed in by those nearby

**33.** The most effective way of protecting a whole community against meningitis during an outbreak is

A. asking everybody to drink plenty of hot tea
B. a vaccination campaign organised by the health authorities
C. spraying the rooms against mosquitoes
D. closing all the boreholes in the town

**34.** Which of the following is the duty of an individual in the control of bacterial diseases?

A. Washing the hands with soap and reporting early to a health facility when ill
B. Passing laws on food safety
C. Supplying vaccines to all the regions
D. Building hospitals in every district

**35.** Which of the following is mainly the duty of the government in the control of bacterial diseases?

A. Sweeping the compound every morning
B. Washing one's own hands before eating
C. Providing vaccines, health facilities and trained health workers
D. Covering food in the kitchen at home

**36.** Communal labour to clear choked gutters and clean a market helps to control disease because it

A. makes the town larger
B. removes the dirt and stagnant water in which germs and pests thrive
C. keeps the traders away from the market
D. increases the price of food in the market

**37.** A pupil who wants to educate the community about meningitis would find a poster useful mainly because a poster

A. removes the need for vaccination
B. can be understood only by health workers
C. is cheaper than speaking to one person

**38.** Which of the following is the BEST message for a poster on the prevention of food poisoning?

A. Buy food only from your own relatives
B. Boil all fruits before eating them
C. Eat only once a day
D. Cook it well, cover it, eat it hot

**39.** A patient stops taking the antibiotics for a bacterial disease as soon as he feels better. The likely result is that

A. the bacteria that are left may survive, become resistant and make the illness return
B. the patient will never fall ill again
C. the remaining drugs will change into vitamins
D. the disease will be passed on only to animals

**40.** A town has many cases of food poisoning after a funeral. The MOST useful first action by the health team is to

A. close the town's only school for a month
B. find out what the people ate and how the food was prepared and stored
C. arrest the family that organised the funeral
D. ask everybody in the town to take antibiotics
