## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** Science is best described as

A. the making of machines for factories only
B. the selling of goods produced in a country
C. the orderly study of nature to find out how and why things happen
D. the repair of broken tools in a workshop

**2.** Technology is best described as

A. the writing down of the results of an experiment
B. the study of living things in their habitat
C. the use of scientific knowledge to make tools, machines and methods that meet human needs
D. the collection of taxes from factories

**3.** Innovation means

A. repeating an old experiment exactly as before
B. copying a machine without changing anything
C. writing a report on a scientific discovery
D. introducing a new or improved product, method or idea that people actually use

**4.** Which of the following shows the usual order in which new things reach the public?

A. Society, then innovation, then technology
B. Innovation, then scientific knowledge, then technology
C. Technology, then society, then scientific knowledge
D. Scientific knowledge, then technology, then innovation used by society

**5.** The discovery that an electric current in a wire produces a magnetic field is an example of

A. an innovation in a market
B. scientific knowledge
C. a business plan
D. a government policy

**6.** Using the knowledge above to build an electric fan is an example of

A. a natural resource
B. pure science
C. technology
D. an environmental hazard

**7.** Which of the following best explains why science and technology depend on each other?

A. Science supplies the knowledge technology uses, and the tools technology makes allow science to investigate further
B. Science is practised only in schools and technology only in factories
C. Science and technology are two names for the same activity
D. Technology was invented before any science was known

**8.** A farmer who fixes a plastic bottle to a rope to make a simple drip waterer for his seedlings is showing

A. a scientific law, because the bottle holds water
B. innovation, because he has created a new way of solving a problem with what he has
C. pure science, because he has carried out an experiment
D. a natural process, because water always flows downwards

**9.** Which of the following is the MAIN benefit of science and technology to a society?

A. They help to solve problems and improve the quality of people's lives
B. They make all work unnecessary
C. They remove the need for education
D. They make every citizen wealthy at once

**10.** The use of a tractor instead of a hoe on a large farm mainly

A. prevents rain from falling on the farm
B. increases the area that can be ploughed in a day
C. makes the soil lose all its nutrients
D. reduces the amount of food the farm can produce

**11.** Mobile money services have improved life in Ghana chiefly because they

A. remove the need for people to work
B. stop thieves from entering any house
C. make all goods in the market free
D. allow people to send and receive money quickly without travelling to a bank

**12.** Which technology has done most to improve the storage of vaccines at a rural clinic?

A. The solar-powered refrigerator
B. The mobile telephone
C. The bicycle
D. The loudspeaker

**13.** A borehole fitted with a hand pump improves the health of a village mainly because it

A. keeps mosquitoes away from the houses
B. provides safe drinking water, so fewer people catch water-borne diseases
C. makes the village land more fertile
D. supplies electricity for the houses

**14.** Which of the following is an example of technology used in health care?

A. The periodic table
B. The weather forecast
C. The multiplication table
D. The X-ray machine

**15.** A cassava processing machine helps a farming community mainly by

A. making the cassava grow faster on the farm
B. removing the need to plant cassava again
C. turning the cassava into gari quickly, so less of the crop is wasted
D. changing cassava into maize

**16.** Which of the following best shows how technology has changed communication in Ghana?

A. A message that once took days by letter is now sent in seconds by phone
B. People now travel more slowly than before
C. Letters are now carried by donkeys
D. Only the government may send messages

**17.** A refrigerator preserves food mainly because the low temperature

A. adds extra nutrients to the food
B. removes all the water from the food
C. kills every germ in the food at once
D. slows down the growth of the bacteria that spoil food

**18.** The MAIN reason why a factory in Tema uses machines rather than hand labour alone is that machines

A. never need any maintenance
B. work without any source of energy
C. work faster and produce goods of a more even quality
D. remove the need for safety rules

**19.** Which of the following is a harmful effect of technological advancement on the environment?

A. A rise in the amount of clean water in rivers
B. An increase in the number of trees in the forest
C. Pollution of air, water and land by wastes from industry
D. A fall in the amount of waste produced

**20.** Smoke from factories and vehicles pollutes the air chiefly because it contains

A. oxygen only
B. harmless dust that settles at once
C. water vapour only
D. harmful gases and tiny particles that people breathe in

**21.** Old televisions, computers and mobile phones that have been thrown away are known as

A. organic manure
B. industrial fertiliser
C. scrap timber
D. electronic waste (e-waste)

**22.** Burning the plastic covering of old cables to get the copper inside is dangerous because it

A. releases poisonous fumes that damage the lungs and pollute the air
B. cools the air around the fire
C. turns the copper into gold
D. makes the copper useless

**23.** Which of the following is the BEST way to deal with old computers and phones?

A. Collect them for proper recycling so that the metals are recovered safely
B. Throw them into a stream
C. Bury them whole in a farm
D. Burn them in an open yard

**24.** Illegal small-scale mining with heavy machines, known as galamsey, has harmed Ghana's rivers chiefly by

A. making the water safe to drink without treatment
B. making them flow faster to the sea
C. increasing the number of fish in them
D. filling them with mud and chemicals such as mercury

**25.** The MAIN effect of clearing a large area of forest for a new factory is

A. an immediate improvement in the fertility of the soil
B. the loss of habitats for plants and animals and an increase in soil erosion
C. a fall in the temperature of the whole country
D. an increase in the yearly rainfall of the area

**26.** Plastic sachets and bottles thrown into gutters cause flooding in Ghanaian towns because they

A. make the water in the gutters evaporate faster
B. block the gutters and drains so that rain water cannot flow away
C. attract rain to the town
D. dissolve and thicken the water

**27.** Which of the following gases, released when fuels are burnt, is mainly responsible for the warming of the earth?

A. Water vapour from a kettle
B. Nitrogen
C. Oxygen
D. Carbon dioxide

**28.** Noise from a corn mill sited close to a classroom block is a form of

A. conservation, because the mill saves time
B. pollution, because it disturbs learning and can damage hearing
C. recycling, because the maize is reused
D. innovation, because the mill is modern

**29.** Technology can also help to repair the damage it causes. Which of the following is an example?

A. Using machines to cut down more trees
B. Pumping untreated waste water into a lagoon
C. Using machines to recycle plastic waste into roofing sheets and pavement blocks
D. Burning refuse in the open to save space

**30.** Which of the following sources of electricity does LEAST harm to the environment?

A. A petrol engine
B. A diesel generator
C. A solar panel
D. A coal-fired station

**31.** The chief advantage of using a solar dryer instead of drying fish in the open is that the dryer

A. adds salt to the fish automatically
B. keeps out flies, dust and rain while drying the fish faster
C. makes the fish grow bigger
D. removes the need to catch fish

**32.** A school that collects rain water from its roof into a tank is using technology to

A. store a free supply of water for use in the dry season
B. prevent lightning from striking the roof
C. cool the classrooms during lessons
D. increase the rainfall over the school

**33.** Before a new machine is brought into a community, the MOST important question to ask is

A. what effect it will have on the people, their work and their environment
B. what colour the machine has been painted
C. how heavy the machine is
D. who owns the shop that sells it

**34.** A pupil reads on social media that a certain herb cures every disease. The BEST action is to

A. accept it because many people have shared it
B. buy the herb and try it immediately
C. forward the message to all the pupils at once
D. check the claim with a health worker or a trusted scientific source before believing it

**35.** Which of the following is the best evidence that a piece of information about a new technology is reliable?

A. It promises results that sound surprising
B. It is written in very large letters
C. It comes from a recognised institution and agrees with other trusted sources
D. It has been shared by many people online

**36.** Science, technology and society are said to be connected because

A. society has no influence at all on science
B. the needs of society direct what is studied and invented, and inventions in turn change society
C. scientific knowledge never changes the way people live
D. technology is practised only by governments

**37.** Which of the following best describes sustainable use of technology?

A. Using technology to meet today's needs without destroying the resources of future generations
B. Using only the machines made in other countries
C. Replacing all workers with machines as quickly as possible
D. Using every machine until the fuel of the country is finished

**38.** A factory sited beside a river discharges its waste water into the river untreated. The MOST useful first step for the community is to

A. ask the factory to work only at night
B. fetch the water and boil it for drinking
C. report the matter to the Environmental Protection Authority and the assembly for action
D. move the whole village to another place

**39.** A group of pupils wants to design a device that will warn a farmer when his water tank is full. The FIRST step in their design is to

A. buy the most expensive materials they can find
B. state clearly the problem to be solved and what the device must do
C. paint the device in bright colours
D. give the device a name

**40.** Which of the following statements about technological advancement in Ghana is MOST balanced?

A. It brings real benefits, but it must be managed so that it does not damage health and the environment
B. It is wholly bad and should be stopped at once
C. It affects only the people who live in the cities
D. It is wholly good and should never be questioned

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** Climate is best described as

A. the condition of the atmosphere of a place at one moment
B. the temperature recorded at noon on one day
C. the average pattern of weather of a place taken over many years
D. the amount of rain that falls in a single storm

**2.** Climate change means

A. the change from morning coolness to afternoon heat
B. the difference in temperature between two towns
C. the change of wind direction during a storm
D. a long-term change in the average pattern of temperature and rainfall of a place

**3.** Which of the following is a sign of climate change?

A. A cold morning during the Harmattan
B. Seasons that no longer begin at the times farmers expect
C. A heavy downpour in the rainy season
D. A cloudy sky in the afternoon

**4.** Which of the following is NOT a sign of climate change?

A. The daily rise in temperature from morning to midday
B. The rise in the average temperature of the earth over many years
C. The retreat of ice at the poles
D. The rise in the level of the sea

**5.** The melting of ice at the poles and on high mountains is evidence that

A. the earth is moving closer to the moon
B. the sun has stopped shining on the poles
C. the oceans are becoming shallower
D. the average temperature of the earth is rising

**6.** A rise in the level of the sea along the coast of Ghana is caused mainly by

A. the melting of ice and the expansion of sea water as it warms
B. the pumping of water out of the lagoons
C. the building of harbours at Tema and Takoradi
D. the digging of boreholes in the coastal towns

**7.** Which record would be MOST useful in showing that the climate of a town has changed?

A. The temperature taken every hour for one day
B. The amount of rain that fell last week
C. The wind speed recorded during one storm
D. Rainfall and temperature figures collected over the past fifty years

**8.** A farmer says, 'The rains used to come in March, but for the past ten years they begin in May.' This statement describes

A. a change in climate
B. a change in crop variety
C. a single weather event
D. a change in soil type

**9.** The gases that trap heat in the atmosphere of the earth are known as

A. inert gases
B. noble gases
C. greenhouse gases
D. respiratory gases

**10.** Which of the following is the greenhouse gas released in the greatest quantity by human activity?

A. Hydrogen
B. Carbon dioxide
C. Oxygen
D. Nitrogen

**11.** Carbon dioxide is added to the atmosphere mainly by

A. the evaporation of water from lakes
B. the burning of wood, charcoal, petrol, diesel and other fuels
C. the breathing of green plants at night only
D. the weathering of rocks on a hillside

**12.** Methane, another greenhouse gas, comes mainly from

A. the burning of solar panels
B. the grinding of maize in a mill
C. rotting refuse in landfill sites, cattle and flooded rice fields
D. the freezing of water in a refrigerator

**13.** Cutting down large areas of forest adds to climate change chiefly because

A. the soil becomes too soft for farming
B. the remaining trees grow much taller
C. fewer trees are left to take in carbon dioxide from the air
D. the rivers begin to flow more slowly

**14.** Which of the following human activities adds LEAST to climate change?

A. Burning refuse in the open
B. Drying clothes in the sun
C. Running a diesel generator all night
D. Clearing a forest by fire for farming

**15.** Bush burning before the planting season adds to climate change because it

A. releases carbon dioxide and destroys the plants that would absorb it
B. increases the number of earthworms in the soil
C. cools the surface of the soil
D. brings the rains earlier in the year

**16.** Which of the following best explains why the earth is warming?

A. The earth has moved nearer to the sun
B. The atmosphere has lost all its oxygen
C. Human activity has increased the greenhouse gases, so more heat is held in the atmosphere
D. The earth now spins faster on its axis

**17.** A likely effect of climate change on farming in Ghana is

A. an increase in the fertility of every soil
B. poor harvests because the rains come late or stop early
C. a fall in the number of pests on the farm
D. the ripening of all crops at the same time

**18.** Longer and more severe dry spells in northern Ghana are likely to lead to

A. a rise in the number of fish in the rivers
B. a fall in the price of water in the towns
C. an increase in the depth of the White Volta
D. the drying up of streams and a shortage of water for people and animals

**19.** Which of the following is an effect of a rise in sea level on a coastal town such as Keta?

A. Flooding of houses and the washing away of land by the sea
B. An increase in the area of land for building
C. A fall in the salt content of the lagoon
D. A rise in the number of trees on the shore

**20.** Climate change can increase disease in a community because

A. germs can no longer live in warm places
B. warmer, wetter conditions allow mosquitoes and other disease carriers to spread
C. people stop drinking water when it is hot
D. hospitals close during the dry season

**21.** Heavy, unusual rainfall in a Ghanaian city often leads to

A. a rise in the quality of the roads
B. a permanent improvement in the drainage system
C. floods that destroy property and lives, especially where gutters are choked
D. a fall in the number of people in the city

**22.** Which of the following groups of people in Ghana is MOST at risk from climate change?

A. Office workers in air-conditioned buildings
B. Small-scale farmers and fishers who depend directly on the rains and the sea
C. Traders who sell goods in a covered market
D. Pupils who attend school in the morning

**23.** Climate change threatens the production of cocoa in Ghana mainly because cocoa

A. is harvested only during the Harmattan
B. grows only on land covered by sea water
C. cannot grow where there are any trees
D. needs steady rainfall and shade, and suffers when the dry season is long and hot

**24.** The drying up of a dam that supplies a hydroelectric station leads to

A. an increase in the amount of power produced
B. an improvement in the quality of the water
C. a shortage of electricity for homes and industries
D. a fall in the price of petrol in the country

**25.** Which statement about the effects of climate change is TRUE?

A. Only the countries that produce the gases are affected
B. The countries that produce the least greenhouse gas often suffer its effects most
C. The effects are felt only at the poles
D. The effects can be seen within a single week

**26.** A direct effect of climate change on biodiversity is that

A. all animals move to the same habitat
B. every species produces more young than before
C. some plants and animals die out because their habitats change faster than they can adapt
D. plants no longer need sunlight to grow

**27.** Adaptation to climate change means

A. changing the way we live and work so that we can cope with the changes already happening
B. measuring the temperature of the earth every day
C. moving every community to another country
D. stopping the release of all gases from factories

**28.** Which of the following is an adaptation measure for a farming community?

A. Using more firewood for cooking
B. Cutting down the trees along the stream
C. Burning the bush before every planting season
D. Planting early-maturing and drought-resistant varieties of maize

**29.** The building of small dams and the harvesting of rain water in northern Ghana is an example of

A. adaptation, because it stores water for the longer dry season
B. pollution, because it changes the river
C. mitigation, because it reduces greenhouse gases
D. deforestation, because land is cleared

**30.** Planting trees along the shore and rebuilding sea defences at Keta is mainly intended to

A. provide timber for export
B. protect the town from the advancing sea
C. raise the temperature of the lagoon
D. increase the number of fish caught

**31.** A farmer who now keeps part of his harvest in an improved store, instead of selling it all at once, is adapting because he

A. is preparing for a season in which the harvest may fail
B. wants to reduce the carbon dioxide in the air
C. is obeying a law about bush burning
D. expects the price of maize to fall

**32.** Legislation against bush burning helps a country to deal with climate change because it

A. increases the number of farms in the forest
B. makes the rains fall at the same time every year
C. removes the need for weeding
D. protects the trees and grass that take in carbon dioxide and hold the soil

**33.** Which of the following shows a community adapting to a longer dry season?

A. Burning refuse in the open every evening
B. Clearing more forest for new farms
C. Buying more firewood for the kitchen
D. Changing the planting calendar and using irrigation from a small dam

**34.** Mitigation of climate change means

A. reducing the amount of greenhouse gas released, or taking it out of the air
B. storing grain for a season of poor harvest
C. learning to live with the effects of a warmer world
D. moving a village away from a flooded river

**35.** Which of the following is a mitigation measure?

A. Replacing a diesel generator with solar panels
B. Storing rain water in a tank
C. Building a higher wall round a flooded house
D. Planting a crop that ripens earlier

**36.** A green economy is one in which

A. only green vegetables are grown for sale
B. all factories are closed down permanently
C. people earn a living in ways that do not destroy the environment
D. every building in the town is painted green

**37.** Which of the following is a green job?

A. Felling timber without replanting
B. Installing and repairing solar panels
C. Burning old tyres to recover steel wire
D. Mining gold in the bed of a river

**38.** Planting trees helps to slow climate change chiefly because growing trees

A. lower the level of the sea directly
B. prevent the sun from reaching the earth
C. take in carbon dioxide and store the carbon in their wood
D. release large amounts of oxygen at night

**39.** Which of the following household changes would do MOST to reduce a family's greenhouse gas release?

A. Sweeping the compound twice a day
B. Washing plates in cold water instead of warm
C. Painting the kitchen a lighter colour
D. Cooking with an improved, fuel-saving stove or gas instead of an open wood fire

**40.** A Basic 8 class wants to help its community act on climate change. The MOST effective action is to

A. write the words 'stop climate change' on the school wall
B. ask the pupils to stay at home on hot days
C. wait until the government solves the problem
D. plant and care for trees on the school compound and teach others why it matters

---

## SECTION B: THEORY (60 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Write your answers in your answer booklet. The marks for each question are shown in brackets.*

### Question 1  [10 marks]

Fig. 1 shows how the earth is kept warm. The three arrows are lettered P, Q and R.

![Fig. 1: The sun, the layer of gases round the earth, the surface of the earth, and the three arrows P, Q and R.](/home/user/figures/pencil_fig42.png)

*Fig. 1: The sun, the layer of gases round the earth, the surface of the earth, and the three arrows P, Q and R.*

**(a)** State what each of the arrows **P**, **Q** and **R** in Fig. 1 represents.

**(b)** Name **two** gases found in the layer shown in Fig. 1 that trap heat in this way.

**(c)** Explain what happens to the temperature of the earth when the amount of these gases in the layer increases, and say why.

**(d)** State **two** human activities that increase the amount of these gases in the air.

---

### Question 2  [10 marks]

Fig. 2 shows the average yearly temperature recorded at a weather station in northern Ghana every ten years from 1980 to 2020. Study it carefully and answer the questions that follow.

![Fig. 2: Average yearly temperature recorded at the station, 1980 to 2020.](/home/user/figures/pencil_fig43.png)

*Fig. 2: Average yearly temperature recorded at the station, 1980 to 2020.*

**(a)** Read from the graph the average temperature in **1980** and in **2020**.

**(b)** Calculate the rise in the average temperature over the forty years.

**(c)** Describe the pattern shown by the graph, and state what it suggests about the climate of the area.

**(d)** State **two** other signs, apart from temperature, that would show the people of the area that the climate is changing.

**(e)** Your group is writing a report on climate change. Explain why the record from this one station is **not** enough on its own, and state what else you would do.

---

### Question 3  [12 marks]

A radio programme says that climate change is 'the greatest problem facing farmers and fishers in Ghana today'.

**(a)** Explain what is meant by **climate change**, and state **one** way in which climate is different from weather.

**(b)** State **four** human activities that are causing climate change, and in each case name the gas or the process involved.

**(c)** Explain **three** ways in which climate change is already affecting farming in Ghana.

**(d)** State **two** effects of climate change on a coastal community such as Keta or Ada.

---

### Question 4  [10 marks]

Countries deal with climate change in two different ways. Ghana does both.

**(a)** Explain the difference between **adaptation** and **mitigation**, and give **one** example of each.

**(b)** State **three** adaptation measures that a farming community in northern Ghana could take.

**(c)** State **three** mitigation actions that the same community could take.

---

### Question 5  [8 marks]

Ghana, like other tropical countries, is trying to build a green economy.

**(a)** Explain what is meant by a **green economy**.

**(b)** Name **three** kinds of work in a green economy, and say briefly what each one does for the environment.

**(c)** Describe **three** things your own school could do to become greener, and state the benefit of each.

---

### Question 6  [10 marks]

Each year Ghana sets aside a day on which citizens plant trees, and the law forbids the careless burning of the bush. Your class has been asked to lead the tree-planting exercise in your school.

**(a)** Give **two** reasons why planting trees helps a country to deal with climate change.

**(b)** Describe, in order, **three** steps your class would take to plan and carry out the exercise.

**(c)** State **one** difficulty your class is likely to meet, and say how you would overcome it.

**(d)** Ghana has a law against the careless burning of the bush. Explain why such a law is needed, and state **two** ways in which a community can help to make it work.

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** Soil is best described as

A. the loose material on the surface of the earth in which plants grow
B. the water held in a stream bed
C. the solid rock that lies deep under the ground
D. the dead leaves lying on a forest floor only

**2.** Which of the following is a physical property of a soil?

A. The name of the farmer who owns it
B. The number of farms in the village
C. The price of the land on which it lies
D. Its texture, that is how coarse or fine it feels

**3.** The four main constituents of a fertile soil are

A. clay, plastic, metal and water
B. mineral particles, humus, water and air
C. rock, petrol, air and humus
D. sand, salt, sugar and water

**4.** Humus in a soil is formed from

A. the broken pieces of plastic in the soil
B. the decayed remains of plants and animals
C. the water held between the soil particles
D. the smallest grains of sand

**5.** The MAIN importance of humus in a soil is that it

A. gives the soil its red colour only
B. makes the soil heavier to dig
C. supplies plant nutrients and helps the soil to hold water
D. prevents earthworms from entering the soil

**6.** The air in a soil is important to a plant because it

A. supplies oxygen for the respiration of the roots and of soil organisms
B. pushes the roots deeper into the soil
C. dissolves the rock particles into nutrients
D. keeps the soil cool during the night

**7.** A soil is described as having a coarse texture when its particles are

A. equal in size to the particles of clay
B. large and can be felt separately between the fingers
C. so fine that they stick together when wet
D. made entirely of humus

**8.** A pupil who wants to compare the texture of three soils should

A. rub a moist sample of each soil between the fingers and feel the particles
B. count the stones in each sample
C. measure the temperature of each sample
D. weigh each sample on a balance

**9.** Which of the following soils has the largest particles?

A. Clay soil
B. Sandy soil
C. Silty soil
D. Loamy soil

**10.** Clay soil holds the most water because its particles are

A. made entirely of humus
B. coated with oil that traps water
C. very fine and tightly packed, leaving tiny spaces
D. very large with wide spaces between them

**11.** Water drains fastest through

A. clay soil
B. loamy soil
C. sandy soil
D. waterlogged soil

**12.** Which soil is described as the best for growing most crops?

A. Loamy soil
B. Gravelly soil
C. Sandy soil
D. Clay soil

**13.** Loamy soil is the best soil for most crops because it

A. contains no air at all
B. holds enough water and nutrients while still allowing water and air to pass
C. is made only of very fine particles
D. never needs any manure

**14.** A soil that is waterlogged harms a crop mainly because

A. the soil becomes too light for the roots
B. the water fills the air spaces, so the roots cannot get oxygen
C. the roots take in too much humus
D. the water washes the leaves off the plant

**15.** Clay soil is difficult to work on a farm chiefly because it

A. has no mineral particles in it
B. is always too light to hold a plant
C. becomes sticky when wet and very hard when dry
D. contains too many large stones

**16.** A farmer can improve a sandy soil by

A. adding more sand to it
B. watering it only once in a season
C. burning the grass on it every year
D. adding organic manure or compost to help it hold water and nutrients

**17.** Adding sand and well-rotted manure to a heavy clay soil helps because it

A. turns the clay into rock
B. removes all the nutrients from the soil
C. makes the soil hold even more water
D. opens up the soil so that water can drain and air can enter

**18.** Plants take in water from the soil mainly through the

A. lower surface of the leaves
B. root hairs
C. stem bark
D. flowers

**19.** The movement of water from the soil into a root hair takes place by

A. evaporation
B. combustion
C. osmosis
D. respiration

**20.** Water passes into the root hair because the solution inside the root hair is

A. more concentrated than the soil water outside it
B. at a higher temperature than the soil
C. held in a vacuum
D. the same strength as the soil water

**21.** A plant wilts on a hot afternoon mainly because

A. its roots have stopped growing
B. the leaves have taken in too much oxygen
C. the soil has become too rich in humus
D. it is losing water from the leaves faster than the roots can take it in

**22.** Besides water, a plant also obtains from the soil

A. the energy it needs to grow
B. carbon dioxide for photosynthesis
C. mineral salts (nutrients) dissolved in the soil water
D. the chlorophyll in its leaves

**23.** A farmer who waters a sandy soil more often than a loamy soil does so because sandy soil

A. loses water quickly by drainage
B. holds water for a very long time
C. contains more humus than loam
D. has no air spaces at all

**24.** In an experiment, maize seedlings were grown in sandy, loamy and clay soils and watered equally. The seedlings in the loamy soil grew tallest. The BEST conclusion is that

A. maize can grow only in loamy soil
B. sandy and clay soils contain no water at all
C. loamy soil supplied the balance of water, air and nutrients that the seedlings needed
D. the seedlings in loam were given more water

**25.** A rock is best described as

A. a piece of concrete broken from a building
B. any hard object buried in the ground
C. a lump of dried clay from a river bed
D. a naturally occurring solid material made of one or more minerals

**26.** The three main types of rock are

A. igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic
B. wet, dry and damp
C. hard, soft and medium
D. surface, middle and deep

**27.** Igneous rocks are formed when

A. layers of sediment are pressed together
B. molten rock material cools and becomes solid
C. plant remains decay in a swamp
D. a rock is changed by heat and pressure

**28.** Granite is an example of

A. a sedimentary rock
B. an igneous rock
C. a metamorphic rock
D. a mineral fuel

**29.** Sedimentary rocks are formed when

A. soil is ploughed and left in the sun
B. an existing rock is changed by great heat and pressure
C. hot liquid rock cools inside the earth
D. layers of sand, mud and shell are deposited and pressed together over a long time

**30.** Which of the following is a sedimentary rock?

A. Marble
B. Basalt
C. Granite
D. Limestone

**31.** A rock that shows clear layers, or bands of different materials pressed together, is most likely

A. volcanic
B. igneous
C. sedimentary
D. molten

**32.** Metamorphic rocks are formed when

A. humus mixes with sand in a garden
B. lava cools quickly on the surface
C. sediments settle at the bottom of a lake
D. an existing rock is changed by great heat and pressure inside the earth

**33.** When a pupil makes a rock identification guide, the MOST useful features to record for each sample are

A. the day on which it was collected only
B. the name of the pupil who found it
C. its price in the market and its owner
D. its colour, hardness, texture and whether it shows grains or layers

**34.** Weathering is best described as

A. the breaking down of rocks into smaller pieces where they lie
B. the burning of grass on a hillside
C. the ploughing of a field before planting
D. the carrying away of soil by running water

**35.** Which of the following is the parent material of a soil?

A. The air trapped between its particles
B. The humus added by farmers
C. The rock beneath it, broken down over a long time
D. The water held in its spaces

**36.** A rock splits when it is heated strongly by day and cooled at night because the rock

A. expands and contracts repeatedly until it cracks
B. absorbs oxygen from the atmosphere
C. dissolves in the cold night air
D. is eaten away by soil organisms

**37.** The roots of a tree growing in the crack of a rock help in weathering because they

A. carry the rock away to the river
B. widen the crack as they grow and force pieces of the rock apart
C. dissolve the whole rock into water
D. make the rock harder as they grow

**38.** Rain water helps to break down some rocks chiefly because it

A. is always boiling hot when it falls
B. freezes solid in tropical countries
C. contains sand that scratches the rock
D. is slightly acidic and slowly dissolves certain minerals in the rock

**39.** Which of the following gives the correct order in the formation of a soil?

A. Solid rock, cracked rock, broken pieces, fine particles mixed with humus
B. Broken pieces, humus, solid rock, fine particles
C. Humus, fine particles, broken pieces, solid rock
D. Fine particles, solid rock, humus, broken pieces

**40.** Soil formation is described as a very slow process because

A. rocks do not break down at all in the tropics
B. only farmers can make soil from rock
C. it may take hundreds of years for a thin layer of soil to form from rock
D. soil forms only during the rainy season

| 5 (d) | Shine a beam of light through the drink in a clear glass: in a true solution the path of the light is not visible and no particles settle; in a suspension the path is visible and particles settle. | Choosing and Performing Separation Methods | Create |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) For procedures and calculations, award method marks. (4) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required.)*

### Question 1 (12 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- A mixture is a combination of **two or more substances** that are **not chemically joined together**.
- The substances in a mixture **keep their own properties** and can be **separated by physical means** (filtration, evaporation, sieving, etc.).
- The substances of a mixture can be mixed in **any ratio**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks). Award 1 mark for ‘two or more substances mixed together’ only if the idea that they are not chemically combined is present. Do NOT accept ‘two things put together’ on its own.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- In a **mixture** the substances are **not chemically joined**; in a **compound** the elements are **chemically joined**.
- A mixture can be **separated by physical means**; a compound can only be separated by **chemical means**.
- The parts of a mixture **keep their own properties**; a compound has **new properties** different from its elements.
- The parts of a mixture can be mixed in **any ratio**; the elements of a compound combine in a **fixed ratio**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct differences (2 marks). The difference must be stated as a comparison, not as a description of only one of them. Do NOT accept ‘a compound is harder’ or answers that describe the appearance alone.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- (i) air - **homogeneous**
- (ii) sand and water - **heterogeneous**
- (iii) salt solution - **homogeneous**
- (iv) groundnut and rice mixture - **heterogeneous**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). The wording and the letter of the mixture must be matched correctly before the mark is given.*

**(d)** [4 marks]

- (i) air - **fractional distillation** (accept ‘cooling the air’, accept ‘distillation’)
- (ii) sand and water - **filtration** (accept ‘decantation’ or ‘sedimentation’)
- (iii) salt solution - **evaporation** (accept ‘distillation’ or ‘crystallisation’)
- (iv) groundnut and rice mixture - **sieving** (accept ‘hand-picking’)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). Accept any method that is scientifically suitable for the mixture named, even if it is not the commonest one.*

### Question 2 (14 marks)

**(a)** [6 marks]

- (i) **Medium-sized** particles (between about 1 nm and 1000 nm)
- (ii) **Does not settle** (remains permanently mixed)
- (iii) **Does not settle**
- (iv) **Settles on standing** (particles settle at the bottom)
- (v) **Does not scatter** light
- (vi) **Scatters** light
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for all SIX blanks correctly filled (6 marks). The blank number must be matched to the correct answer. Accept clear equivalents, e.g. ‘intermediate size’ for (i) and ‘never settles’ for (ii).*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- Solution particles are **smaller than 1 nm** (about 1 nm or less).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Accept ‘less than 1 nm’ or ‘about 1 nanometre’.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) Solution: salt solution, sugar solution, sea water, soft drink, vinegar, air, brass.
- (ii) Colloid: milk, blood, fog, smoke, starch solution, jelly, paint, mayonnaise, Milo drink.
- (iii) Suspension: muddy water, chalk and water, sand and water, tomato juice, kerosene and water.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct examples of each group (3 marks). Do NOT give a mark for an example repeated from another part of the question. Accept any correct example from the local environment.*

**(d)** [4 marks]

- (i) **29 g** of sugar
- (ii) The mass of sugar that dissolves **increases** as the temperature of the water rises (the higher the temperature, the more sugar dissolves).
- (iii) **No**, not all the sugar will dissolve.
- (iii) Reason: only **36 g** of sugar can dissolve in 100 cm³ of water at 80 °C, so the remaining **4 g** stays at the bottom as undissolved sugar.
  - *Marking note: (i) 1 mark; (ii) 1 mark; (iii) 1 mark for the correct decision and 1 mark for the reason (4 marks in all). In (iii) do not award the reason mark for repeating the question; the number 36 g or 4 g must appear.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- A: the path of the light is **not visible** - the light passes straight through.
- B: the **path of the light is clearly visible** inside the liquid as a bright track.
- C: the path of the light is **not clearly visible** - the light is blocked and the mixture is opaque.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (3 marks). The answer must name the mixture or its letter; an answer that gives only ‘visible’ or ‘not visible’ with no link to A, B or C earns no mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- The particles of milk are **large enough to scatter the light** in all directions (1 mark).
- The scattered light reaches the eye from the side, so the **path of the beam becomes visible** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark for each point. Accept ‘the particles reflect the light’ if scattering in all directions is implied. Do NOT accept ‘milk is white’ on its own.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- A - **solution**
- B - **colloid**
- C - **suspension**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (3 marks). All three must be correctly matched to A, B and C; a correct list in the wrong order earns no mark.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- The **Tyndall effect** (accept ‘the scattering of light’).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for the correct name.*

**(e)** [1 marks]

- Any one of: blood, fog or mist, smoke, starch solution, jelly, Milo drink, hair spray, paint.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any correct example. Do NOT accept salt solution, sea water or muddy water - these are not colloids.*

### Question 4 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- I - **thermometer**
- II - **round-bottom flask**
- III - **Liebig condenser**
- IV - **beaker** (accept ‘receiver’ or ‘conical flask’)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). Accept ‘flask’ for II and ‘condenser’ for III. Do NOT accept ‘flask’ for IV or ‘test tube’ for IV.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- I (thermometer): **measures the temperature** of the vapour or liquid so that the boiling point can be checked (1 mark).
- III (condenser): **cools the vapour** and changes it back into a liquid - it condenses the vapour (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The function must be linked to the correct part; a correct statement attached to the wrong letter earns no mark.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- **Evaporation** (accept ‘vaporisation’).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. If a candidate writes ‘boiling’, award 0 here but allow the mark in (d) if the reason given refers to the boiling point.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Ethanol** is collected first in IV (1 mark).
- Reason: ethanol has a **lower boiling point** (about 78 °C) than water (100 °C), so it vapourises first (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. Award the second mark only if a comparison of boiling points is given. Do NOT accept ‘because ethanol is lighter’.*

**(e)** [1 marks]

- To **cool (condense) the vapour** into a liquid; also to prevent the vapour from escaping into the air.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one correct reason.*

**(f)** [1 marks]

- The mixture in the flask contains **two liquids**; the liquid in IV contains **only one** (pure) liquid.
- The mixture boils over a **range of temperatures**; the liquid in IV boils at a **fixed temperature**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one correct difference. The answer must be a comparison, not a description of only one of them.*

**(g)** [1 marks]

- The water would **evaporate and escape** into the air instead of being collected, and the **salt would be left behind** in the flask.
- Distillation is used to recover the **liquid** from a mixture, not the solid; to obtain salt, **evaporation to dryness** should be used instead.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any answer that identifies that the salt would be left in the flask and that evaporation is the correct method.*

### Question 5 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) Iron filings and sand - **magnetic separation**
- (ii) Ground pepper and groundnut soup - **filtration**
- (iii) Salt and water - **evaporation**
- (iv) Salt, sand and water - **filtration, then evaporation** (both must be named)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). In (iv) both processes must be named for the mark. Do NOT accept ‘distillation’ for (iii) unless the candidate shows that the water is to be collected.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Iron is magnetic** (attracted by a magnet) while sand is not, so the iron filings are picked out and the sand remains.
- (ii) **Pepper is insoluble** in the soup and its particles are large enough to be caught on the filter paper as the residue, while the soup passes through as the filtrate.
- (iii) **Salt is dissolved** in the water and cannot be caught by a filter; on heating, the water escapes as vapour and the salt is left behind.
- (iv) The sand is **insoluble**, so filtration removes it first; the salt is **dissolved**, so the filtrate must then be **evaporated** to recover the salt.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks each for any TWO correctly explained choices (4 marks): 1 mark for the correct reason and 1 mark for linking it clearly to the method chosen. A reason that would fit any method earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Filtration:** pour the mixture through **filter paper in a funnel**. The **sand** is trapped as the residue and the salt solution passes through as the filtrate.
- **Evaporation:** pour the filtrate into an **evaporating dish** and heat gently (or leave it in the sun). The water evaporates and **salt crystals** are left behind. Dry the sand and the salt.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for each stage correctly described, and the order must be filtration first. Accept ‘leave the filtrate in the sun’ instead of heating. Maximum 2 marks.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Pour a little of the drink into a **clean, transparent glass** and shine a **torch or beam of light** through it (1 mark).
- In a **true solution** the path of the light is **not visible** and the drink stays clear; if it were a **suspension**, the light path would be **visible (scattered)** and **particles would settle** on standing (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. Accept a ‘leave it to stand and observe whether particles settle’ test if it is fully described. Look for the comparison between what is seen in a solution and in a suspension.*

**Strand:** 1: Diversity of Matter | **Sub-strand:** 1: Materials | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

| Appropriate for the class | Yes - B8 level; particle sizes are used only as a comparison between the three groups and NO advanced colloid chemistry (Brownian motion, dialysis, the mole) is examined. |
| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, a diagram question, a data table and a table for pupils to complete. |
| Sufficient application and reasoning | Yes - 50 of 100 marks (50%) at Apply level or above (Apply 30, Analyse 13, Evaluate 5, Create 2). |
| Plausible MCQ distractors | Yes - drawn from the same content family as the key: the other class of mixture, the wrong separation method, reversed solute/solvent, and confusion between residue, filtrate and distillate. |
| Single best answer per MCQ | Yes - reviewed item by item; special care with A29 (only colloid and suspension scatter light) and A34 (boiling to dryness is the decisive test). |
| Marks internally consistent | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40; Section B 12 + 14 + 10 + 12 + 12 = 60; every sub-question total matches the marking scheme. |
| Total adds up correctly | Yes - 40 + 60 = 100. |
| Answer key correct | Yes - all 40 keys verified item by item against the paper, and all Section B answers verified against the marking scheme. |
| Marking scheme matches questions | Yes - expected answers plus marking notes covering partial credit, accepted alternatives, common wrong answers and method marks. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - open items are anchored with ‘state two’, ‘give two’ and the mark allocation; Question 2(a) numbers every blank (i) to (vi); Question 3 letters the beakers A, B and C. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - gari, fufu, dawa dawa, groundnut soup, Milo, palm wine, Kaneshie market, harmattan and kebabs; everyday separation at home (sieving gari, decanting palm wine, straining soup). |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the abstract terms ‘Tyndall effect’ and the particle-size range are the only additions and both sit inside the supplied indicator on classifying mixtures; no chromatography or industrial fractional distillation is examined. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - definition, classification, table completion, diagram interpretation, data interpretation, naming apparatus, explaining, choosing and justifying a method, and designing a simple test. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand has ONE content standard (B8/JHS2.1.1.1) carried by two indicators, so every blueprint row shows both the standard and the indicator that applies to it.
- Question 3 is the light-scattering (Tyndall) question. The expected level is ‘the particles of a colloid are large enough to scatter the light’; do not expect any detail about particle diameters beyond 1 nm - 1000 nm.
- Question 2(a) turns the comparison of solutions, colloids and suspensions into a completion table with six numbered blanks, (i) to (vi), so marking is quick and fair: 1 mark each, and the blank number must be matched to the answer.
- Question 5(d) is a design task, so award method marks: any sensible test that lets a customer see that no particles settle and the light path is not visible earns credit. If your class actually performs the test, accept what they did as evidence.
- The word ‘sulfur’ is used (IUPAC/British spelling). Accept ‘sulphur’ from candidates.
- Question 4 uses ethanol (b.p. 78 °C) and water (b.p. 100 °C). The expected reason is the difference in boiling points; do not expect fractional-distillation detail, which sits above B8.
- The two figures in this paper are hand-drawn sketches, matching the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) In calculations, award method marks: accept the correct working even if the final figure is wrong. (4) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required.)*

### Question 1 (7 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- The **proton**
- The **neutron**
- The **electron**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (3 marks). All three must be named. Do NOT accept ‘nucleus’ or ‘shell’ - these are parts of the atom, not sub-atomic particles.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Positive** (+1)
- (ii) **Nucleus**
- (iii) **No charge** (neutral / 0)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for (i) with (ii) and 1 mark for (iii), giving 2 marks. A candidate who writes ‘positive’ for the neutron or ‘outside the nucleus’ for the proton earns no mark.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- An **atom is electrically neutral** (equal numbers of protons and electrons); an **ion carries a charge** because the numbers are unequal.
- An atom may **gain or lose electrons to become an ion**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one correct difference. Do NOT accept ‘an ion is smaller’ or ‘an ion is charged’ alone without saying why.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- The number of **protons equals the number of electrons**, so the **positive and negative charges cancel out**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. The answer must mention both protons and electrons and the idea of the charges cancelling.*

### Question 2 (6 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) The atomic number is the number of **protons in one atom** of the element (accept ‘number of protons’, or ‘number of electrons in a neutral atom’) - 1 mark.
- (ii) **16** protons - 1 mark.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). In (ii) the figure 16 must appear; ‘sixteen’ in words is accepted.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 32 − 16 = **16 neutrons**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for 16. Award the method mark for correct working even if the final figure is wrong, but do not award a mark for a wrong figure with no working.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- **16 electrons** (the atom is neutral, so electrons = protons)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for 16. Do NOT accept 32, which confuses the mass number with the number of electrons.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- **2, 8, 6**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. The shells must be filled in order: 2, then 8, then the remainder. Do NOT accept 8, 8 or 2, 6, 8.*

**(e)** [1 marks]

- **6** valence electrons
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Do NOT accept 16, which is the total number of electrons.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- Atom X: atomic number **11**
- Atom Y: atomic number **17**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). The figures must be matched to the correct atom; do NOT accept 23 or 35 here - those are mass numbers.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Atom X: mass number = 11 + 12 = **23**
- Atom Y: mass number = 17 + 18 = **35**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). Award the mark for the correct total; accept the correct addition shown without a final figure only if the figure is then given.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Atom X: **2, 8, 1**
- Atom Y: **2, 8, 7**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). Each configuration must be matched to the correct atom.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Atom X: **1** valence electron
- Atom Y: **7** valence electrons
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). Do NOT accept the total number of electrons (11 and 17).*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- Atom X **loses its single (valence) electron** from the outermost shell (1 mark).
- It then has **11 protons but only 10 electrons**, so the charge on the ion is **+1** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The reason must refer to the numbers of protons and electrons, or state that a positive ion forms because a negative electron has been lost. Do NOT accept ‘it becomes positive’ with no reason.*

### Question 4 (12 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- A molecule is the **smallest particle of a substance that can exist on its own**, made up of **two or more atoms chemically joined together**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Award the mark for the idea that two or more atoms are chemically combined. Do NOT accept ‘a small particle’ alone.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- An **atom** is a single particle; a **molecule** is made up of **two or more atoms joined together**.
- A molecule of an element contains atoms of the same kind; a molecule of a compound contains atoms of different kinds.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one correct difference, stated as a comparison.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **H₂**
- (ii) **O₂**
- (iii) **CO₂**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (3 marks). Accept the formulae with correct subscripts only; do NOT accept 2H, 2O or Co₂.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- (i) Carbon (C) = **6 atoms**; Hydrogen (H) = **12 atoms**; Oxygen (O) = **6 atoms** (2 marks for all three correct).
- (ii) 6 + 12 + 6 = **24 atoms** altogether (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) award 2 marks only when all three figures are correct; award 1 mark if only carbon and oxygen are right. (ii) earns 1 mark for 24.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- (i) Hydrogen molecule, H₂ - **covalent bond**
- (ii) Sodium chloride, NaCl - **ionic bond**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). A candidate who reverses the two earns no mark.*

**(f)** [2 marks]

- Each chlorine atom has **7 valence electrons** and needs **one more** to complete its outermost shell (1 mark).
- The two atoms each contribute one electron, forming a **shared pair** which is **attracted by both nuclei** - this is a single covalent bond (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Look for the idea of sharing (not transfer) and for both atoms reaching a complete outer shell. Do NOT accept ‘chlorine gives an electron to the other chlorine’.*

### Question 5 (12 marks)

**(a)** [5 marks]

- (i) Sodium - **2, 8, 1**
- (ii) Magnesium - mass number **24**
- (iii) Chlorine - atomic number **17**
- (iv) Chlorine - **17** electrons
- (v) Chlorine - **2, 8, 7**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for all FIVE blanks (5 marks). The blank number must be matched to the correct answer. In (ii) accept 24 from ‘12 protons + 12 neutrons’.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- (i) Magnesium is in **Period 3** (its electrons occupy 3 shells) - 1 mark.
- (ii) Sodium is in **Group 1** (it has 1 electron in its outermost shell) - 1 mark.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). Accept the reason drawn from the electron configuration: 2, 8, 2 has three shells; 2, 8, 1 has one outer electron. Do NOT accept Group 3 for magnesium.*

**(c)** [5 marks]

- (i) Neutrons = 39 − 19 = **20** (1 mark)
- (ii) Electron configuration = **2, 8, 8, 1** (1 mark)
- (iii) Valence electrons = **1** (1 mark)
- (iv) The charge on the ion is **+1** (1 mark)
- (iv) Reason: the atom has only **one electron in its outermost shell**, and it loses this electron easily to form a stable ion, K⁺ (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 5 marks: 1 mark each for (i), (ii) and (iii); in (iv) 1 mark for the charge and 1 mark for the reason. Do NOT accept −1 or +19.*

### Question 6 (13 marks)

**(a)** [10 marks]

- (i) Sodium atom: **1** valence electron; chlorine atom: **7** valence electrons (2 marks, 1 each).
- (ii) The sodium atom **loses (transfers) its single outermost electron** to the chlorine atom (1 mark); the chlorine atom **gains** this electron and now has a complete outer shell of 8 (1 mark); the **positive and negative ions formed are held together by their opposite charges** (1 mark).
- (iii) Sodium ion: **+1** (Na⁺); chloride ion: **−1** (Cl⁻) (2 marks, 1 each).
- (iv) Type of bond: **ionic (electrovalent) bond** (1 mark); formula: **NaCl** (1 mark).
- (v) Any one of: flavouring food; preserving meat and fish (salting); oral rehydration salt (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 10 marks in all, marked against the brackets shown in the question. In (ii) award the third mark only for the idea that the ions are held together by their opposite charges. In (v) do NOT accept ‘it is used for cooking’ alone without a use such as flavouring.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- The compound is **magnesium chloride** (1 mark).
- A magnesium atom (2, 8, 2) **loses 2 outermost electrons** to form **Mg²⁺**, while **each** chlorine atom gains 1 electron to form **Cl⁻** (1 mark).
- **Two** chlorine atoms are therefore needed for every magnesium atom, giving the formula **MgCl₂** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. The last mark requires the formula MgCl₂ WITH the 1 : 2 ratio explained. Do NOT accept MgCl or Mg₂Cl.*

The periodic-table items are traced to the content standard itself. |

| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, a shell-diagram question, a table for pupils to complete and a design/reasoning question. |
| Sufficient application and reasoning | Yes - 40 of 100 marks (40%) at Apply level or above (Apply 33, Analyse 7). The high Apply weighting matches the indicators themselves, which require pupils to use atomic and mass numbers and work out formulae. |
| Plausible MCQ distractors | Yes - drawn from the same content family as the key: the mass number given as the number of neutrons, the nucleus said to contain electrons, and confusion among the symbols K, Ca, Cl and Cu. |

| Marking scheme matches questions | Yes - expected answers plus marking notes covering partial credit, accepted alternatives, common wrong answers and method marks in the calculations. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - open items are anchored with ‘state two’, ‘give one’ and the mark allocation; Question 5(a) numbers every blank (i) to (v); Question 6 gives the proton, neutron and electron numbers in a table so that no item depends on memory of the Periodic Table. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - table salt and the salting of fish and meat, oral rehydration salt (ORS), and familiar school-laboratory apparatus; the potassium and sulfur examples follow the food and farming context of the syllabus. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - isotope ideas were deliberately left out because they are not named in the three indicators supplied; only the atom, sub-atomic particles, atomic and mass numbers, electron configuration, ions, molecules and the Periodic Table as a chart are examined. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - naming particles, completing a charge/location table, calculations, diagram interpretation, completing a data table, explaining ion formation, writing formulae, naming bonds and explaining a use. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand has ONE content standard (B8/JHS2.1.1.2) carried by three indicators, so every blueprint row shows both the standard and the indicator that applies to it; the periodic-table rows are traced to the content standard itself, since the table is named there and not in the indicators.
- Isotopes were deliberately excluded: the earlier draft had an isotope sub-question in Question 2, but isotopes are not named in the indicators supplied by the school, so the item was removed and Question 2 now totals 6 marks. Add it back only if your scheme of work covers it.
- Use the 2, 8, 8 rule for the first twenty elements. Potassium (Z = 19) is the highest element examined, so pupils are never asked for configurations beyond what the rule supports.
- Question 5(a) turns the atomic data into a completion table with five numbered blanks, (i) to (v), so marking is quick and fair: 1 mark each, and the blank number must be matched to the answer.
- Question 6 is the ionic-bond question. Award method marks in (b): the formula MgCl₂ earns its mark only when the 1 : 2 ratio is explained from the charges.
- The figure in Question 3 is a hand-drawn sketch of two shell diagrams, matching the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Accept the correct chemical symbols written without subscripts as long as the intended formula is clear (for example CO2 for CO₂, H2 for H₂).
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) In explanations, award method marks for correct reasoning even if the wording differs from the scheme. (4) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required.)*

### Question 1 (8 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- A cell is the **basic (smallest) unit of all living things**.
- **All living things are made up of one or more cells.**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks). Award 1 mark for ‘the smallest part of a living thing’ if the idea of a unit of life is present. Do NOT accept ‘a small thing’ on its own.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) Nucleus - **controls all the activities of the cell** (and contains the genetic material).
- (ii) Cell membrane - **controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell**.
- (iii) Cytoplasm - the **living material** in which the other organelles are found; most cell activities take place there.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (3 marks). The function must be matched to the correct part; a correct statement attached to the wrong part earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Chloroplast** (accept ‘chloroplasts’)
- (ii) **Cell wall**
- (iii) **Vacuole** (accept ‘large central vacuole’)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (3 marks). Do NOT accept ‘cell membrane’ for (ii) or ‘cytoplasm’ for (iii).*

### Question 2 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Chloroplasts**
- **Cell wall**
- **Large central vacuole** (accept ‘large vacuole’)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE (3 marks). Accept ‘plastids’ for chloroplasts. Do NOT accept nucleus, cytoplasm or cell membrane - these are found in both cells.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- **Centriole** (accept ‘small vacuoles’ or ‘centrosome’)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Do NOT accept ‘mitochondria’, which are found in both cells.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Both have a **cell membrane** and **cytoplasm**.
- Both have a **nucleus** and other organelles such as mitochondria and ribosomes.
- Both are **living** and carry out life processes such as respiration.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct similarities (2 marks). The similarity must be true of BOTH cells; a difference given as a similarity earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- It **stores cell sap** (water with dissolved sugars and salts).
- It helps to **keep the cell firm (turgid)** and therefore gives the plant support.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct functions (2 marks). Do NOT accept ‘it makes food’ - that is the work of chloroplasts.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- I - **cell wall**
- II - **cell membrane**
- III - **cytoplasm** (accept ‘cytoplasm with ribosomes’)
- IV - **nuclear material** (accept ‘DNA’, ‘loop of DNA’, ‘genetic material’)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). The label must be matched to the correct part. Do NOT accept ‘nucleus’ for IV - a prokaryotic cell has no true nucleus.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- I (cell wall): **gives the cell its fixed shape** and **protects** the cell (1 mark).
- II (cell membrane): **controls the movement of substances** into and out of the cell (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The function must be matched to the correct label.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- **Prokaryotic organisms** (accept ‘prokaryotes’)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for the correct group.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- A bacterial cell has **no true nucleus** - its genetic material lies loose in the cytoplasm.
- It has **no membrane-bound organelles** such as mitochondria and chloroplasts.
- It has **no chloroplasts and no large central vacuole**, and some bacteria have a capsule and flagellum.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct differences (3 marks). Accept ‘it is much smaller’ or ‘it is unicellular’ paired with a structural difference, but do not award a mark for size or ‘unicellular’ alone.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- V - **nucleus**
- VI - **chloroplast**
- VII - **mitochondrion**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (3 marks). Do NOT accept ‘cell’ for V or ‘vacuole’ for VII.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- The chloroplast **traps light energy** (through chlorophyll) and uses it to **make food** during photosynthesis.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for either point, or for ‘it makes food for the plant by photosynthesis’.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- It has a **true nucleus** enclosed by a **nuclear membrane** (1 mark).
- It has **membrane-bound organelles** such as mitochondria, chloroplasts and a vacuole (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept ‘it has a nucleus’ for the first mark only if the enclosed/true nucleus idea is clear.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Plants **make their own food** by photosynthesis, and the chloroplast (with chlorophyll) is needed to **trap light energy** (1 mark).
- Animals **feed on ready-made food**, so they have no need for chloroplasts (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The answer must contrast how plants and animals obtain food.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- **Water enters the cell** (through the partially permeable membrane) and the cell becomes **firm and swollen (turgid)** (1 mark).
- Explanation: water moves from where it is in plenty into the cell, and the **strong cell wall prevents the cell from bursting** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept ‘the vacuole fills up with water and pushes on the cell wall’ as the explanation. Do NOT accept ‘the cell bursts’ for a plant cell.*

### Question 5 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A **prokaryotic cell** is a cell with **no true nucleus**: its genetic material lies loose in the cytoplasm (1 mark), and it has **no membrane-bound organelles** (1 mark).
- A **eukaryotic cell** has a **true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane** (1 mark) and **membrane-bound organelles** such as mitochondria and chloroplasts (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 4 marks, 1 mark for each of the four ideas. Accept ‘a bacterium is prokaryotic’ for one mark only if the structural idea is given as well.*

**(b)** [6 marks]

- **Prokaryotic cell:** a bacterium; a blue-green alga.
- **Eukaryotic cell:** Amoeba; a mushroom; a human cheek cell; a maize leaf cell.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for each organism placed in the correct column (6 marks). The columns must be correct: a bacterium and a blue-green alga are the ONLY prokaryotic organisms listed. Do NOT award a mark for an organism placed in the wrong column.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- A prokaryotic cell has **no true nucleus**; a eukaryotic cell has a **true nucleus**.
- A prokaryotic cell has **no membrane-bound organelles**; a eukaryotic cell has **membrane-bound organelles**.
- Prokaryotes are usually **unicellular** small cells; eukaryotes may be unicellular or multicellular and are larger.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct differences (2 marks). The difference must be stated as a comparison.*

### Question 6 (6 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- Any two of: **cholera, tuberculosis, typhoid fever, tetanus, whooping cough, leprosy** (also accept ‘boils’ or ‘food poisoning’).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct diseases (2 marks). Do NOT accept malaria, measles or sleeping sickness - these are not caused by bacteria.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Wash your hands with soap** under running water, especially before eating and after visiting the toilet.
- **Boil drinking water** (or treat it) and **cover food** to keep flies away.
- **Keep the surroundings clean**, use a toilet properly and bury or dispose of waste well.
- **Cook food well** and wash fruits and vegetables before eating them.
- **Visit the hospital** for treatment when you are sick so that you do not spread the disease.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE sensible measures (3 marks). The measure must really prevent the spread of bacterial disease. Do NOT accept ‘take medicine every day’ without a reason, or ‘stay away from people’ on its own.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- Bacteria are useful in **fermenting milk into yoghurt** (also accept: fermenting maize dough for kenkey; making cheese; producing some medicines; helping to decompose waste to form manure).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one correct use. Do NOT accept ‘they are used for food’ on its own.*

### Question 7 (6 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Prokaryotic organisms** - made up of cells with **no true nucleus**.
- **Eukaryotic organisms** - made up of cells with a **true nucleus**.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for naming the two groups and 1 mark for a correct description of at least one of them. Accept ‘prokaryotes and eukaryotes’.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Observe and list** the organisms (or pictures of them) to be studied.
- Look at the **type of cell** each organism is made of (with a microscope or from charts), **record the results in a table**, and place each organism in the correct group.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sensible steps (2 marks). Look for observing, recording in a table, and using the cell type as the criterion.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- A plant cell has a **cell wall**, **cell membrane** and **cytoplasm**.
- It also has a **nucleus**, **chloroplasts** and a **large central vacuole**.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for any three correctly named parts, 1 mark for the remaining parts. Do NOT award a mark for parts that belong to animal cells only.*

## QUALITY-CONTROL SUMMARY

| Check | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Every question within supplied curriculum scope | Yes - all items fall under Strand 1, Sub-Strand 2 (Living Cells), Content Standard B8/JHS2.1.2.1, mapped to the two indicators quoted from the NaCCA curriculum: examine and describe the structure of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells (B8/JHS2.1.2.1.1); and classify organisms as prokaryotic or eukaryotic based on the type of cells they are made of (B8/JHS2.1.2.1.2). |
| Appropriate for the class | Yes - B8 level; pupils name parts and functions, compare cells and classify organisms. No organelle biochemistry, no cell division detail and no membrane transport terminology beyond ‘water enters the cell’ and ‘partially permeable’. |
| Content outside the standard deliberately excluded | Yes - an earlier draft carried eight items on large molecules (macromolecules, monomers, carbohydrates and proteins). These were removed because the NaCCA curriculum places food nutrients under a different strand and they do not appear in content standard B8/JHS2.1.2.1; they were replaced with items on cell structure, cell classification and the health impact of micro-organisms. |
| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, two cell diagrams, a classification table for pupils to complete and a safety-measures question. |
| Sufficient application and reasoning | Yes - 30 of 100 marks (30%) at Apply level or above (Apply 23, Analyse 7, Evaluate 3). |
| Plausible MCQ distractors | Yes - drawn from the same content family as the key: parts that belong to the other cell type, organisms of the other cell group, and diseases that are not caused by bacteria. |
| Single best answer per MCQ | Yes - reviewed item by item; special care with A7 (centriole is the animal-cell part), A31 (mitochondria are absent from prokaryotic cells) and A38 (only the maize plant and mushroom pair have cell walls and a true nucleus). |
| Marks internally consistent | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40; Section B 8 + 8 + 10 + 10 + 12 + 6 + 6 = 60; every sub-question total matches the marking scheme. |
| Total adds up correctly | Yes - 40 + 60 = 100. |
| Answer key correct | Yes - all 40 keys verified item by item against the paper; biological facts re-checked: cell wall/cellulose, chloroplast/chlorophyll, centriole in animal cells, prokaryotes = bacteria and blue-green algae, eukaryotes = Amoeba, fungi, plants and animals. |
| Marking scheme matches questions | Yes - expected answers plus marking notes covering partial credit, accepted alternatives and common wrong answers. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - open items are anchored with ‘name three’, ‘state two’ and the mark allocation; Question 5(b) fixes the six organisms to be classified so that no item depends on an open list. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - maize, cassava dough (kenkey), yoghurt from fermented milk, onion skin for the microscope, hospital treatment and community hygiene; the organisms named are those pupils meet in the syllabus. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - naming parts, stating functions, classifying into a table, diagram interpretation, comparing two cell types, explaining osmosis in a plant cell, naming diseases and evaluating safety measures. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand has ONE content standard (B8/JHS2.1.2.1) carried by two indicators, so every blueprint row shows both the standard and the indicator that applies to it.
- Use the school's own coding side by side with the NaCCA coding: the paper prints B8/JHS2.1.2.1 (NaCCA 2021, Basic 8, page 56); the school's content-standard sheets use the shorter form B8.1.x.x.
- The eight macromolecule items that appeared in the first draft were withdrawn: the NaCCA curriculum places food nutrients in a different strand, so they fall outside this content standard. Do not re-insert them unless your scheme of work covers that strand.
- Question 5(b) is a classification task with a fixed list of six organisms, so marking is quick and fair: 1 mark each, and the organism must be in the correct column.
- Question 6(b) is an evaluation task, so award method marks: any sensible hygiene measure that really prevents bacterial disease earns credit. Listen for the reason as well as the measure.
- In Question 4(e) the expected answer is that a plant cell becomes firm and turgid, NOT that it bursts - the cell wall prevents bursting. This is a common pupil error and worth teaching before the examination.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, matching the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.
