## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) In explanations, award method marks for correct reasoning even if the wording differs from the scheme. (4) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required.)*

### Question 1 (8 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- The carbon cycle is the **continuous movement (circulation) of carbon** between the air, living things, the soil and **back to the air again**.
- Carbon passes from carbon (IV) oxide in the air into green plants, then to animals, and back into the air, repeatedly.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks). Award 1 mark for ‘carbon moving round and round’ if the idea of movement between air and living things is present. Do NOT accept ‘the cycle of carbon’ alone.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Photosynthesis**
- **Respiration**
- **Burning** (combustion)
- **Decay** (decomposition)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for all FOUR processes (4 marks). Accept ‘combustion’ for burning and ‘decomposition’ for decay. Do NOT accept ‘eating’ or ‘food chain’ as one of the four processes.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The **same carbon atoms are used again and again** - carbon is not destroyed or used up at any stage.
- The **processes repeat themselves over and over** in nature (carbon returns to the air and is taken up again).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct reasons (2 marks). Accept ‘it goes round and round’ only when the idea of repetition or of reuse is stated.*

### Question 2 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Carbon (IV) oxide** (carbon dioxide)
- **Water**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). Do NOT accept oxygen or sunlight, which are needed but are not raw materials taken in by the plant.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- **Oxygen**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for oxygen.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The plant uses the carbon (IV) oxide with water to **make food (carbohydrates)** (1 mark).
- The **carbon becomes part of the plant's body** - it is stored in the food made, and oxygen is given out (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept ‘the carbon is trapped in the plant’ or ‘the carbon changes into food’. Do NOT accept ‘the carbon disappears’.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The carbon taken from the air is stored in the **food made by the plant** (1 mark).
- When the goat **eats the plant**, the food passes into the goat, so the carbon becomes part of the **goat's body** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Look for the idea that the carbon is in the food the plant made, and that eating transfers it to the animal.*

**(e)** [1 marks]

- It **produces food** for the plant and for animals (including humans), and it **gives out oxygen** for living things to breathe.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for either point, or for both.*

**(f)** [2 marks]

- **Little or no food** will be made (1 mark).
- Reason: there is **no light** in the cupboard, and light is needed for photosynthesis (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark for the correct prediction and 1 mark for the reason. Accept ‘the plant will use up the food it has stored and may die’ as the reason if light is named.*

### Question 3 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- Respiration is the process by which living things **obtain energy from food**.
- It uses **oxygen** and gives out **carbon (IV) oxide** (and water) - it happens in all living cells, day and night.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks). Award 1 mark for ‘getting energy from food’ on its own; do NOT accept ‘breathing’ without the idea of energy from food.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Photosynthesis **takes in carbon (IV) oxide** and gives out oxygen; respiration **takes in oxygen** and gives out carbon (IV) oxide.
- Photosynthesis **needs light** and takes place only in **green plants**; respiration takes place in **all living things**, in light or in darkness, day and night.
- Photosynthesis **stores energy** in food; respiration **releases energy** from food.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks each for any TWO correct differences (4 marks): 1 mark for each half of the comparison. Do NOT award a mark for a difference that describes only one process without contrasting it with the other.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any two of: **firewood (wood), charcoal, kerosene, petrol, diesel, natural gas (LPG)**, dry grass, crop residue or household refuse.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct fuels (2 marks). Accept any fuel really burnt in Ghana.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- It **adds a lot of carbon (IV) oxide** to the air (and destroys useful plants, soil organisms and the nutrients in the soil).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one correct reason. Do NOT accept ‘it is bad’ or ‘it can burn the farm’ on its own.*

### Question 4 (6 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Bacteria**
- **Fungi** (moulds, mushrooms, yeast)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). Do NOT accept insects or earthworms as the main groups, although they help to break up the material.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Any two of: **carbon (IV) oxide, methane**, water vapour (also accept ‘heat’ as energy given out).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct gases (2 marks). Do NOT accept oxygen or nitrogen - these are not given out during decay.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Dead plants and animals would **pile up (not decay)** in the environment (1 mark).
- The **carbon trapped in their bodies would not return to the air**, so less carbon (IV) oxide would be added to the air and **the carbon cycle would not continue** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Look for both the pile-up of dead matter and the break in the cycle.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- a - **photosynthesis**
- b - **respiration**
- c - **burning** (combustion)
- d - **decay** (decomposition)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). The process must be matched to the correct letter. Do NOT accept ‘breathing’ for b.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- e - **feeding** (the animals eat the green plants)
- f - **decay** (decomposition) of dead plants and animals in the soil
- g - **burning of fossil fuels** (combustion)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (3 marks). Accept ‘feeding’ or ‘eating’ for e, and ‘combustion of fossil fuels’ for g.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The group is **fossil fuels** (coal, crude oil and natural gas) (1 mark).
- Use: they **burn to give energy** - for cooking, for vehicles (petrol and diesel), for generating electricity, and in industry (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the name of the group, 1 mark for any correct use.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- Because **photosynthesis takes carbon (IV) oxide out of the air** and uses the carbon to make food, so the amount of the gas in the air is reduced.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. The answer must say that the gas is taken from the air and used to make food.*

### Question 6 (7 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- The **maize plant**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Do NOT accept ‘the rat’ or ‘the snake’.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Primary consumer - the **rat**
- Secondary consumer - the **snake**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). The two must be matched to the correct terms; a reversed answer earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The carbon is stored in the **body (flesh and other tissues) of the rat** (1 mark).
- When the snake **eats (feeds on) the rat**, the carbon passes into the snake's body (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept ‘the snake eats the rat, so it takes in the carbon that was in the rat’ for full marks if the idea of eating is clear.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Bacteria and fungi (decomposers)** break down the body of the dead snake (1 mark).
- Carbon (IV) oxide is **given out during the decay** and released into the air, so the carbon returns to the air (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The two ideas required are the decomposers doing the breaking down and the carbon returning to the air as carbon (IV) oxide.*

### Question 7 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- The greenhouse effect is the **trapping (holding) of heat** from the sun by gases in the air.
- This heat is kept near the **earth's surface**, so the earth stays warm enough for life.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks). Award 1 mark for ‘gases trap heat’ on its own; do NOT accept ‘the earth is hot’.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Too much carbon (IV) oxide **traps too much heat** in the atmosphere (1 mark).
- The earth therefore becomes **warmer than normal (global warming)**, which changes the climate (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The chain of reasoning (more gas - more heat trapped - earth warms) must be present for both marks.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- Green plants **remove carbon (IV) oxide** from the air and **give out oxygen** during photosynthesis (1 mark).
- Respiration in living things, burning and decay **add carbon (IV) oxide** to the air and use up oxygen (1 mark).
- Because the two sets of processes **go on at the same time**, the gases that are removed are replaced (1 mark).
- This keeps the amounts of carbon (IV) oxide and oxygen in the air **fairly constant (balanced)**, which keeps life on earth going (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 4 marks, 1 mark each. Award marks for the pairs of processes named and for the idea of balance. A candidate who names only one side of the cycle earns a maximum of 2 marks.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Suggestion:** planting trees and keeping them on the farm (agroforestry), or using an improved (LPG) cooker instead of firewood, or **composting crop waste instead of burning it** (1 mark).
- **Benefit:** the trees remove carbon (IV) oxide from the air and give out oxygen - and they also give shade, fruit, fodder, firewood or extra income (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for a sensible suggestion, 1 mark for a real benefit. This is a design task, so award method marks for any practical suggestion that would genuinely reduce carbon (IV) oxide in the air.*

All four exemplars of the standard are used (stages of the cycle, a flow chart/diagram, the four processes, and the reasons why it is a repeated pattern). |

No chemical equations, no carbon sinks/sources terminology and no quantitative treatment of greenhouse gases are required. |

The reasoning load sits in the items that ask pupils to explain the balance of gases, to reason about a plant kept in the dark, and to judge the effect of burning a forest. |

| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the carbon cycle, its four processes and its role in the environment are exactly what the standard sets out; the greenhouse effect and global warming are named in exemplar 3 of indicator B8/JHS2.2.1.1.2 (the relationship between greenhouse gases and the carbon cycle). |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand has ONE content standard (B8/JHS2.2.1.1) carried by two indicators, so every blueprint row shows both the standard and the indicator that applies to it.
- The syllabus wording ‘Carbon (IV) oxide’ is used throughout, with ‘carbon dioxide’ accepted from candidates.
- Question 5 is the flow-chart/diagram exemplar (exemplar 2). Award the naming marks (a) and (b) only when the process is matched to the correct letter on Fig. 1.
- Question 7(c) is the balance-of-gases item from exemplar 1 of indicator B8/JHS2.2.1.1.2 and carries the heaviest reasoning load in the paper; expect pupils to name both sides of the cycle (removal by photosynthesis; addition by respiration, burning and decay) before the balance idea.
- Question 7(d) is a design task, so award method marks: any practical suggestion that really reduces carbon (IV) oxide (tree planting, composting instead of burning, using LPG, improved cookstoves) earns the first mark, with the second mark for a real benefit.
- Do not expect chemical equations or percentages of gases in the air; the strand is about the process and its role in the environment, not about quantitative chemistry.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, matching the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers (their flow charts for exemplar 2 can be drawn the same way); redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) For procedures and design tasks, award method marks. (4) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required.)*

### Question 1 (8 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- A vector is an **organism (insect or other animal) that carries a disease-causing organism** from one host to another.
- The vector itself may not become sick; it only carries the germ to the person or animal it bites.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks). Award 1 mark for ‘an insect that carries disease’ if it is not developed further. Do NOT accept ‘an animal that causes disease’ on its own - the vector carries the germ, it does not make the germ.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Egg**
- **Larva** (wriggler)
- **Pupa**
- **Adult** (imago)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for all FOUR stages in the correct order (4 marks). The order must be correct for full marks; an order that puts the pupa before the larva earns a maximum of 2 marks and a comment.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Water:** the egg, the larva and the pupa
- **Land/air:** the adult mosquito
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for naming the water stages and 1 mark for the adult stage (2 marks). Accept ‘the young stages (egg, larva, pupa) live in water’.*

### Question 2 (9 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **eggs** (laid on the surface of water)
- (ii) **larva** (wriggler)
- (iii) **pupa**
- (iv) **adult mosquito**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). The stage must be matched to the correct number. Accept ‘wriggler’ for (ii) and ‘imago’ for (iv).*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- **Complete metamorphosis**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Do NOT accept ‘incomplete metamorphosis’ or ‘metamorphosis’ alone.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The **larva lives in water** and has **no wings**; the **adult lives on land** and **has wings**.
- The larva **breathes through a tube** at the water surface and feeds on tiny water plants or animals; the adult feeds on **nectar (male) or blood (female)**.
- The larva **crawls (wriggles)** while the adult **flies**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct differences (2 marks). The difference must be a comparison between (ii) and (iv); a statement about only one of them earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The **young stages (egg, larva and pupa) can only develop in water** - they need water to live (1 mark).
- The larva and pupa **breathe air at the surface** of the water, so the eggs must be laid where there is water (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept ‘the young ones cannot live outside water’ for the first mark and ‘they need water to breathe and grow’ for the second.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- I - **proboscis**
- II - **antenna** (antennae)
- III - **wings**
- IV - **abdomen**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). The label must be matched to the correct part. Do NOT accept ‘nose’ for I or ‘tail’ for IV.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- The proboscis **pierces the skin** and is used for **sucking blood** (1 mark).
- In the female Anopheles it also **passes the plasmodium (the malaria germ) into the blood** of the person she bites (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Award the first mark for piercing/sucking; the second mark is for the link with malaria. Accept ‘it is the mouth part of the mosquito’ only with piercing or sucking.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Only the **female bites human beings and takes blood** (1 mark).
- She needs the blood for the **development of her eggs**, and the **plasmodium in her body is passed into the person's blood** when she bites (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Do NOT award a mark for ‘the male has no proboscis’ - that statement is wrong.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- It rests with its **body at an angle (sloping) to the surface**, not flat on it.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. The key idea is the angled (tilted) resting posture; accept a correct drawing that shows the tilted body.*

**(e)** [1 marks]

- The **adult has wings and flies (lives on land)**; the larva has **no wings, lives in water and crawls**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one correct difference. Do NOT accept ‘the adult is bigger’ on its own.*

### Question 4 (12 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- The **economic importance** of an organism is the way it **affects people's money, work and wealth** (whether it helps or harms them).
- It is the **value** of the organism to humans: what it costs or gives in money, work and health, and to farming and industry.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks). Award 1 mark for ‘how it is useful or harmful to people’. Do NOT accept ‘how many there are’.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Mosquito **larvae and adults are food** for fishes, birds, bats and other animals in the **food chain**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for each correct point, maximum 2 marks. Accept ‘they are part of the food chain’ with an example. Do NOT accept ‘they make honey’ or ‘they add nutrients to the soil’.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- They **spread malaria** (the female Anopheles carries the plasmodium).
- Their **bites are painful and disturb sleep**, and they are a **nuisance** at home.
- Time and money are **lost through sickness and treatment** - people miss work, school and farming.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct points (3 marks). Do NOT accept ‘they are bad’ or ‘they bite’ without a stated harm.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- The pupil **stays away from school** while sick, so lessons are **missed** (1 mark).
- Weakness and fever make **concentration hard**, so performance in class and in examinations **falls** (1 mark).
- Money is spent on **treatment and medicine** instead of on school needs such as books or fees; repeated sickness may even make the pupil **drop out** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each for any three sound points. Look for the loss of lessons, the effect on performance, and the cost or drop-out risk.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- **Workers and farmers stay away from work and farms**, so less is produced and national income falls.
- **Large sums are spent on treating and preventing the disease** (drugs, nets, hospital care), money that could build schools, roads and hospitals.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks). The answer must name an effect on work, production or money.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- The stages found in water are the **egg, the larva and the pupa** (1 mark).
- They are **concentrated in the water** and **cannot fly away**, so they can be killed or poured away easily - unlike the adult mosquitoes that fly about (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept ‘the young stages live in water’ for the first mark.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Drain or pour away stagnant water** and fill up the hollows where water collects.
- **Cover all water storage containers** (barrels, pots, tanks) so that mosquitoes cannot lay eggs in them.
- **Clear the bushes and weeds** around the house, and **cut the grass** short.
- **Spray the rooms with insecticide** (or use mosquito coils) and fix **wire mesh** on the windows.
- **Sleep under a treated mosquito net**, and visit the hospital early when you feel feverish.
- Put **fishes (such as tilapia)** in ponds and wells to eat the larvae.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR correct methods (4 marks). Accept any practical method really used in Ghana. Do NOT accept ‘praying’, ‘drinking herbal medicine’ or ‘taking malaria drugs regularly’ as control methods - the last one is treatment, not control.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Certain **fishes (for example tilapia) are put into the pond** and they **feed on the mosquito larvae and pupae** in the water (1 mark).
- This reduces the number of larvae that develop into adult mosquitoes, so fewer mosquitoes bite people (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The method is called **biological control**; accept the term with the correct explanation.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Prevention is **cheaper and safer** than cure - treating malaria costs money and the illness can become serious, causing **death or long absence from work and school** (1 mark).
- When mosquitoes are controlled, **the whole family stays healthy**, so no money or time is lost; the measures (net, clearing water, spraying) protect everyone, not only the sick person (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each for any two sound points. Accept ‘prevention is better than cure because you do not fall sick at all’ if supported with a reason such as cost, time lost or danger of death.*

### Question 6 (11 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Walk round** the school compound and the nearby houses **looking for water that is standing still** (drains, pits, open barrels, wells, old tyres, bottles, broken pots).
- **Check each place carefully** (using a spoon or a small net) to see whether there are **wrigglers (larvae) or pupae** in the water.
- **Record the findings** in a table or a map of the compound: where the water is, what container holds it, and whether young mosquitoes were found.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE sensible steps (3 marks). This is a design task, so award method marks for any practical step that would really find breeding sites. Look for searching for standing water, confirming the presence of the young stages, and recording.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Collect eggs or wrigglers** from a pond or gutter with a little water, put them in a **glass jar** and cover the jar with a piece of cloth (to keep the adults in).
- **Observe the jar every day**, and **draw and label** each stage as it appears (egg, larva, pupa, adult), recording the changes in a table with dates.
- Alternatively, **draw and label the four stages on a chart** and arrange them in a circle with arrows to show the cycle, and present it to the class.
  - *Marking note: 3 marks: 1 mark for the breeding/observation method, 1 mark for drawing and labelling each stage, 1 mark for recording or presenting the cycle in order. Accept a correctly labelled flow chart as evidence.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- A **drawing of the four stages** of the life cycle with their names.
- The **breeding places** (stagnant water, open barrels, old tyres, drains) shown crossed out or marked with a big X.
- The **control methods** in pictures: pouring away water, covering containers, sleeping under a net, spraying, clearing bushes.
- A **short clear message and a title** (for example: “No stagnant water, no mosquitoes, no malaria!”).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE sensible features (3 marks). This is a design task, so award method marks for any feature that would really teach someone how to control mosquitoes.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Cover the breeding jar always** so that adult mosquitoes cannot escape and bite the class.
- **Wash hands with soap after handling pond water** or the young stages, and **do not drink or taste** the water; wear a long-sleeved shirt when going round the compound.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sensible precautions (2 marks). The key idea is protection from bites and from dirty water. Do NOT accept ‘do not fall in the water’ on its own.*

## QUALITY-CONTROL SUMMARY

| Check | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Every question within supplied curriculum scope | Yes - all items fall under Strand 2, Sub-Strand 2 (Life Cycle of Organisms), Content Standard B8/JHS2.2.2.1, mapped to the two indicators quoted from the curriculum: describe the life cycle and economic importance of the Anopheles mosquito (B8/JHS2.2.2.1.1); and discuss the impact of the Anopheles mosquito on humans and how it can be controlled (B8/JHS2.2.2.1.2). All four exemplars are used: observing/drawing the stages (breeding in a jar), the economic importance, the female Anopheles as a vector of plasmodium, and generating solutions to control malaria in Ghana. |
| Appropriate for the class | Yes - B8 level; pupils describe and draw the stages, identify parts of the adult, and discuss the control of malaria in simple, practical terms. The biology of the plasmodium life cycle inside the human body (liver and blood stages) is NOT examined, because it sits outside this indicator. |
| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, two diagram questions (life cycle and parts of the adult), and design tasks (breeding the mosquito and a community poster). |
| Sufficient application and reasoning | Yes - 28 of 100 marks (28%) at Apply level or above (Apply 12, Analyse 9, Evaluate 5, Create 2). The reasoning load sits in the items on why the female transmits malaria, why water stages are easier to control, and why prevention is better than treatment. |
| Plausible MCQ distractors | Yes - drawn from the same content family as the key: the other disease, the wrong causal organism, the wrong stage of the life cycle, and insects that undergo incomplete metamorphosis. |
| Single best answer per MCQ | Yes - reviewed item by item; special care with A11 (maggot is the housefly larva, not a mosquito stage), A30 (the housefly is the complete-metamorphosis insect; grasshoppers and cockroaches are not) and A36 (only the female Anopheles spreads malaria). |
| Marks internally consistent | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40; Section B 8 + 9 + 10 + 12 + 10 + 11 = 60; every sub-question total matches the marking scheme. |
| Total adds up correctly | Yes - 40 + 60 = 100. |
| Answer key correct | Yes - all 40 keys verified item by item against the paper; the science re-checked: the female Anopheles lays eggs singly on water, the larva is the wriggler, the pupa does not feed, the adult emerges from the pupa, Anopheles rests at an angle to the surface, and plasmodium is the cause of malaria. |
| Marking scheme matches questions | Yes - expected answers plus marking notes covering partial credit, accepted alternatives and common wrong answers (including ‘the male has no proboscis’ and ‘taking malaria drugs’ as a control method). |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - open items are anchored with ‘name four’, ‘state two’ and the mark allocation; the life-cycle figure numbers its stages (i) to (iv) and the adult figure labels its parts I to IV, and both are repeated in the questions. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - treated mosquito nets, mosquito coils, insecticide spraying, open barrels and old tyres in compounds, drains and gutters, maize and cocoa farm work, school attendance, hospital treatment costs and ‘no stagnant water, no malaria’ campaign messages. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the life cycle, the parts of the adult, the economic importance and the control of malaria are exactly what the standard sets out; the teacher-level detail of the plasmodium life cycle in humans and the difference between the four species of plasmodium are excluded. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - recalling stages, matching stages to a diagram, naming parts, reasoning about metamorphosis and breeding, classifying control methods, evaluating prevention against treatment, and designing a breeding demonstration and a community poster. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand has ONE content standard (B8/JHS2.2.2.1) carried by two indicators, so every blueprint row shows both the standard and the indicator that applies to it.
- Question 2(a) and Question 3(a) mark the two figures: the stages are numbered (i) to (iv) on Fig. 1 and the adult parts are labelled I to IV on Fig. 2. Award the mark only when the name is matched to the correct number or letter.
- Question 6(b) is the activity exemplar (breeding the mosquito in a glass jar). If your class actually breeds the mosquito, accept what they did as evidence - a labelled set of drawings with dates is worth full marks.
- Question 6(c) is the ‘generate solutions to control malaria in Ghana’ exemplar. Award method marks for any practical feature on the poster; look first for the breeding places and the control methods.
- In Question 5(b) note carefully that **taking malaria drugs is treatment, not control**. Do not award a control mark for it, although ‘visiting the hospital early’ is accepted under prompt treatment.
- The syllabus calls the larva a **wriggler**; the term is used in the paper and in the marking scheme. Accept ‘mosquito larva’ from candidates.
- Do not expect the pupils to know the names of the four species of Anopheles or the stages of plasmodium in the human body; the indicator is about the mosquito, its life cycle, its importance and its control.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, matching the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers (their drawings of the four stages count as the activity evidence); redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) For procedures, investigations and design tasks, award method marks. (4) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required.)*

### Question 1 (8 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- A seed bed is a **piece of land that has been prepared (cleared, dug, levelled)** for planting.
- The soil in it is made **loose and fine** so that seeds can germinate and the young roots can grow easily.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks). Award 1 mark for ‘land prepared for planting’ alone. Do NOT accept ‘a place where seeds are stored’.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Flat bed**
- **Raised bed**
- **Sunken bed**
- (Also accept: **nursery bed**, **ridges**, **mounds**)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct types (3 marks). Accept ridges and mounds, which are used in many farming communities in Ghana.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- To **loosen the soil** so that seeds germinate easily and roots can spread.
- To **remove weeds, stumps and stones** that would compete with the crops or obstruct the work.
- To **improve drainage and the movement of air** in the soil, and to **mix in manure** so the soil is more fertile.
- To make **planting, weeding and harvesting easier** for the farmer.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct reasons (3 marks). Do NOT accept ‘to make the farm beautiful’.*

### Question 2 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- A - **flat bed** (the soil is level with the surrounding ground)
- B - **raised bed** (the soil is heaped above the surrounding ground)
- C - **sunken bed** (the soil is dug below the surrounding ground)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (3 marks). The name must be matched to the correct letter. Accept ‘flat seed bed’, ‘raised seed bed’ and ‘sunken seed bed’.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **B - the raised bed** (1 mark).
- Because the bed stands above the ground, **excess water drains away** and the roots **get air instead of rotting** in the water (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the correct bed and 1 mark for the reason. If the bed named is wrong, no marks are awarded even if the reason is sound.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **C - the sunken bed** (1 mark).
- Because it lies below the ground it **holds water (and moisture) around the roots for a longer time**, which the crops need in dry weather (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the correct bed and 1 mark for the reason. Accept ‘it conserves moisture’ for the reason mark.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- It is **easy and quick to prepare** (little soil has to be moved), so a large area can be planted; it suits most crops on **well-drained land**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one correct advantage.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- The soil of **B is heaped above the ground** while the soil of **C is dug below the ground**.
- **B drains water away** from the crops, whereas **C holds water** around the crops.
- **B is used in wet or waterlogged places**, while **C is used in dry places**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct differences (2 marks). The answer must compare the two beds; a statement about only one of them earns no mark.*

### Question 3 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) Cassava - **stem cuttings**
- (ii) Maize - **seeds** (grains)
- (iii) Plantain - **suckers**
- (iv) Yam - **setts** (pieces cut from the tuber)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). Accept ‘stem’ for cassava, ‘grains’ for maize and ‘tuber pieces’ for yam. Do NOT accept ‘seeds’ for cassava, plantain or yam.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Transplanting is the **lifting of young seedlings from a nursery bed** (or seed box) (1 mark)
- and **planting them in the main field** or in their permanent position (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Award 1 mark only for ‘moving plants from one place to another’ without reference to the nursery or the main field.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Water the nursery bed before lifting** the seedlings, and lift them with **soil (a ball of earth) around the roots** so that the roots are not damaged.
- **Transplant in the evening or on a cool, cloudy day**, not in the hot sun.
- **Water the seedlings immediately after planting** and **provide shade** for a few days until they are established.
- **Firm the soil gently** around each seedling and keep the correct spacing.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct precautions (3 marks). Award method marks for any sensible practice that protects the seedling from damage or from drying up.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- Tomato **seeds are very small** and need **close attention** (watering, shade and protection from pests), which is easier on a small nursery bed (1 mark).
- The **weak seedlings can be sorted out** and only the **strong, healthy ones transplanted** (1 mark).
- The seedlings can be planted in the field at the **correct spacing**, and **seed is not wasted**; the main field is also free for other use while the seedlings grow (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each for any three sound reasons.*

### Question 4 (11 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- **18 cm**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. The unit must be given; award the mark for ‘18’ with cm.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- **Bed B**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Accept ‘B’.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Tallest = 26 cm (Bed B); shortest = 18 cm (Bed A) (1 mark)
- Difference = 26 cm - 18 cm = **8 cm** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the correct working (26 - 18) and 1 mark for the answer with the unit. Award full marks for a correct answer of 8 cm even if no working is shown.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- Bed B **drained better**, so the roots got **enough air** and did not rot (1 mark).
- The soil in Bed B was **deeper, looser and more fertile** (it may have had more manure), so the plants obtained more nutrients (1 mark).
- The **roots could spread more easily** in the loose soil and so took in more water and nutrients for growth (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each for any three sound reasons. Accept ‘fewer weeds competed with the crops on Bed B’.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- The **number of flowers** on each plant and the **number of fruits** produced.
- The **number of leaves**, the **thickness (girth) of the stem** or the **weight of the fruits harvested**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct measurements (2 marks). The curriculum names height, size, number of flowers and number of fruits. Do NOT accept ‘the colour of the plant’, which is not a measurement.*

**(f)** [2 marks]

- So that **other pupils, teachers and farmers in the community learn** which seed bed gives the best growth and can **use the findings** on their own farms.
- So that the work can be **checked, questioned and repeated** by others, which is how scientists share and confirm results.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sound reasons (2 marks). Accept ‘to practise explaining ideas clearly’, which is the communication aim of the exemplar.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- The **same crop (same variety of pepper)** and the **same number of plants** at the **same spacing**.
- The **same amount of water and manure**, and the **same sunlight and weather** for both beds.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks). Do NOT award a mark for ‘the type of seed bed’ - that is the thing being changed.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- The **type of seed bed** - one bed is raised and the other is flat.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. This is the only thing that may be different in a fair test.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Stand the **metre rule (or tape measure) upright beside the plant with the zero mark at the soil surface** (1 mark).
- **Read the mark at the tip of the plant** with the eye level with the reading, and **record the height in centimetres** in the table (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Award method marks for any correct, careful procedure; look for measuring from the soil level and reading correctly.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Plants do not all grow at the same rate**; a single plant may happen to be unusually tall or unusually short (1 mark).
- The **average of several plants is fairer and more reliable**, because it represents the whole bed and reduces the effect of one odd plant (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The key idea is the variation between plants and the reliability of the average.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- A table with the **weeks (1, 2, 3, 4) in the first column** (1 mark)
- and a **column for each bed** - average height on the raised bed (cm) and average height on the flat bed (cm), with the **units given in the headings** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. Award 1 mark for a ruled table with the time (weeks) as one heading and 1 mark for both beds shown with the unit (cm). A table drawn the other way round (beds as rows, weeks as columns) is equally correct. The table need not contain any readings.*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Clear the land**: cut down the weeds and remove the rubbish and stones from the piece of land.
- **Mark out the bed** with pegs and a line to the size required (for example 1 m by 3 m).
- **Dig and loosen the soil** inside the marked area with a hoe, removing roots and stumps, and **mix in manure or compost**.
- **Heap the soil above the level of the ground** to form the raised bed, then **level and firm the top** of the bed and water it before planting.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR sensible steps in a workable order (4 marks). This is a practical design task, so award method marks for any step that would really produce a raised bed. The heaping of the soil above the ground must appear somewhere in the answer for full marks.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Cutlass** - for **clearing the weeds and bushes** from the land.
- **Hoe** - for **digging, loosening and heaping up the soil** to form the bed.
- **Rake** - for **levelling the top of the bed** and removing stones and rubbish.
- **Watering can** - for **watering** the bed and the young plants.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for each tool correctly named WITH its use, maximum 2 marks. A tool named without a use earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Handle the cutlass and hoe carefully** and **stand well apart** while working so that nobody is struck.
- **Wear shoes or boots** (and gloves where possible), **do not play with the tools**, and **wash the hands with soap** after the work.
- **Report any cut or injury to the teacher at once**, and work in the cool of the morning or evening.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sensible precautions (2 marks). Accept any practical safety measure for garden work. Do NOT accept ‘be careful’ on its own.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Water the crops regularly**, especially in the dry season, and **mulch the bed** with dry grass to keep the soil moist.
- **Weed the bed regularly**, **apply manure or compost**, **control pests and diseases**, and **fence the garden** to keep goats and fowls out.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct practices (2 marks). Accept staking of tomato or pepper plants and thinning where it applies.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 2: Cycles | **Sub-strand:** 3: Crop Production | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.2.3.1** - Demonstrate knowledge and skills in planting crops on different seed beds. **B8/JHS2.2.3.2** - Demonstrate understanding of the differences in height, size, and flowering of crops grown in different seed beds.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 2: Cycles, Sub-Strand 3: Crop Production, Basic 8, pages 60-61, content standards B8/JHS2.2.3.1 and B8/JHS2.2.3.2. The indicators and their exemplars are quoted from the curriculum, not invented: observe and discuss different seed beds for planting different crops; list and compare the differences and similarities among seed beds in the community; match the types of seed beds with the types and stages of crops planted in the community; select different plant parts (seeds, seedlings, cuttings, leaves, roots) and plant them in different seed beds; measure the heights, sizes, number of flowers and number of fruits of plants grown in different seed beds; discuss the differences and similarities using tables and graphs; and write and give presentations on the reasons for the differences.

> Note: The NaCCA document prints these standards as 'B8/JHS2.2.3.1' and 'B8/JHS2.2.3.2'. The school's content-standard sheets use the shorter coded form (B8.2.3.1 and B8.2.3.2 for the same standards); both forms are given in the blueprint so that the paper matches your records and the curriculum document. This is the first sub-strand in the series with TWO content standards, so the blueprint carries a standard column as well as an indicator column.

Every exemplar is examined, including matching seed beds to crops, planting with seeds, seedlings, cuttings and suckers, measuring heights and numbers of flowers and fruits, using tables and graphs, and presenting the reasons for the differences. |

Soil chemistry, fertiliser formulations (NPK ratios) and crop rotation theory are NOT examined, since they sit outside this sub-strand. |
| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, two figure-based questions (a cross-section of three seed beds and a bar chart), a data-handling calculation, a fair-test design and a practical garden-planning task. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand carries TWO content standards. Questions 1 to 3 and the Section A items on beds and planting materials assess B8/JHS2.2.3.1; Questions 4 and 5 and the data items assess B8/JHS2.2.3.2. The blueprint shows which standard each item belongs to.
- Question 2 depends on Fig. 1: the beds are labelled A, B and C and the ground line is drawn in each bay. Award the mark only when the name is matched to the correct letter.
- Question 4 depends on Fig. 2. The value of each bar is printed above it, so no mark should be lost through difficulty in reading the scale; 4(c) must show 26 - 18 = 8 cm.
- Question 5 is the fair-test item. Watch for candidates who name the type of seed bed as something to keep the same in 5(a) - that is the variable being changed and earns no mark.
- Question 5(e) asks for headings only. A table drawn with the beds as rows and the weeks as columns is equally correct, and the table need not contain any readings.
- Question 6 is the practical exemplar. Award method marks generously for any workable step, but the heaping of soil above ground level must appear for full marks in 6(a), since that is what makes the bed a raised bed.
- Accept ridges and mounds as seed bed types in Question 1(b). They are widely used for yam and cassava in Ghanaian farming communities and fall within the exemplar on seed beds in the community.
- If your class actually planted crops on different beds and measured them, accept their own records and charts as evidence for Questions 4 and 5; this sub-strand is practical and the exemplars expect measuring, tabulating and presenting.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, matching the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) In calculations, award a method mark for correct working even where the final answer is wrong. (4) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- Animal feed is the **food given to farm animals** (1 mark)
- to keep them **alive, healthy and productive** - for growth, reproduction and the production of meat, milk and eggs (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Award 1 mark for ‘food given to farm animals’ alone. Do NOT accept ‘grass’ by itself.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) Cattle - **grass, forage, hay or silage**
- (ii) Laying hen - **layer mash**
- (iii) Pig - **pig grower mash or pellets** (accept kitchen and farm waste)
- (iv) Day-old chick - **chick mash (starter mash)**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). The feed must suit the animal AND its age. Do NOT accept ‘layer mash’ for a day-old chick or ‘silage’ for a chick.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Proteins**
- **Carbohydrates**
- **Fats and oils**
- **Mineral salts**
- **Vitamins** (also accept **water** and **roughage/fibre**)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct classes (3 marks). Do NOT accept named feedstuffs such as ‘maize’ or ‘fish meal’ here - those are sources, not classes of nutrients.*

### Question 2 (11 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- **Carbohydrate** (55 %)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Accept ‘carbohydrate’ with or without the percentage.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Protein = 22 % of 50 kg = (22 ÷ 100) x 50 (1 mark)
- = **11 kg** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 method mark for the correct working and 1 mark for the answer with the unit. Award the method mark even if the arithmetic is wrong. A bare correct answer of 11 kg scores both marks.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Chicks are growing rapidly**, and protein is the nutrient that **builds body tissues, muscles and feathers** (1 mark).
- **Adult birds have finished growing**, so they need mainly energy and maintenance feed and need a smaller proportion of protein (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The first mark is for linking protein to growth or body building; the second is for the comparison with adult birds.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- To check that the **proportions of nutrients suit the type and age** of his animals (for example starter mash for chicks).
- To **compare the quality and price** of different brands, and to check the **net mass** and the **expiry (or manufacturing) date** so that stale feed is not bought.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sound reasons (2 marks). This is the curriculum exemplar on selecting feed from the proportions shown on the label.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- **Mineral salts** - calcium and phosphorus (1 mark)
- used by a laying hen to form **strong egg shells** (also accept **strong bones**) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept ‘calcium’ for the nutrient mark. The egg-shell answer is the expected use for a laying hen.*

**(f)** [2 marks]

- To stop the feed from **taking up moisture and going mouldy** - mouldy feed can **poison the animals**.
- To **keep out rats, weevils and other pests**, and to **preserve the nutrients** so that the feed stays fresh until it is used.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct reasons (2 marks).*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) Protein - **builds and repairs body tissues**, for growth, muscle and the production of milk and eggs
- (ii) Carbohydrate - **supplies energy** for movement, work and warmth
- (iii) Mineral salts - **form strong bones, teeth and egg shells** and keep the blood healthy
- (iv) Vitamins - **protect the animal from diseases** and keep the body working properly
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). Accept any one correct use for each nutrient. Do NOT accept ‘it makes the animal strong’ for more than one of them.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- (i) Protein - **fish meal**, groundnut cake, soya bean meal or blood meal
- (ii) Carbohydrate - **maize**, cassava, rice bran, wheat bran or millet
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). Any one correct feedstuff per nutrient earns the mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Hay is dried** grass or fodder, while **silage is kept moist (green)**.
- Hay is **stored dry in a barn or stack**, while silage is **stored in a pit or silo where it ferments**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct differences (2 marks). The answer must compare the two; a statement about only one of them earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- A concentrate supplies a **high proportion of nutrients (especially protein) in a small quantity**, making up for what grass and forage lack.
- It makes the animals **grow faster and produce more meat, milk and eggs**, and keeps them healthier.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct reasons (2 marks).*

### Question 4 (12 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- **1000 g** (1 kg)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. The unit must be given. Accept 1 kg.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- **750 g**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. The unit must be given. Accept 0.75 kg.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Group P = 1500 g and Group Q = 750 g at the end of week 5 (1 mark)
- Difference = 1500 g - 750 g = **750 g** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 method mark for the subtraction and 1 mark for the answer with the unit. A bare correct answer of 750 g scores both marks.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- They **grew much more slowly** and gained far less mass than Group P (1 mark).
- Their growth **almost stopped (levelled off) after about week 3**, while Group P kept growing steadily (1 mark).
- Without enough water they **could not digest and absorb the feed properly**, so they would be weak, dull and unhealthy (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. At least one mark must come from the graph itself (slower growth, or the levelling off of the Group Q curve).*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- They would **stop growing and begin to lose mass**, stop feeding and become very weak, with sunken eyes and dry skin (1 mark).
- Within a few days the chicks would **die** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. This is the curriculum exemplar on predicting what happens to animals not provided with adequate water; death must appear for the second mark.*

**(f)** [2 marks]

- **Water is necessary for the proper growth of animals** (1 mark).
- Animals given **enough clean water grow much faster** than those given too little, **even when they are given the same feed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The conclusion must refer to water AND to growth. Do NOT accept ‘Group P is better than Group Q’, which merely restates the result.*

**(g)** [1 marks]

- The **type and quantity of feed** given to both groups (also accept the **breed, age and number of chicks** or the **housing and temperature**).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Do NOT award a mark for ‘the amount of water’ - that is the factor being changed.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- It **helps in the digestion** of food and softens the feed in the gut.
- It **dissolves nutrients and carries them round the body** in the blood.
- It helps to **control the body temperature** of the animal through sweating and panting.
- It forms a large part of the **blood, milk and body fluids**, and helps in **removing waste** from the body as urine.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR correct uses (4 marks). Do NOT award two marks for the same idea stated twice in different words.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Dry nose, muzzle and mouth**, with **sunken eyes** and a dull, rough coat.
- **Loss of appetite and loss of body mass**, with weakness and slow movement.
- **Little urine passed, and it is dark and strong-smelling**; the animals crowd round the trough whenever water is brought.
- A **fall in the production of milk or eggs**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct signs (3 marks). Accept any observable sign of dehydration.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Wash the drinking troughs daily** and **change the water regularly** (at least twice a day).
- **Place the troughs where droppings, dust and litter cannot fall in** (raise them slightly), and **cover the water storage tank**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO practical ways (2 marks).*

### Question 6 (9 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Give the right feed for the age of the birds** (starter mash first, then grower and finisher) at **fixed times each day**.
- **Measure out the correct quantity** of feed for the fifty birds, so that there is neither shortage nor waste.
- **Wash the drinkers and feeders** and **provide clean, fresh water at all times**, changing it at least twice a day.
- **Remove stale, wet or mouldy feed** and soiled litter, and **observe the birds**, reporting any that look sick or are not eating.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR sensible daily practices (4 marks). This is a practical design task, so award method marks. Water must be mentioned somewhere in the answer for full marks.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- The **quantity of feed used** each day or week and the **money spent** on it.
- The **body mass of the birds each week** (to check their growth), and the **number of birds that are alive, sick or dead**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO useful records (2 marks). Accept a record of sales or of vaccination dates.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Keep the bags in a **cool, dry, well-ventilated room** so that the feed does not absorb moisture and go mouldy.
- **Stack the bags on pallets or planks off the floor** and away from the wall, and **keep rats and insects out** of the store.
- **Use the oldest bags first** and check the expiry date; **never store feed together with insecticides, fertilisers or other chemicals**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct precautions (3 marks). Accept any sound storage practice that protects the feed from damp, pests or contamination.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 2: Cycles | **Sub-strand:** 4: Animal Production | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.2.4.1** - Recognise the different types of feed for different types of animals. **B8/JHS2.2.4.2** - Demonstrate understanding of the importance of water and animal feed to the growth of animals.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 2: Cycles, Sub-Strand 4: Animal Production, Basic 8, pages 62-63, content standards B8/JHS2.2.4.1 and B8/JHS2.2.4.2. The indicators and their exemplars are quoted from the curriculum, not invented: match the different types of feed with different types of animals; discuss the types of nutrients and their sources in the different types of animal feed; select and discuss appropriate feed for animals based on the proportions of nutrients indicated on the package or labels; list and discuss the usefulness of water and feed for the growth and reproduction of animals; and predict what will happen to animals who are not provided with adequate water.

## QUALITY-CONTROL SUMMARY

| Check | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Every question within supplied curriculum scope | Yes - all items fall under Strand 2, Sub-Strand 4 (Animal Production) and are mapped to the two content standards of the sub-strand: B8/JHS2.2.4.1 (recognise the different types of feed for different types of animals) through indicator B8/JHS2.2.4.1.1, and B8/JHS2.2.4.2 (importance of water and animal feed to growth) through indicator B8/JHS2.2.4.2.1. Every exemplar is examined, including matching feed with animals, discussing nutrients and their sources, selecting feed from the proportions shown on a label, discussing the usefulness of water and feed, and predicting what happens to animals not given adequate water. |
| Appropriate for the class | Yes - B8 level; pupils match feed to animals, read a feed label, interpret a growth graph and explain why water matters. Ruminant digestion (the four-chambered stomach), feed formulation by Pearson square and the chemistry of digestion are NOT examined, since they sit outside this sub-strand. |
| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, two figure-based questions (a feed-bag label and a growth graph), two calculations, a prediction item and a practical poultry-management task. |
| Sufficient application and reasoning | Yes - 33 of 100 marks (33%) at Apply level or above (Apply 13, Analyse 11, Evaluate 5, Create 4). The reasoning load sits in the percentage calculation, the interpretation of the two growth curves and the prediction in Question 4(e). |
| Plausible MCQ distractors | Yes - drawn from the same content family as the key: the feed meant for a different animal or a different age, the neighbouring nutrient (protein against carbohydrate against mineral), and hay against silage against concentrate. |
| Single best answer per MCQ | Yes - reviewed item by item; special care with A18 (only layer mash for a laying hen is correctly matched), A21 (22% of 50 kg is exactly 11 kg, not 2.2 kg) and A35 (in the water investigation the factor changed is the amount of water, not the feed). |
| Marks internally consistent | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40; Section B 9 + 11 + 10 + 12 + 9 + 9 = 60; every sub-question total matches the marking scheme. |
| Total adds up correctly | Yes - 40 + 60 = 100. |
| Answer key correct | Yes - all 40 keys verified item by item against the paper; the animal science re-checked: chick mash for young chicks and layer mash for laying hens, fish meal and groundnut cake as protein sources, maize and bran as energy sources, bone meal and oyster shell for calcium, hay as dried fodder and silage as fermented green fodder. |
| Marking scheme matches questions | Yes - expected answers plus marking notes covering partial credit, method marks for the two calculations, accepted alternatives, and the common errors, including offering a feedstuff when a class of nutrient is asked for, and naming the changed factor as a control variable. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - open items are anchored with ‘name three’, ‘state four’ and the mark allocation; Fig. 1 prints every proportion as a percentage and the net mass of the bag, and Fig. 2 carries a key, labelled axes with units and readings that fall on the gridline values. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and poultry; a feed company in Kumasi; a poultry farmer in Dormaa; groundnut cake, fish meal, maize and rice bran; goats that browse all day; and a school broiler project behind the science laboratory. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - types of feed, nutrients and their sources, reading feed labels, and the importance of water and feed to growth are exactly what the two standards set out; disease diagnosis, veterinary drugs and the economics of livestock marketing are excluded. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - recalling feed types, matching feed to animals, stating nutrient functions, calculating a percentage from a label, reading and comparing two curves on a graph, predicting the effect of withholding water, drawing a conclusion from an investigation, and planning the daily feeding, record-keeping and feed storage for a school poultry unit. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand carries TWO content standards. Questions 1 to 3 and the Section A items on feed and nutrients assess B8/JHS2.2.4.1; Questions 4 and 5 and the water items assess B8/JHS2.2.4.2. Question 6 draws on both. The blueprint shows which standard each item belongs to.
- Question 2 depends on Fig. 1. The proportions add up to 100%, so 2(b) is a clean calculation: 22% of 50 kg = 11 kg. Award the method mark for correct working even where the arithmetic slips.
- Question 4 depends on Fig. 2. All the readings asked for fall exactly on gridline values (1000 g, 750 g, 1500 g), so no mark should be lost through difficulty in reading the scale.
- Question 4(e) is the curriculum exemplar on predicting what happens to animals that are not provided with adequate water. The answer must reach death for the second mark; ‘they will be weak’ alone earns one mark.
- In Question 4(g), watch for candidates who name the amount of water as something kept the same. That is the factor being changed in the investigation and earns no mark.
- In Question 1(c), insist on classes of nutrients (protein, carbohydrate, fats and oils, minerals, vitamins). Named feedstuffs such as maize or fish meal are sources, not classes, and belong in Question 3(b).
- Accept local feedstuffs freely throughout: groundnut cake, soya bean meal, fish meal, copra cake, rice and wheat bran, cassava peels, palm kernel cake and kitchen waste are all used on Ghanaian farms.
- If your class keeps poultry, rabbits or small ruminants, accept their own feeding records and weight charts as evidence for Questions 4 to 6; this sub-strand is practical and the exemplars expect pupils to handle real feed labels.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, matching the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) For descriptions, demonstrations and design tasks, award method marks. (4) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Crown**
- **Neck**
- **Root**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (3 marks). These are the three regions named in the curriculum. Do NOT accept enamel, dentine and pulp - those are the layers, not the regions.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- (i) Crown - the part **above the gum** that **bites, tears or grinds the food**
- (ii) Root - **fixes and holds the tooth firmly** in the socket of the jaw bone
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). Accept ‘the part used for chewing’ for the crown and ‘anchors the tooth’ for the root.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- **32**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Do NOT accept 20, which is the number of milk teeth.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Milk teeth are the **first set and are 20 in number**, while permanent teeth are the **second set and are 32 in number**.
- Milk teeth are **smaller and fall out (are replaced)**, while permanent teeth are **larger and stronger and are not replaced** when they are lost.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct differences (2 marks). The answer must compare the two sets; a statement about only one of them earns no mark.*

**(e)** [1 marks]

- **Enamel**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Do NOT accept ‘bone’ or ‘dentine’.*

### Question 2 (11 marks)

**(a)** [6 marks]

- I - **enamel**
- II - **dentine**
- III - **pulp cavity**
- IV - **gum**
- V - **cement**
- VI - **nerve and blood vessels**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (6 marks). The name must be matched to the correct number. Accept ‘pulp’ for III, ‘gums’ for IV and ‘cementum’ for V. For VI accept either ‘nerve’ or ‘blood vessels’ alone.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- The enamel is the **hard outer covering that protects the crown** of the tooth from wear, from damage during chewing and from decay.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for protection or hardness of the crown.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- It contains the **nerves**, which make the tooth **sensitive to pain, heat and cold** (1 mark).
- It contains the **blood vessels**, which **supply food and oxygen** to the living cells of the tooth and keep it alive (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Both the nerve function and the blood supply must appear for full marks.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The **pulp cavity contains the nerves** of the tooth, while the enamel and dentine outside it have no nerves (1 mark).
- When the decay reaches the pulp the **nerves are exposed and irritated** by food, acid, heat and cold, and the pulp may become infected, so **severe pain (toothache) is felt** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The first mark is for locating the nerves in the pulp; the second is for the exposure or irritation of those nerves.*

### Question 3 (11 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- W - **incisor**
- X - **canine**
- Y - **premolar**
- Z - **molar**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). The name must be matched to the correct letter. Accept ‘eye tooth’ for the canine.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- (i) W (incisor) - **cuts and bites** off pieces of food
- (ii) Z (molar) - **grinds and chews** the food into small pieces
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). Do NOT accept ‘chewing’ for the incisor or ‘cutting’ for the molar.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **X is pointed (has one sharp cusp)** while **Z is broad with a large, ridged grinding surface**.
- **X is used for tearing** food, while **Z is used for grinding and chewing** it.
- **X has one root** and stands **near the front** of the mouth, while **Z has two or more roots** and stands **at the back**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct differences (2 marks). The answer must compare the two teeth; a statement about only one of them earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **A dog** (also accept a cat, lion, leopard or any named carnivore) (1 mark).
- It is a **flesh eater (carnivore)**, so it needs long, pointed canines to **hold its prey and tear flesh from the bones** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for a correct carnivore and 1 mark for the reason. A herbivore such as a cow or goat earns no mark, since its canines are poorly developed or absent.*

**(e)** [1 marks]

- The **jaw presses most strongly at the back**, so the broad molars can **grind the food thoroughly** after it has been cut and torn at the front of the mouth.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any sound reason linked to the force of the jaw or to the order of cutting, tearing and then grinding.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- Tooth decay is the **gradual breaking down or destruction of the hard parts of a tooth** (enamel and dentine) (1 mark)
- by the **acids produced by bacteria** acting on food left on the teeth, so that **holes (cavities) are formed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Award 1 mark for ‘holes in the teeth’ alone. The acid or bacteria must appear for the second mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Sugar from the sweets remains on the teeth** and, together with bacteria and saliva, forms a sticky layer called **plaque** (1 mark).
- The **bacteria in the plaque feed on the sugar and produce acid** (1 mark).
- The **acid dissolves the enamel and then the dentine**, forming a hole (cavity) which may finally reach the pulp cavity and cause toothache (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each, and the steps must be in a sensible order. The words plaque and acid should both appear; award the marks for the correct science even where the term plaque is missing.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The gums are **red, swollen and painful** and **bleed easily** when the teeth are brushed.
- There is **bad breath**, the **gums shrink away from the teeth**, and the **teeth become loose** in their sockets.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct signs (2 marks).*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- The pain **prevents proper chewing**, so the pupil **eats poorly** and may become weak and undernourished (1 mark).
- The pupil **misses school or cannot concentrate** in class because of the toothache, so performance falls (1 mark).
- **Money is spent on treatment**, and **bad breath or missing front teeth** may make the pupil shy and lose confidence among friends (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each for any three sound effects. Accept loss of sleep. Do NOT award two marks for the same idea stated twice.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Brush the teeth properly at least twice a day**, especially last thing before going to bed.
- **Reduce the eating of sweets, toffees and sugary drinks**, particularly between meals, and **rinse the mouth with clean water after eating**.
- **Eat foods rich in calcium** (milk, small fish eaten with the bones) and plenty of **fresh fruits and vegetables**.
- **Visit the dentist regularly** (at least twice a year) for check-ups, and **avoid using the teeth to open bottle tops** or crack hard objects.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR correct ways (4 marks). Do NOT accept ‘take medicine’ or ‘remove the tooth’ - these are treatments, not prevention.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Wet the brush and put a little toothpaste on it** (or chew the end of the chewing stick until it is soft and brush-like) (1 mark).
- **Brush all the surfaces** - the outer, the inner and the biting surfaces - using **short up-and-down (and circular) strokes, brushing away from the gum**, not only across the front teeth (1 mark).
- **Brush for about two minutes**, also **clean the tongue**, then **rinse the mouth with clean water** and rinse the brush; replace the brush when the bristles spread (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. This is the ‘demonstrate proper ways of cleaning the teeth’ exemplar, so award method marks for a sound procedure. The idea of reaching ALL surfaces must appear for full marks.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Milk** (and other dairy foods such as cheese and yoghurt)
- **Small fishes eaten with their bones**, eggs, beans, green leafy vegetables such as kontomire, and fresh fruits
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct foods (2 marks). The food should be a source of calcium, vitamins or phosphorus. Do NOT accept sweets or soft drinks.*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **‘Brush your teeth twice every day - and never miss bedtime.’**
- **‘Cut down on toffees and fizzy drinks; rinse your mouth after eating.’**
- **‘Eat milk, small fish and fruits for strong teeth.’**
- **‘Visit the dentist twice a year; never use your teeth to open bottles.’** (with a clear drawing of a tooth or a brushing action)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR sensible points (4 marks). This is a design task; award method marks for any message that would really help a Basic 4 pupil care for the teeth. A drawing or slogan may earn one of the marks.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- A **toothbrush with toothpaste**
- A **chewing stick (sokodua)**; also accept **salt with clean water** or dental floss
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO materials genuinely available locally (2 marks). The chewing stick is widely used in Ghana and must be accepted.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Put a clean egg shell into a cup containing the fizzy drink**, and an identical shell into a cup of **clean water as a control** (1 mark).
- **Leave both cups for a day or two**, then remove the shells and compare them (1 mark).
- The shell from the fizzy drink is **soft, rough, stained and partly dissolved**, while the one from the water is unchanged - showing that the **acid in the drink attacks the hard material of the tooth (the enamel)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. This is a design task, so award method marks for any workable procedure. The control (shell in water) earns a mark, and the conclusion must link the change to acid acting on the enamel. The egg shell is used because it is made of a hard mineral material like enamel.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- **Do not allow the pupils to drink the liquid or taste the egg shells**, and **wash the hands with soap** after handling them (keep the cups covered and labelled).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one sensible precaution. Do NOT accept ‘be careful’ on its own.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 3: Systems | **Sub-strand:** 1: The Human Body System | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.3.1.1** - Demonstrate knowledge of parts of the mammalian tooth and the functions of the different types of teeth in relation to feeding in man.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 3: Systems, Sub-Strand 1: The Human Body System, Basic 8, pages 64-65, content standard B8/JHS2.3.1.1. The three indicators and their exemplars are quoted from the curriculum, not invented: label parts such as crown, neck and root of a mammalian tooth; explain the functions of each part of the mammalian tooth of humans; discuss the functions of the different types of human teeth; draw the different types of teeth; describe the causes of tooth decay, gum diseases and the formation of plaque and the proper way of preventing tooth decay; and demonstrate proper ways of cleaning the teeth.
