| Check | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Every question within supplied curriculum scope | Yes - all items fall under Strand 3, Sub-Strand 1 (The Human Body System), content standard B8/JHS2.3.1.1, and are mapped to its three indicators: identify parts of a mammalian tooth (B8/JHS2.3.1.1.1); discuss the functions of the different types of teeth - incisors, canines, premolars and molars (B8/JHS2.3.1.1.2); and explain the causes and prevention of tooth and gum decay (B8/JHS2.3.1.1.3). Every exemplar is examined, including labelling the crown, neck and root, explaining the function of each part, drawing and identifying the types of teeth, the formation of plaque, and demonstrating the proper way of cleaning the teeth. |
| Appropriate for the class | Yes - B8 level; pupils label a tooth section, match the four types of teeth to their feeding functions, explain how decay happens and plan a dental-care talk. The dental formula notation, the names of the individual cusps and the histology of enamel are NOT examined, since they sit outside these indicators. |
| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, two labelled-diagram questions (a vertical section of a tooth and the teeth of a half jaw), a sequencing item on how decay occurs, and a demonstration-design task with a control. |
| Sufficient application and reasoning | Yes - 32 of 100 marks (32%) at Apply level or above (Apply 10, Analyse 9, Evaluate 8, Create 5). The reasoning load sits in explaining why pain is felt only when decay reaches the pulp, why molars sit at the back of the mouth, and the egg-shell demonstration. |
| Plausible MCQ distractors | Yes - drawn from the same content family as the key: the neighbouring layer of the tooth (enamel against dentine against cement), the neighbouring type of tooth, and the neighbouring region (crown against neck against root). |
| Single best answer per MCQ | Yes - reviewed item by item; special care with A13 (cartilage is not a part of a tooth), A21 (32 is the adult number and 20 the number of milk teeth) and A29 (decay attacks the enamel first, not the pulp). |
| Marks internally consistent | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40; Section B 9 + 11 + 11 + 10 + 9 + 10 = 60; every sub-question total matches the marking scheme. |
| Total adds up correctly | Yes - 40 + 60 = 100. |
| Answer key correct | Yes - all 40 keys verified item by item against the paper; the biology re-checked: enamel is the hardest substance in the body and covers the crown only, cement covers the root, the pulp cavity holds the nerves and blood vessels, canines are well developed in carnivores such as the dog, and an adult has 32 permanent teeth against 20 milk teeth. |
| Marking scheme matches questions | Yes - expected answers plus marking notes covering partial credit, accepted alternatives (pulp for pulp cavity, cementum for cement, eye tooth for canine, chewing stick for toothbrush) and the common errors, including naming the layers when the three regions are asked for, and offering a herbivore in Question 3(d). |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - open items are anchored with ‘name three’, ‘state two’ and the mark allocation; Fig. 1 numbers its parts I to VI and marks the crown, neck and root regions with brackets, and Fig. 2 letters the four tooth types W to Z and shows which end is the front of the mouth. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - the chewing stick (sokodua), small fishes eaten with their bones, kontomire, toffees and fizzy drinks sold near the school, a Basic 4 dental-care talk, and the advice to visit the dentist early. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the parts of the tooth, the functions of the four types of teeth and the causes and prevention of tooth and gum decay are exactly what the standard sets out; the dental formula, orthodontics and the detailed anatomy of the jaw are excluded. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - recalling regions and layers, labelling a sectional diagram, matching tooth types to feeding functions, comparing a canine with a molar, sequencing the stages of tooth decay, evaluating the effects of toothache on a pupil, describing the proper brushing procedure, and designing a poster and an egg-shell demonstration with a control. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This standard carries THREE indicators. Questions 1 and 2 assess B8/JHS2.3.1.1.1 (parts of the tooth); Questions 1(c), 1(d) and 3 assess B8/JHS2.3.1.1.2 (types of teeth and their functions); Questions 4, 5 and 6 assess B8/JHS2.3.1.1.3 (causes and prevention of tooth and gum decay). The blueprint shows the indicator for every item.
- In Question 1(a) insist on the three REGIONS - crown, neck and root. Candidates who give enamel, dentine and pulp have named the layers and earn no mark there; those layers are asked for in Question 2(a).
- Question 2 depends on Fig. 1, where the parts are numbered I to VI and the crown, neck and root are bracketed. Award the mark only when the name is matched to the correct number.
- Question 3(d) must name a carnivore. A cow, goat or sheep earns no mark, because the canines of herbivores are poorly developed or absent.
- Question 5(b) and Question 6(c) are the two practical exemplars - demonstrating the proper way of cleaning the teeth, and showing the effect of acid. Award method marks generously, but the idea of brushing ALL surfaces must appear in 5(b), and the control shell in clean water earns a mark in 6(c).
- The egg shell is used in Question 6(c) because it is made of a hard mineral material much like the enamel of a tooth. Accept a chicken bone or a discarded tooth as an alternative if your class used one.
- Accept the chewing stick (sokodua) throughout as a proper means of cleaning the teeth; it is in daily use in many Ghanaian homes and should never be marked wrong.
- In Question 4(b) look for the order: food and sugar remain on the teeth, plaque forms, bacteria produce acid, the acid dissolves the enamel and then the dentine. Award the marks for the correct science even where the word plaque is missing.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, matching the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers (the exemplar asks them to draw the different types of teeth); redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) In calculations, award a method mark for correct working even where the final answer is wrong. (4) For design and modelling tasks, award method marks. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- The solar system is the **Sun together with all the bodies that move round it** (1 mark).
- These bodies are the **eight planets and their moons, the asteroids, comets and meteors** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Award 1 mark for ‘the Sun and the planets’; the second mark needs other members such as moons, asteroids or comets.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Jupiter**
- **Saturn**
- **Uranus**
- **Neptune**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each, and the order must be correct for full marks (4 marks). All four named but in the wrong order scores a maximum of 2 marks.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- The **asteroid belt**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Accept ‘belt of asteroids’.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The planets **do not produce light of their own**, unlike the Sun and the other stars (1 mark).
- They are seen because they **reflect the light of the Sun** that falls on them towards the Earth (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The word **reflect** (or ‘the Sun's light bounces off them’) must appear for the second mark.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- I - **Jupiter**
- II - **Saturn**
- III - **Uranus**
- IV - **Neptune**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). The name must be matched to the correct number. Candidates should use the clues in the figure: I is the largest and II carries the rings.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- The **great red spot** (1 mark)
- It is a **huge storm** whirling in the atmosphere of the planet, larger than the Earth and lasting for hundreds of years (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept ‘red spot’ for the name. The second mark requires the idea of a storm; ‘a big red mark’ earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The **rings** (of Saturn) (1 mark)
- They are made up of **many pieces of ice, dust and rock** moving round the planet (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Do NOT award the second mark for ‘solid metal’ or ‘a solid band’ - the rings are not solid.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- **IV** - Neptune
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Accept either the number or the name.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- The inner planets are **small and rocky with solid surfaces**, while the outer planets are **very large and made mainly of gases**.
- The inner planets are **nearer the Sun and warmer**, while the outer planets are **far from the Sun and very cold**.
- The inner planets have **few or no moons**, while the outer planets have **many moons** (and rings).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct differences (2 marks). The answer must compare the two groups; a statement about only one group earns no mark.*

**(f)** [1 marks]

- They are **extremely large (giant)** and are made up **mainly of gases**, not of solid rock.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Both the size and the gas must appear; ‘they are big’ alone earns no mark.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- **143 thousand km** (about 143 000 km)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. The unit must be given; accept 143 000 km.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- **IV** (Neptune)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Accept either the number or the name.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Difference = 143 - 49 (1 mark)
- = **94 thousand km** (about 94 000 km) (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 method mark for the subtraction and 1 mark for the answer with the unit. A bare correct answer scores both marks.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- 143 ÷ 51 (1 mark)
- = about 2.8, that is **roughly 3 times** as wide (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 method mark for the division and 1 mark for the answer. Accept any answer between 2.5 and 3 described as ‘about 3 times’. The answer has no unit, since it is a comparison.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- They are all **much larger than the Earth** and are **made up mainly of gases** (no solid surface to stand on).
- They are all **very far from the Sun and very cold**, all have **many moons**, and each takes **many Earth years** to go round the Sun once.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct shared properties (2 marks). Do NOT accept ‘they are all planets’, which is given in the question.*

**(f)** [2 marks]

- It means that the **sizes of the planets and the distances between them are not in their true proportions** in the drawing (1 mark).
- It is necessary because the **real distances and sizes are far too vast** to be drawn in proportion on one page - the small planets would be invisible (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The first mark is for explaining the phrase; the second is for the reason.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) Jupiter - the **largest planet** in the solar system, with the **great red spot** (a giant storm)
- (ii) Saturn - famous for its **bright, wide rings** of ice and rock
- (iii) Uranus - **rotates on its side**, so that it appears to roll along its orbit; it looks blue-green
- (iv) Neptune - the **farthest planet from the Sun**, deep blue, with the strongest winds and the longest orbit
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). The property must be peculiar to that planet. Do NOT award a mark for ‘it is big and cold’, which is true of all four.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- They are **very far away from the Sun** compared with the Earth (1 mark).
- So **very little of the Sun's heat and light reaches them** - the heat spreads out and is very weak at that distance (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Do NOT accept ‘they are covered with ice’ as the reason - the ice is a result of the cold, not its cause.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Neptune is **much farther from the Sun** than Jupiter (1 mark).
- So its **orbit (path round the Sun) is very much longer**, and it has a far greater distance to cover to complete one journey (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept the additional point that it also travels more slowly along its orbit. Do NOT accept ‘it is lazy’ or ‘it is heavier’.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- A moon (natural satellite) is a **natural body that moves round a planet** (1 mark).
- The outer planets are **very large and have a strong pull (force of gravity)**, so they can hold many moons in orbit round them (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept ‘satellite’ for moon. Do NOT accept ‘a moon is a small star’.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Air (oxygen) to breathe**
- **Water**
- **Food** and a **suitable, moderate temperature** (not extremely hot or cold)
- A **suitable surface or habitat** to live on
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct conditions (3 marks).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- It is **extremely cold**, because it is very far from the Sun.
- It has **no solid surface** and **no liquid water** - it is made up mainly of gases.
- Its **atmosphere has no oxygen** to breathe (it is mainly hydrogen and helium, with poisonous gases), and **violent storms** blow there constantly.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct reasons (3 marks). The reasons must be about conditions on the planet. Do NOT accept ‘it is too far to travel to’ - that is about reaching it, not about life existing there.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Saturn is made up **mainly of gases and has no solid surface**, so there is nothing firm to stand on and the astronaut would **sink into the planet** (1 mark).
- Besides, the **extreme cold, the crushing pressure and the absence of oxygen** would make survival impossible (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The absence of a solid surface must appear for the first mark.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- The **journey takes many years and the conditions would kill a human being**; a probe needs **no air, food or water**, is cheaper and safer, and can send back pictures and readings without returning.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one sound reason.*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Balls of different sizes** (or moulded clay, paper mâché, calabash pieces) - to **represent the four planets and the Sun**.
- **Wire, string or thin sticks and a cardboard or wooden base** - to **hold the planets in position** at their different distances; **paint and paper labels** to colour and name them.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for each material correctly named WITH its use, maximum 2 marks. A material named without a use earns no mark. Accept any local material that would really work.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Find out the correct order, relative sizes and distances** of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune from books or the internet.
- **Make or choose balls of the right relative sizes** - the biggest for Jupiter, a slightly smaller one for Saturn, and two smaller ones for Uranus and Neptune.
- **Paint each planet in its colour** and add a card ring round Saturn.
- **Fix the planets with wire or string to the base in the correct order**, spacing them out from the Sun, then **label each one, write a title and display the model** for the class to discuss.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR sensible steps in a workable order (4 marks). This is the ‘construct a model and display it for discussion’ exemplar, so award method marks. The correct ORDER of the planets must appear somewhere for full marks.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The **correct order** of the planets from the Sun, with each in **its own separate orbit**.
- The **relative sizes** - Jupiter the largest, then Saturn, with Uranus and Neptune much smaller - and the **rings round Saturn**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The **sizes and the distances are not to true scale** - the real distances are far too vast to show on a table.
- The planets in the model are **held by wire and do not move**, whereas the real planets **move freely in orbit and rotate**; the model also cannot show the gases, the storms, the many moons or the extreme cold.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct limitations (2 marks). This item rewards candidates who understand that a model is only a representation; accept any sound limitation.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 3: Systems | **Sub-strand:** 2: The Solar System | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.3.2.1** - Demonstrate knowledge of the outer planets of the solar system.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 3: Systems, Sub-Strand 2: The Solar System, Basic 8, page 66, content standard B8/JHS2.3.2.1. The indicator and its five exemplars are quoted from the curriculum, not invented: describe the composition of the solar system using charts, pictures and digital content; identify and draw the planets that form the outer solar system; discuss the properties that are peculiar to each of the planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune; search and explain why there is no life on Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune; and construct a model of the outer solar system and display it for discussion.

> Note: The NaCCA document prints this standard as 'B8/JHS2.3.2.1' with the single indicator B8/JHS2.3.2.1.1. The school's content-standard sheets use the shorter coded form (B8.3.2.1 for the same standard); both forms are given in the blueprint so that the paper matches your records and the curriculum document. Because the sub-strand carries only one indicator, the blueprint separates the items by exemplar instead, so that you can see which of the five exemplars each item serves.

## QUALITY-CONTROL SUMMARY

| Check | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Every question within supplied curriculum scope | Yes - all items fall under Strand 3, Sub-Strand 2 (The Solar System), content standard B8/JHS2.3.2.1 and its single indicator B8/JHS2.3.2.1.1 (identify the outer planets of the solar system and describe their properties). All five exemplars are examined: describing the composition of the solar system using charts and pictures; identifying and drawing the planets of the outer solar system; discussing the properties peculiar to Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune; explaining why there is no life on those four planets; and constructing a model of the outer solar system and displaying it for discussion. |
| Appropriate for the class | Yes - B8 level; pupils identify the outer planets from a chart, read a bar chart of diameters, describe the peculiar features of each planet and plan a model. Orbital mechanics, the law of gravitation, planetary mass calculations and the dwarf-planet debate are NOT examined, since they sit outside this indicator. |
| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, two figure-based questions (a chart of the solar system and a bar chart of diameters), two calculations, and a modelling task that includes the limitations of the model. |
| Sufficient application and reasoning | Yes - 34 of 100 marks (34%) at Apply level or above (Apply 11, Analyse 10, Evaluate 9, Create 4). The reasoning load sits in comparing the inner and outer planets, explaining why Neptune's year is so long, why an astronaut could not stand on Saturn, and in judging what a model can and cannot show. |
| Plausible MCQ distractors | Yes - drawn from the same content family as the key: a neighbouring outer planet, an inner planet, and the common confusions between star, planet, moon and comet. |
| Single best answer per MCQ | Yes - reviewed item by item; special care with A5 (there are eight planets, since Pluto is no longer counted as a planet), A28 (Neptune does have an orbit, so that is the statement which is NOT a reason) and A29 (the Milky Way is a galaxy, not a member of the solar system). |
| Marks internally consistent | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40; Section B 9 + 12 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 10 = 60; every sub-question total matches the marking scheme. |
| Total adds up correctly | Yes - 40 + 60 = 100. |
| Answer key correct | Yes - all 40 keys verified item by item against the paper; the astronomy re-checked: eight planets; the asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter; Jupiter is the largest and carries the great red spot; Saturn's rings are ice, dust and rock; Uranus rotates on its side and appears blue-green because of methane; Neptune is the farthest from the Sun and has the longest orbit. |
| Marking scheme matches questions | Yes - expected answers plus marking notes covering partial credit, method marks for the two calculations, accepted alternatives (satellite for moon), and the common errors, including giving a property shared by all four planets when a peculiar one is asked for, and explaining the cold by the ice rather than by the distance from the Sun. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - open items are anchored with ‘name four’, ‘state two’ and the mark allocation; Fig. 1 numbers the four outer planets I to IV, names the inner planets and marks the asteroid belt, and Fig. 2 uses the same I to IV labels and prints the value above every bar. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - a class project to build and display a model from locally available materials, observing the night sky, and the use of charts and pictures in the science lesson. The topic is by nature a universal one, so contexts are kept to the classroom and the school science club rather than forced. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the composition of the solar system, the identity and properties of the four outer planets, the reasons for the absence of life, and the construction of a model are exactly what the standard sets out; the inner planets appear only for comparison, as the composition exemplar requires. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - recalling the members of the solar system, identifying planets from a chart, reading and calculating from a bar chart, describing features peculiar to each planet, explaining the cold and the long orbit, reasoning about why life cannot exist there, planning the construction of a model, and evaluating the limitations of that model. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand has ONE content standard and ONE indicator, so the blueprint separates the items by exemplar instead, showing which of the five exemplars each item serves.
- Question 2 depends on Fig. 1 and Question 3 on Fig. 2. The same labels I to IV are used in both figures and refer to the same planets, so a candidate who names them correctly in 2(a) can carry the names into Question 3.
- Teach candidates to read the clues in Fig. 1: I is drawn largest (Jupiter) and II carries the rings (Saturn). The figure is deliberately marked ‘not drawn to scale’, and Question 3(f) asks them to explain what that means.
- There are EIGHT planets. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 and is not counted; if a candidate writes nine, mark it wrong but explain why in class.
- In Question 4(a) the property must be PECULIAR to that planet. ‘It is large and cold’ is true of all four and earns no mark; look for the great red spot, the rings, the sideways rotation and the greatest distance from the Sun.
- In Question 4(b) the cold is caused by the great distance from the Sun. Candidates who answer ‘because they are covered with ice’ have reversed cause and effect and earn no mark.
- Question 6 is the modelling exemplar. Award method marks generously for any workable procedure, but the correct ORDER of the four planets must appear for full marks in 6(b). Part 6(d) rewards pupils who understand that a model is only a representation.
- If your class actually built a model, accept it as evidence for Question 6 and let the pupils present it; the exemplar asks for the model to be displayed for discussion.
- Encourage the use of charts, pictures and digital content for this sub-strand, as the first exemplar directs. Where there is no internet, a drawn chart on manila card works just as well.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, matching the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers (the exemplar asks them to draw the outer planets); redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) In food chains, the arrows must point from the organism eaten towards the organism that eats it. (4) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- An ecosystem is **all the living organisms (plants, animals and micro-organisms) in a particular place** (1 mark)
- **together with the non-living parts of their surroundings** - soil, water, air, light and temperature - all **interacting with one another** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Award 1 mark for the living things alone; the second mark needs the non-living surroundings or the interaction.*

**(b)** [6 marks]

- (i) **Producer** - an organism, usually a **green plant, that makes its own food** using energy from the Sun by photosynthesis (2 marks)
- (ii) **Primary consumer** - an animal that **feeds directly on producers (green plants)**; it is a herbivore, for example a grasshopper or a goat (2 marks)
- (iii) **Secondary consumer** - an animal that **feeds on primary consumers**, for example a lizard that eats grasshoppers (2 marks)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks for each term (6 marks): 1 mark for the basic idea and 1 mark for a correct example or for the link with the level below it. These three terms are named directly in the curriculum exemplar.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- **Water** (also accept air, soil, sunlight, rocks or temperature)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. The thing named must be non-living. Do NOT accept a dead animal or a fallen leaf, which were once living.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Maize plant**
- **Grass**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). They are the producers because the arrows begin from them and they are green plants.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **maize plant → grasshopper → lizard → hawk**
- or **grass → rat → snake → hawk**
- or **maize plant → rat → snake → hawk**
- or **grass → grasshopper → lizard → snake**
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for four organisms correctly taken from the web and 1 mark for the arrows pointing in the right direction (from the eaten to the eater). A chain written in reverse order scores a maximum of 1 mark.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- **Grasshopper** (or **rat**)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Both feed directly on the producers. Do NOT accept the lizard, the snake or the hawk.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The lizard** (also accept **the snake**) (1 mark).
- It **hunts and eats the grasshopper**, so it is a **predator**; but it is **itself eaten by the snake and the hawk**, so it is also a **prey** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for a correct organism and 1 mark for the explanation. The explanation must show both roles. Do NOT accept the hawk, which nothing in the web eats, or the maize plant.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- The arrows show the **direction in which food and energy flow** through the web (1 mark).
- Each arrow points **from the organism that is eaten towards the organism that eats it** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The direction of the arrow must be explained correctly for the second mark; ‘it shows who eats who’ earns 1 mark only.*

**(f)** [2 marks]

- The number of grasshoppers would **increase** (1 mark),
- because the **lizards that feed on them would no longer be there to control their numbers** (1 mark). (Accept the further point that the grasshoppers would then destroy more maize and grass.)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the correct prediction and 1 mark for the reason. A reason without the prediction, or a prediction of ‘decrease’, earns no mark.*

**(g)** [1 marks]

- **Most organisms feed on more than one kind of food** (and are eaten by more than one kind of animal), and a web **shows all those links together**, so it is a truer picture of the ecosystem.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for the idea of several feeding links rather than one.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- P is the **producer** level (the green plants) (1 mark)
- Example: **maize plant** (accept grass, cassava, algae or any named green plant) (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The example must be a green plant. Do NOT accept a mushroom, which is not a producer.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- **R**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. P is the producers, Q the primary consumers, R the secondary consumers and S the top consumers.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- As **heat**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Do NOT accept ‘light’ or ‘sound’.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- At each level the organisms **use most of the energy for respiration, movement, growth and other life activities**, and much of it **escapes to the surroundings as heat** (1 mark).
- Only the **small part that remains stored in their bodies is passed on** when they are eaten, so less and less energy is available at each higher level (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept the point that parts of the organism (bones, fur, roots) are not eaten or digested.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- **So much energy is lost at every stage** that after four or five levels **very little is left** (1 mark).
- There would **not be enough energy to feed and support another level** of consumers, so the chain ends (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The answer must connect the loss of energy with the inability to support a further level.*

**(f)** [2 marks]

- They **trap the energy of the Sun and make food**, which every other organism in the ecosystem depends on, directly or indirectly.
- They **release oxygen** into the air for other organisms to breathe, and **provide shelter and habitats** for animals (and their roots hold the soil together).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks). The food-making point should appear; award the second mark for oxygen, shelter or soil protection.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Green plants absorb the sunlight** that falls on their leaves, using the green substance **chlorophyll** (1 mark).
- They use that energy, with **carbon dioxide and water**, to make food by **photosynthesis**, and the energy is **stored in the food** they make (1 mark).
- When **animals eat the plants**, the stored energy passes into their bodies, and so into the rest of the food chain (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. The word photosynthesis should appear; award the mark for a correct description even where the term is missing.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- The Earth would become **extremely cold and dark**, and water would freeze, stopping the water cycle (1 mark).
- **Photosynthesis would stop**, so green plants would die and no new food would be made (1 mark).
- **Animals would starve** as the food chains broke down, and in time **almost all life on Earth would come to an end** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each for any three sound changes. This is the curriculum exemplar ‘discuss how life on earth will be like without the sun’; accept any well-reasoned consequence.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- They are the **only organisms that can trap the Sun's energy and make their own food** (1 mark).
- **Every other organism depends on them** for food, directly or indirectly, so the chain must start with them (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Animals **have no chlorophyll**, the green substance needed to absorb and trap sunlight (1 mark).
- They **cannot carry out photosynthesis** at all, so they must take in **ready-made food** by eating plants or other animals (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Chlorophyll (or the inability to photosynthesise) must appear for full marks.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- Interdependence means that the organisms in an ecosystem **depend on one another for food, shelter, oxygen and other needs** (1 mark).
- None of them can live entirely on its own, so **a change that affects one organism affects the others too** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Plants provide **shelter, shade and nesting places** for animals, while animals **pollinate flowers and scatter seeds** for the plants.
- Plants **release oxygen** that animals breathe, and animals **release carbon dioxide** that plants use; **animal droppings and dead bodies enrich the soil** for plants.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points that are NOT about feeding (2 marks). An answer about eating earns no mark here.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Decomposers **break down dead plants and animals and their waste** (1 mark),
- **returning the nutrients to the soil** so that green plants can use them again, and **clearing away dead matter** that would otherwise pile up (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Named examples such as bacteria, fungi and mushrooms may support the answer but do not earn a mark on their own.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- The **number of rats would increase greatly**, because the snakes that fed on them are gone (1 mark).
- The rats would **destroy much more maize**, so the farmer's **harvest would fall** (1 mark).
- **Hawks and other animals that feed on snakes would lose a source of food** and reduce in number, so the **balance of the whole ecosystem is upset** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each for any three sound effects. Credit any answer that traces a correct chain of consequences through the food web.*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Mark out a small area** of the grass (for example one metre square) with pegs and string, so that the study area is clear.
- **Search the area carefully** - in the grass, under stones and leaves - and **identify and list the organisms** found there.
- **Observe quietly over several days** to see what each organism feeds on, looking for clues such as bitten leaves, droppings and remains of prey.
- **Record the findings in a table** (organism, what it feeds on, what feeds on it), then **use the records to draw food chains and a food web**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR sensible steps in a workable order (4 marks). Award method marks for any step that would really reveal feeding relationships. Observation and recording must both appear for full marks.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- A chain of **four organisms beginning with a green plant**, for example **grass → grasshopper → lizard → hawk** (1 mark).
- **Arrows drawn pointing from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it** (1 mark).
- **Every organism clearly named (labelled)**, and the organisms chosen are ones that could really be found in grass behind a school (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks as shown. A chain that begins with an animal loses the first mark; arrows drawn in the wrong direction lose the second. This is the ‘illustrate with diagrams’ exemplar.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Do not touch or handle snakes, scorpions or any unfamiliar animal**, and **wear shoes and long sleeves** against bites and stings.
- **Do not taste any plant, fruit or seed**, **wash the hands with soap** after the study, and **stay with the teacher** throughout.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sensible precautions (2 marks). Do NOT accept ‘be careful’ on its own.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- **Every organism has its own part to play** in the ecosystem; if they are removed or killed the **feeding relationships and the balance of the ecosystem are upset**, and the organisms would die away from their habitat.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for the idea of balance, or of respect for living things.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 3: Systems | **Sub-strand:** 3: Ecosystem | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.3.3.1** - Demonstrate an understanding of the interdependence of organisms in an ecosystem and their interaction.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 3: Systems, Sub-Strand 3: Ecosystem, Basic 8, page 67, content standard B8/JHS2.3.3.1. The indicator and its three exemplars are quoted from the curriculum, not invented: discuss how life on earth will be like without the sun; explain the terms producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, food chain and food web as applied in energy transfer in an ecosystem; and illustrate with diagrams how energy from the sun flows through a food chain and food web in an ecosystem.

Because the sub-strand carries only one indicator, the blueprint separates the items by exemplar, so that you can see which of the three exemplars each item serves. The five terms named in Exemplar 2 - producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, food chain and food web - are each examined directly.

## QUALITY-CONTROL SUMMARY

| Check | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Every question within supplied curriculum scope | Yes - all items fall under Strand 3, Sub-Strand 3 (Ecosystem), content standard B8/JHS2.3.3.1 and its single indicator B8/JHS2.3.3.1.1 (explore the feeding relationships within an ecosystem). All three exemplars are examined: how life on Earth would be without the Sun (Question 4(b) and Section A items 27 and 28); the terms producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, food chain and food web (Question 1(b), Question 2 and Section A items 5 to 15); and illustrating with diagrams how energy flows through a food chain and a food web (Question 2, Question 3 and Question 6(b)). |
| Appropriate for the class | Yes - B8 level; pupils interpret a food web, name trophic levels, trace the consequences of removing an organism and draw a food chain. Numerical energy-transfer percentages, pyramids of biomass and the nitrogen cycle are NOT examined, since they sit outside this indicator. |
| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, two figure-based questions (a food web and an energy-flow pyramid), prediction items, and a fieldwork task that requires the candidate to draw a labelled food chain. |
| Sufficient application and reasoning | Yes - 33 of 100 marks (33%) at Apply level or above (Apply 7, Analyse 15, Evaluate 8, Create 3). The reasoning load sits in predicting what happens when the lizards or the snakes are removed, explaining why energy decreases up the chain, and why food chains are short. |
| Plausible MCQ distractors | Yes - drawn from the same content family as the key: the neighbouring trophic level, the neighbouring feeding term (herbivore, carnivore, omnivore, decomposer), and predator against prey. |
| Single best answer per MCQ | Yes - reviewed item by item; special care with A13 (grass is a producer, so the chain has three consumers, not four), A28 (the statement that plants would grow faster is the one that would NOT happen) and A36 (the snake is both predator and prey, while the hawk is only a predator). |
| Marks internally consistent | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40; Section B 9 + 12 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 10 = 60; every sub-question total matches the marking scheme. |
| Total adds up correctly | Yes - 40 + 60 = 100. |
| Answer key correct | Yes - all 40 keys verified item by item against the paper and against Fig. 1; the ecology re-checked: food chains begin with producers, arrows run from the eaten to the eater, energy is lost as heat at each stage, decomposers return nutrients to the soil, and removing a predator increases the number of its prey. |
| Marking scheme matches questions | Yes - expected answers plus marking notes covering partial credit, the direction of the arrows in a food chain, accepted alternatives, and the common errors, including giving a feeding answer in Question 5(b) where non-feeding links are asked for, and naming the hawk in Question 2(d). |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - open items are anchored with ‘name two’, ‘state three’ and the mark allocation; Fig. 1 names every organism and states beneath it that the arrows show the direction of energy flow, and Fig. 2 letters the four levels P to S and marks the energy lost at each stage. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - a grassland beside a maize farm with grasshoppers, rats, lizards, snakes and hawks; a farmer who kills the snakes on his maize farm; a pond with algae and fishes; and a fieldwork study in the grass behind the school. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - feeding relationships, the five named terms, energy transfer and the role of the Sun are exactly what the indicator sets out. Decomposers and the predator-prey relationship appear because the content standard is about the interdependence of organisms and their interaction; they are kept to a small number of items and are not treated as a separate topic. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - defining the key terms, extracting a food chain from a food web, identifying trophic levels on a pyramid, predicting the effect of removing an organism, discussing a world without the Sun, explaining interdependence and the work of decomposers, planning a fieldwork study, and drawing a labelled food chain. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand has ONE content standard and ONE indicator, so the blueprint separates the items by exemplar, showing which of the three exemplars each item serves.
- The five terms named in the curriculum exemplar - producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, food chain and food web - are each examined directly. Question 1(b) carries two marks per term: one for the idea and one for a correct example.
- Arrows matter. In Question 2(b) and Question 6(b), the arrow must point FROM the organism eaten TO the organism that eats it. A chain written in reverse order scores a maximum of half the marks.
- Question 2(d) asks for an organism that is both predator and prey. The lizard and the snake both qualify; the hawk does not, because nothing in the web feeds on it.
- In Question 2(f), the prediction and the reason are marked separately. A candidate who predicts a decrease earns nothing, even if the reasoning is neatly written.
- In Question 5(b) the two ways must NOT be about feeding - look for shelter, pollination, seed dispersal, oxygen and carbon dioxide, or the enriching of the soil.
- Question 4(b) is the curriculum exemplar on life without the Sun. Accept any well-reasoned consequence; the strongest answers link the cold and darkness to the stopping of photosynthesis and then to the collapse of the food chains.
- Question 6 is fieldwork. If your class actually carried out such a study, accept their own records, tables and drawn food webs as evidence, and let them present the work.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, matching the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers (the exemplar asks them to illustrate energy flow with diagrams); redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

| 1 (a) | A farming system is the particular way in which a farmer combines crops, animals and land, with his labour and other resources, to produce food and other farm products. | Types of Farming Systems | Understand |
| 1 (b) | (i) mixed farming - keeping crops and animals together on the same farm; (ii) mono-cropping - growing only one kind of crop on the same land season after season; (iii) crop rotation - growing different crops one after another on the same land in a planned order. | Types of Farming Systems | Understand |
| 1 (c) | The climate and rainfall of the area, the type and fertility of the soil, the size of land available, the capital and labour the farmer has, the market nearby, or the custom of the community. | Types of Farming Systems | Understand |
| 2 (a) | Mixed farming. | Types of Farming Systems | Understand |
| 2 (b) | The cattle manure is spread on the maize field and the poultry droppings are used as manure on the vegetable plot, improving the fertility of the soil. | Usefulness of the Crops and Animals | Understand |
| 2 (c) | The maize stalks and husks are fed to the cattle, the maize grain is used as poultry feed and the spoilt vegetable leaves are fed to the fowls. | Usefulness of the Crops and Animals | Understand |
| 2 (d) | The oxen plough the fields (they provide draught power). | Usefulness of the Crops and Animals | Understand |
| 2 (e) | Farm wastes are used instead of being thrown away, so he spends less on fertiliser and feed; he has several products and a steady income through the year; the land is used fully and the soil is kept fertile; if one enterprise fails the others still bring in money. | Advantages and Disadvantages of Farming Systems | Analyse |
| 2 (f) | It needs more skill, labour and capital than one enterprise alone; the farmer's attention is divided; animals may stray and damage the crops; diseases and pests must be managed in both crops and animals; housing, water and veterinary care add to the cost. | Advantages and Disadvantages of Farming Systems | Analyse |
| 2 (g) | Nothing is wasted - the waste from one part becomes a resource for another, so the soil is kept fertile and fewer outside inputs are needed, and the farm can go on producing year after year. | Contribution to Sustainability and Soil Care | Evaluate |
| 3 (a) | Crop rotation (with a fallow year). | Types of Farming Systems | Understand |
| 3 (b) | Groundnut is a legume; the bacteria in the nodules on its roots fix nitrogen, so the soil is left richer in nitrogen for the cassava that follows. | Contribution to Sustainability and Soil Care | Analyse |
| 3 (c) | The land is left to rest under bush (fallow); no crop is planted, so that the soil can recover its fertility and its structure naturally. | Contribution to Sustainability and Soil Care | Understand |
| 3 (d) | It keeps the soil fertile and reduces the need for fertiliser; it breaks the life cycle of pests and diseases; it controls weeds; and it gives the farmer different products from the same land. | Advantages and Disadvantages of Farming Systems | Understand |
| 3 (e) | The soil would lose the particular nutrients maize needs, so yields would fall; the pests and diseases of maize would build up in the land; she would have to spend more on fertiliser and chemicals; weeds associated with maize would increase. | Advantages and Disadvantages of Farming Systems | Analyse |
| 3 (f) | Land is now scarce because the population has grown and much land is used for housing, so farmers must crop the small holdings they have every season. | Contribution to Sustainability and Soil Care | Evaluate |
| 4 (a) | Crops provide food for the household, income when sold, raw materials for industry, feed and bedding for the animals, and cover that protects the soil. | Usefulness of the Crops and Animals | Understand |
| 4 (b) | Animals provide meat, milk and eggs; manure for the soil; hides, skins and wool; draught power for ploughing and transport; and income and savings for the household. | Usefulness of the Crops and Animals | Understand |
| 4 (c) | Animal manure and crop residues return nutrients to the soil, so its fertility is maintained without heavy use of bought fertiliser; crop residues feed the animals so less feed is bought; legumes restore nitrogen; and the variety of products keeps the farm earning, so the farmer is not forced to overwork the land. | Contribution to Sustainability and Soil Care | Analyse |
| 4 (d) | He must pay cash for all the feed, which is his largest cost, and he has no crops of his own to fall back on; the farmer with crops feeds his animals on residues and uses the manure on his fields, so his costs are lower and his income comes from more than one product. | Usefulness of the Crops and Animals | Evaluate |
| 5 (a) | In subsistence farming the farmer produces mainly to feed his own household, on a small piece of land with simple tools; in commercial farming he produces on a large scale mainly for sale and for profit. | Types of Farming Systems | Understand |
| 5 (b) | Advantages: the fallow restores soil fertility naturally; little capital, fertiliser or machinery is needed; pests and weeds are left behind on the old plot. Disadvantages: it needs a large area of land, which is now scarce; it destroys forest and encourages erosion, especially where burning is used; yields are low and only small areas can be farmed; the farmer must keep moving. | Advantages and Disadvantages of Farming Systems | Analyse |
| 5 (c) | Practise crop rotation; apply compost, farmyard manure or green manure; leave part of the land to fallow; plant cover crops and mulch; plant trees and grass strips or ridge across the slope to check erosion; avoid burning the bush; use fertiliser according to a soil test. | Contribution to Sustainability and Soil Care | Evaluate |
| 6 (a) | Agree on the purpose and prepare the questions; obtain permission from the teacher, the chief or the farmers to be visited; visit the farms in groups and observe the crops, animals and land use; interview the farmers and record the answers in a table; sort the farms into systems and present the findings to the class. | Crop, Animal and Land Combinations | Apply |

What do you do with the crop residues and the animal droppings? Do you sell your produce or use it at home? | Crop, Animal and Land Combinations | Apply |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) Where a candidate is asked to state a number of points, mark only the first points up to the number asked for. (4) Credit local examples drawn from the candidate's own community. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- A farming system is the **particular way a farmer combines crops, animals and land** on his holding (1 mark),
- using his **labour, capital and other resources to produce food and other farm products** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The combination of the components must appear for the first mark. A list of crops alone earns no mark.*

**(b)** [6 marks]

- (i) **Mixed farming** - the growing of crops and the keeping of farm animals **together on the same holding**, for example maize with cattle (2 marks)
- (ii) **Mono-cropping** - the growing of **only one kind of crop on the same piece of land season after season**, for example maize every year (2 marks)
- (iii) **Crop rotation** - the growing of **different crops one after the other on the same piece of land in a planned order**, so that the same crop does not return to the land every season (2 marks)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks for each term (6 marks): 1 mark for the idea and 1 mark for a correct example or for the point that distinguishes it. Candidates commonly confuse mixed farming with mixed cropping - mixed cropping has no animals in it.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- **The climate and rainfall of the area** (accept the type of soil, the size of land available, the capital and labour the farmer has, the nearby market, or the custom and experience of the community).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one sound reason.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- **Mixed farming** (crops and animals kept together on one holding)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Do NOT accept ‘mixed cropping’, which does not include animals.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- The **cattle manure is spread on the maize field**, adding nutrients and improving the soil.
- The **poultry droppings are used as manure on the vegetable plot** (accept: the oxen plough the fields).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO (2 marks). Both answers must be taken from the arrows in Fig. 1.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The **maize stalks and husks are fed to the cattle**, and the **maize grain is used as poultry feed**.
- The **spoilt vegetable leaves are fed to the fowls**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO feed links shown in Fig. 1 (2 marks).*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- The **oxen plough both fields**, providing draught power that would otherwise cost money to hire.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. The ploughing is stated beneath the diagram; manure is NOT accepted here, as the question excludes it.*

**(e)** [3 marks]

- The **farm wastes are used on the farm itself**, so he **spends less money on fertiliser and on feed** (1 mark).
- He has **several products - maize, vegetables, milk, eggs - and so a steadier income throughout the year** (1 mark).
- The **risk is spread**: if one enterprise fails, the others still bring in money; and the **land and labour are fully used** while the soil is kept fertile (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE sound advantages (3 marks). Credit answers that are clearly drawn from Fig. 1.*

**(f)** [2 marks]

- It needs **more skill, labour and capital**, and the farmer's **attention is divided** between the crops and the animals.
- **Animals may stray and damage the crops**, and **both crops and animals bring pests and diseases** that cost money to control (accept: housing, water and veterinary care are extra costs).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO (2 marks). ‘It is difficult’ on its own earns no mark; the difficulty must be explained.*

**(g)** [1 marks]

- **The waste from one part of the farm becomes a resource for another**, so the soil stays fertile, fewer bought inputs are needed and the land can go on producing year after year.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for the idea of recycling the wastes or of keeping the soil fertile for the future.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- **Crop rotation** (accept crop rotation with a bush-fallow year)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Do NOT accept ‘shifting cultivation’ - the farmer stays on the same piece of land, as the centre of Fig. 2 states.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Groundnut is a **legume**, and the **bacteria in the nodules on its roots fix nitrogen** from the air into the soil (1 mark).
- The soil is therefore **left richer in nitrogen for the crop that follows**, which grows better without bought fertiliser (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The word legume or the mention of root nodules should appear; award the nitrogen mark for a correct description even where the terms are missing.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The land is **left to rest under bush (fallow)** and **no crop is planted** on it (1 mark).
- This allows the **soil to recover its fertility and structure naturally**, as the plants that grow and die add organic matter to it (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- It **keeps the soil fertile**, since different crops take different nutrients and the legume restores nitrogen, so **less fertiliser is needed**.
- It **breaks the life cycle of pests, diseases and weeds** that attack one crop, and it **gives the farmer different products** from the same piece of land.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO advantages (2 marks).*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- The soil would **lose the particular nutrients that maize needs** and her **yields would fall** year after year (1 mark).
- The **pests and diseases of maize would build up in the land**, so she would have to **spend more on fertiliser and chemicals** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO (2 marks). A bare statement that ‘the soil will spoil’ earns no mark unless it is explained.*

**(f)** [1 marks]

- **Land has become scarce**: the population has grown and much land is taken for housing and other uses, so farmers must **crop their small holdings every season** to feed their families.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for the scarcity of land, population pressure, or the need to produce food or income every year.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- They provide **food for the farmer's household** and **income when the surplus is sold** (1 mark).
- They provide **raw materials for industry** (cocoa, cotton, oil palm) and **feed and bedding for the farm animals** (1 mark).
- Their **cover and their roots protect the soil** from erosion, and their residues add organic matter to it (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct uses (3 marks).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- They provide **meat, milk and eggs** - protein food for the family and produce for sale (1 mark).
- They provide **manure that improves the fertility of the soil**, and **hides, skins, horns and feathers** for other uses (1 mark).
- They provide **draught power for ploughing and for carrying loads**, and they are a **form of savings** that can be sold when money is needed (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct uses (3 marks). Do not award two marks for two kinds of food (for example meat and milk) given as separate points.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Animal manure and crop residues return nutrients and organic matter to the soil**, so its fertility is maintained **without heavy use of bought fertiliser**.
- **Crop residues feed the animals** (and legumes restore nitrogen), so **less is bought from outside** and the farm can go on producing for many years.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO (2 marks). The answer must link the practice to the land's ability to go on producing - that is sustainability.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- He **pays cash for all the feed**, which is usually the largest cost in keeping animals, and he has **no crop income to fall back on** if prices rise or the animals fall sick (1 mark).
- The mixed farmer **feeds his animals on his own crop residues and spreads their manure on his fields**, so his **costs are lower and he earns from more than one product** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The comparison with the mixed farmer must be made for the second mark.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- In **subsistence farming** the farmer produces **mainly to feed his own household**, usually on a small piece of land with simple tools, with little left over to sell (1 mark).
- In **commercial farming** the farmer produces **on a large scale mainly for sale and for profit**, often using machinery and hired labour (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. A candidate who describes only one of the two systems scores a maximum of 1 mark.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Advantages:** the **fallow period restores the fertility of the soil naturally**, and **little capital, fertiliser or machinery is needed**; the pests and weeds of the old plot are left behind (2 marks).
- **Disadvantages:** it **needs a large area of land**, which is now scarce; it **destroys forest and leads to soil erosion**, especially where the bush is burnt; and **yields are low**, as only a small area can be cleared and worked by hand (2 marks).
  - *Marking note: 4 marks: 1 mark each for TWO advantages and 1 mark each for TWO disadvantages. A candidate who gives four advantages and no disadvantage scores a maximum of 2 marks.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Practise crop rotation**, including a legume in the cycle.
- **Apply compost, farmyard manure or green manure**, and **mulch or plant cover crops** to protect the soil surface.
- **Avoid burning the bush**, ridge across the slope or plant grass strips and trees to check erosion, and rest part of the land under fallow.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE sound practices (3 marks).*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Agree on the purpose of the study and prepare the questions** and the recording table beforehand.
- **Obtain permission** from the teacher and from the farmers (or the chief) before visiting the farms.
- **Visit the farms in small groups and observe** the crops grown, the animals kept and how the land is used; **interview the farmers** and record their answers.
- **Sort the farms into the different farming systems, summarise the records in a table and present the findings** to the class.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR sensible steps in a workable order (4 marks). Observation or interview, and recording, must both appear for full marks.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- A **ruled table with clear column headings**, for example **Name of farmer | Crops grown | Animals kept | How the land is used (size, fallow, rotation) | Farming system** (2 marks).
- **Rows left blank for the entries**, with the table neatly drawn and the headings written in full (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks: 2 marks for headings that would really allow the systems to be compared (at least three useful headings) and 1 mark for a neat, ruled table with blank rows. A list written without a table scores a maximum of 1 mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- ‘**Which crops do you grow, and which animals do you keep on this land?**’
- ‘**Do you rest the land or change the crop each season, and what do you do with the crop residues and the droppings?**’ (accept: do you farm mainly to eat or to sell?)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO questions that would really help to identify the farming system (2 marks). A question that can be answered without visiting the farm earns no mark.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- **Greet the farmer politely and ask permission before entering the farm** (accept: do not pluck or damage any crop; keep away from the animals and the cutlasses; stay with the teacher; wear shoes and wash the hands afterwards).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one sound courtesy or safety rule. ‘Be careful’ on its own earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 3: Systems | **Sub-strand:** 4: Farming Systems | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.3.4.1** - Demonstrate understanding of the different crop, animal and land combinations under various farming systems.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 3: Systems, Sub-Strand 4: Farming Systems, Basic 8, page 68, content standard B8/JHS2.3.4.1 with indicators B8/JHS2.3.4.1.1 and B8/JHS2.3.4.1.2. The exemplars quoted are: describe the types of crops, animals and land combinations in the different farming systems in your community; discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each farming system identified; explain how the different components of farming systems contribute to each other; and discuss and write down the contributions of crops and animals towards the sustainability of each farming system.

> Note: The NaCCA document prints this standard as 'B8/JHS2.3.4.1' with two indicators, B8/JHS2.3.4.1.1 (the types of crops, animals and land combinations) and B8/JHS2.3.4.1.2 (the usefulness of those crops and animals). The school's content-standard sheets use the shorter coded form (B8.3.4.1); both forms are given in the blueprint. Section A items 1 to 24 and Questions 1, 2, 3 and 5 rest mainly on the first indicator; items 25 to 40 and Question 4 rest mainly on the second.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand has two indicators. Items 1 to 24 and Questions 1, 2, 3 and 5 rest mainly on B8/JHS2.3.4.1.1; items 25 to 40 and Question 4 rest mainly on B8/JHS2.3.4.1.2. The blueprint shows the indicator against every item.
- Mixed farming and mixed cropping are the commonest confusion in this topic. Mixed farming keeps animals and crops together; mixed cropping is two or more crops on the same land with no animals. Mark Question 1(b)(i) strictly on this point.
- Shifting cultivation and bush fallowing are also confused. In shifting cultivation the farmer abandons the plot and moves on; in bush fallowing he stays and returns to the rested plot.
- Fig. 2 shows crop rotation on ONE piece of land, which the centre of the diagram states plainly. Candidates who answer 'shifting cultivation' in Question 3(a) have not read the figure.
- In Question 2(d) the manure is specifically excluded. The expected answer is the ploughing done by the oxen, which is written beneath the diagram.
- Question 5(b) is marked two and two. Read the whole answer before awarding marks, as candidates often mix the advantages and the disadvantages together in one paragraph.
- Question 6(b) asks for a table. Award the headings marks for any set of headings that would genuinely allow two farms to be compared; the exact wording does not matter.
- If your class actually carried out such a survey, accept their own records and completed tables as evidence for Question 6, and let the groups present their findings.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) An energy change must show both the starting form and the final form; a single form earns no mark. (3) Accept 'mechanical energy' for 'kinetic energy' where the body is clearly moving. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- Energy conversion is the **changing of energy from one form into another form** (1 mark),
- for example **electrical energy changing into heat energy in a kettle**; the energy is **not destroyed - it only changes its form** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The second mark may be earned either by a correct example or by the point that the energy is not destroyed.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Electrical energy to heat energy** (1 mark)
- (ii) **Chemical energy to electrical energy to light energy** (accept chemical to light) (1 mark)
- (iii) **Electrical energy to sound energy** (1 mark)
- (iv) **Light (solar) energy to chemical energy** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). Both the starting form and the final form must be given; a single form earns no mark. In (ii) accept the two-step or the three-step chain.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Heat energy** - from the cooking stove or the coal pot.
- **Light energy** - from the electric lamp or the lantern.
- **Sound energy** - from the radio or the television (accept electrical energy at the socket, or chemical energy in food and dry cells).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for each correct pairing of a form of energy with a place where it is used or produced (3 marks). A form named without a place, or a place without a form, earns no mark.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- **Potential energy** (gravitational potential energy), because the water is stored at a high level
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Do NOT accept kinetic energy; the stored water is not yet moving.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- The **dam wall holds back the river**, so that a large volume of water is **stored at a high level** in the reservoir (1 mark).
- The water is released and **rushes down the penstock**, so its potential energy changes into **kinetic energy** (1 mark).
- The fast-moving water **strikes the blades of the turbine and makes it spin** (1 mark).
- The spinning turbine **drives the generator through the shaft**, and the generator **produces electricity**, which is carried away by the transmission lines (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for each correct step in the right order (4 marks). This is the curriculum exemplar on the processes a dammed river goes through to produce electricity. A candidate who merely writes 'water turns turbine, turbine turns generator' earns a maximum of 2 marks.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Kinetic energy of the moving water to mechanical (kinetic) energy of the turbine** (1 mark)
- (ii) **Mechanical (kinetic) energy to electrical energy** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). Both forms must be stated in each case.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The **higher the water is stored above the turbine, the greater its potential energy** (1 mark).
- As it falls, this becomes a **greater kinetic energy**, so the water **strikes the turbine with greater force and more electricity is produced** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The link between the height, the energy and the output must be made; 'so that the water can flow' alone earns 1 mark at most.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- The **water is renewable and free** once the dam has been built, so the **running cost is low** and no fuel has to be bought.
- **No fuel is burnt**, so there is **no smoke or air pollution** (accept: the reservoir also provides fish, water for irrigation and transport).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO (2 marks).*

**(f)** [1 marks]

- **People living in the valley lose their homes and farmland and have to be resettled** (accept: the still water breeds mosquitoes and bilharzia snails; the flow downstream is reduced, affecting farming and fishing).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one sound problem.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) W - **solar energy (light energy from the Sun)** (1 mark)
- (ii) X - **electrical energy** (1 mark)
- (iii) Y - **chemical energy** stored in the battery (1 mark)
- (iv) Z - **light energy** given out by the lamp (accept light and heat energy) (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). In (iii) the battery stores the energy as chemical energy; 'electrical energy' is not accepted there, because the arrow Y shows what the battery sends out after storing it - accept 'electrical energy' only where the candidate has clearly explained that the battery first stores it as chemical energy.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- The **solar panel** on the roof
  - *Marking note: 1 mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The panel **produces electricity only while the Sun is shining** (1 mark).
- The battery **stores the energy produced during the day and gives it out at night or on a cloudy day**, so the lamp can be used when there is no sunshine (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Heat energy** (1 mark).
- The lamp is meant to **give light**, so the energy that escapes as heat **does no useful work and is wasted to the surroundings** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. 'Sound' is not accepted; a lamp gives out negligible sound.*

**(e)** [1 marks]

- The village obtains **light without waiting to be connected to the national grid**; the sunshine is **free and plentiful**, there is **no fuel to buy and no smoke**, and it is safer than a kerosene lamp.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one sound advantage.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- The **moving air (wind) strikes the blades of the wind turbine and makes them spin** (1 mark).
- The spinning blades **turn a shaft that is connected to a generator** (1 mark).
- The generator **changes the mechanical energy into electrical energy**, which is stored in batteries or sent out along cables (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for each correct step in the right order (3 marks).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Animal dung is mixed with water and fed into a closed tank (digester)** from which air is excluded (1 mark).
- **Bacteria break down the dung**, and the **gas produced collects at the top of the digester and is piped off** (1 mark).
- Use: the gas is **burnt for cooking or for lighting** (accept: to run a small generator; the slurry left behind is used as manure) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks: 2 marks for the process and 1 mark for a use. The exclusion of air or the action of bacteria must appear for the second process mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- It **puts natural energy into a form people can actually use** - for lighting, cooking, pumping water, transport and industry.
- It **saves money and fuel and supports schools, clinics and businesses**, and reduces the cutting of firewood and the pollution that comes from burning fuels.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sound reasons (2 marks).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Our **lamps, machines and appliances are made to work on particular forms of energy**, usually electrical energy or heat energy (1 mark).
- Sunlight, wind and flowing water are **not in those forms**, so a device such as a solar panel, a turbine or a generator **must first convert them** before the energy can be used (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Kinetic (mechanical) energy to heat energy** (1 mark)
- (ii) **Potential energy to kinetic energy** (1 mark)
- (iii) **Chemical energy (in the boy) to kinetic energy to electrical energy to light energy** (accept kinetic to electrical to light) (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (3 marks). Both forms must appear in each answer.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **No device changes all the energy supplied to it into the useful form**; some always escapes to the surroundings, mostly as **heat from friction or from the resistance of the wires** (1 mark).
- Example: a **filament bulb becomes very hot** while it is giving light, so part of the electrical energy supplied leaves as heat (accept any suitable example) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the explanation and 1 mark for a suitable example.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Switch off lights, fans and the television when nobody is using them**, and **use energy-saving (LED) bulbs**.
- **Cover pots while cooking** and use the correct size of saucepan, dry clothes in the sun, and keep appliances well maintained.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO practical ways (2 marks).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The LED **changes a much greater part of the electrical energy supplied into light** and **wastes far less of it as heat** (1 mark).
- For the **same brightness it therefore uses less electricity**, so the cells last longer and the electricity bill is lower (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. A candidate who writes only that the LED 'is better' or 'is modern' earns no mark.*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Cut the cardboard into vanes (blades) and fix them evenly round a cork or a cut plastic bottle** to form the wheel.
- **Push the knitting needle through the centre to act as the axle** and rest its ends on two supports (for example two tins) so that the wheel spins freely.
- **Tie one end of the string to the axle and the small load to the other end**, so the string winds on to the axle as the wheel turns.
- **Pour water steadily on to the vanes from a height and observe** the wheel turning and the load being lifted; **repeat with a faster flow and record** what happens.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR workable steps in a sensible order (4 marks). The making of the wheel, the axle, the load and the testing must all appear for full marks.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- A clear sketch showing the **wheel with its vanes and the axle resting on the supports** (1 mark).
- The **string wound on the axle and carrying the load** shown correctly (1 mark).
- The **water being poured from above on to the vanes**, with **all the parts labelled** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks as shown. Award the marks for a workable arrangement, however roughly drawn; an unlabelled diagram scores a maximum of 1 mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The **potential energy of the water held above changes into kinetic energy** as the water falls on to the vanes (1 mark).
- This **turns the wheel (mechanical energy)**, which **lifts the load, so the energy becomes potential energy stored in the raised load** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept a correctly written chain such as 'potential to kinetic to mechanical to potential'.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- **Handle the knitting needle and the cutting tool carefully, keeping the sharp ends away from others** (accept: mop up spilt water at once so that nobody slips; keep water away from electrical sockets).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one sound precaution. 'Be careful' on its own earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 1: Energy | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.4.1.1** - Demonstrate the skill to evaluate the conversion of energy from one form to another.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 1: Energy, Basic 8, page 69, content standard B8/JHS2.4.1.1 with indicators B8/JHS2.4.1.1.1 (describe energy conversion) and B8/JHS2.4.1.1.2 (discuss the importance of conversion of energy). The exemplars quoted are: describe how energy is converted from one form to another; explain the processes that a dammed river goes through to produce electricity; and describe how to harness natural forms of energy into other forms.

> Note: Sub-Strand 1 (Energy) carries three content standards at Basic 8: B8/JHS2.4.1.1 (conversion of energy), B8/JHS2.4.1.2 (renewable energy sources and their sustainable management) and B8/JHS2.4.1.3 (heat and temperature). This paper examines B8/JHS2.4.1.1 only; the other two standards are examined in the companion paper. The school's content-standard sheets use the shorter coded form (B8.4.1.1); both forms are given in the blueprint.
