## QUALITY-CONTROL SUMMARY

| Check | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Every question within supplied curriculum scope | Yes - all items fall under Strand 4, Sub-Strand 1 (Energy), content standard B8/JHS2.4.1.1. Indicator B8/JHS2.4.1.1.1 (describe energy conversion) is served by the items on the forms of energy and the conversions in everyday devices (Questions 1, 3 and 5(a)); indicator B8/JHS2.4.1.1.2 (importance of conversion) is served by the dammed-river question (Question 2), the harnessing of wind and biogas (Question 4), the energy-loss items (Question 5) and the model water-wheel (Question 6). |
| Appropriate for the class | Yes - B8 level; pupils name forms of energy, write energy chains, read a section through a hydroelectric station and build a simple model. No calculations of work, power or efficiency are required, and no formulae are used, since the standard asks pupils to describe and evaluate conversions, not to compute them. |
| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, two figure-based questions, a process-description question drawn from the curriculum exemplar, and a practical design-and-draw task. |
| Sufficient application and reasoning | Yes - 35 of 100 marks (35%) at Apply level or above (Apply 9, Analyse 14, Evaluate 9, Create 3). The reasoning load sits in explaining why the dam wall is built high, why the battery is needed in the solar system, why energy is always lost as heat, and why an LED is more efficient than a filament bulb. |
| Plausible MCQ distractors | Yes - the commonest distractor is the same conversion written backwards (for example 'electrical to chemical' against 'chemical to electrical'), together with the neighbouring part of the power station (turbine, generator, penstock) and the neighbouring form of energy. |
| Single best answer per MCQ | Yes - reviewed item by item; special care with A9 and A14 (a cell in use and a cell being charged are opposite conversions), A19 and A21 (the turbine is turned by the water, the generator produces the electricity) and A35, where the common misconception that a generator 'creates' electricity is tested directly. |
| Marks internally consistent | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40; Section B 9 + 12 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 10 = 60; every sub-question total matches the marking scheme. |
| Total adds up correctly | Yes - 40 + 60 = 100. |
| Answer key correct | Yes - all 40 keys verified item by item against the paper and against Fig. 1 and Fig. 2; the physics re-checked: stored water holds potential energy, the penstock carries it to the turbine, the turbine drives the generator, a battery stores energy chemically, and some energy always leaves a conversion as heat. |
| Marking scheme matches questions | Yes - expected answers plus marking notes covering partial credit, accepted alternatives ('mechanical' for 'kinetic'), and the common errors, including writing only one form of energy where a change is asked for, and naming kinetic energy for the stored water in Question 2(a). |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - the instructions tell candidates to write an energy change in the form 'A energy to B energy'; Fig. 1 names every part of the station, and Fig. 2 letters the four stages W to Z and states beneath it that the letters stand for the forms of energy. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - the Akosombo Dam on the Volta, a solar home system at Bongo, a wind turbine at Ada, a biogas digester fed with animal dung, a bicycle dynamo and a household LED bulb. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the forms of energy, conversions between them, the dammed river and the harnessing of natural energy are exactly what the two indicators set out. The idea that energy is not destroyed but lost as heat appears only in words, since the formal law of conservation of energy belongs to content standard B8/JHS2.4.3.1 and is examined in the paper on that sub-strand. Renewable and non-renewable sources (B8/JHS2.4.1.2) are mentioned only where a conversion requires it. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - defining conversion, writing energy chains for named devices, describing the processes in a hydroelectric station, interpreting a lettered energy chain, describing how wind and biogas are harnessed, judging efficiency and energy waste, and designing, drawing and testing a model water-wheel. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- Sub-Strand 1 (Energy) has three content standards at Basic 8. This paper covers B8/JHS2.4.1.1 only. Renewable and non-renewable sources (B8/JHS2.4.1.2) and heat and temperature (B8/JHS2.4.1.3) are examined in the companion paper, so do not penalise candidates for omitting those topics here.
- Insist on the two-sided form of an energy change. 'Heat energy' alone is not an energy change; 'electrical energy to heat energy' is. This rule is printed in the instructions and applied throughout the marking scheme.
- Accept 'mechanical energy' wherever 'kinetic energy' is expected for a moving part such as the turbine or the water-wheel.
- Question 2(b) is the curriculum exemplar on the processes a dammed river goes through. Mark the four steps separately and in order; a two-line answer naming only the turbine and the generator cannot earn more than half the marks.
- In Question 3(a)(iii) the battery stores energy as chemical energy. Candidates who write 'electrical energy' have missed the storage step; award the mark only where they have shown that they understand the storage.
- Question 5(b) requires both an explanation and an example. Many candidates give one without the other.
- Question 6 is a practical task. If your class actually built the model, mark their own written account and drawing, and let the groups demonstrate the wheel lifting the load.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

### Section B - Theory (summary answers; full detail in the Marking Scheme)

| Question | Expected Answer | Curriculum Area | Cognitive Level |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (a) | (i) A renewable source is one that is replaced by nature as fast as it is used, so it does not run out, for example solar, wind and hydro. (ii) A non-renewable source took millions of years to form and is used up far faster than it can be replaced, for example coal, crude oil and natural gas. | Renewable and Non-Renewable Sources of Energy | Understand |
| 1 (b) | Renewable: wind, hydro, biogas. Non-renewable: coal, crude oil, natural gas. | Renewable and Non-Renewable Sources of Energy | Understand |
| 1 (c) | They are replaced by nature and will not run out; they do not pollute the air with smoke and harmful gases; the source (sun, wind, water) is free, so running costs are low; they can be used in villages far from the national grid. | Managing Renewable Energy Sources Sustainably | Evaluate |
| 2 (a) | P - the inlet (mixing) tank through which the dung and water are fed in; Q - the digester tank holding the slurry; R - the gas outlet pipe; S - the outlet through which the used slurry leaves. | Producing Energy from a Renewable Source | Understand |
| 2 (b) | Biogas (mainly methane); it is burnt in the school kitchen for cooking, and may also be used for lighting. | Producing Energy from a Renewable Source | Remember |
| 2 (c) | Animal dung is mixed with water and fed in through the inlet; the mixture is held in the closed digester where air is kept out; bacteria break down the organic matter and the gas produced collects above the slurry and is piped off. | Producing Energy from a Renewable Source | Understand |
| 2 (d) | The slurry that leaves at S is used as manure on the school farm; the dung that would have littered the compound is cleared, so the surroundings are cleaner and flies are reduced; the school saves the money it spent on firewood or gas. | Producing Energy from a Renewable Source | Evaluate |
| 2 (e) | The animal dung and other organic waste that feed the plant are produced every day as long as the animals are kept, so the source is replaced as fast as it is used and cannot be exhausted. | Renewable and Non-Renewable Sources of Energy | Analyse |
| 3 (a) | Solar: no electricity at night and less on cloudy days; the panels and batteries are expensive to buy and to replace; dust and dirt reduce the output; theft and damage. Hydro: the reservoir level falls during a drought; silting of the reservoir from erosion; the dam is very costly to build; people have to be resettled and the flow downstream is affected. | Managing Renewable Energy Sources Sustainably | Analyse |
| 3 (b) | Plant trees to replace those cut for firewood and protect the forests along the rivers; maintain the equipment - clean the panels, service the turbines and replace worn batteries; use energy sparingly and fit efficient appliances; train local people to repair the systems; prevent erosion so that the reservoir does not silt up. | Managing Renewable Energy Sources Sustainably | Apply |
| 3 (c) | Fossil fuels are non-renewable and will one day be exhausted; burning them pollutes the air and contributes to climate change; their prices rise and fall on the world market, so the country's electricity becomes costly and uncertain; a country that imports them loses foreign exchange. | Managing Renewable Energy Sources Sustainably | Evaluate |
| 4 (a) | Heat: a form of energy that flows from a hotter body to a cooler one; SI unit the joule (J); measured with a calorimeter (or calculated from the mass, the temperature change and the specific heat). Temperature: the degree of hotness or coldness of a body; SI unit the kelvin (K), commonly in degrees Celsius; measured with a thermometer. | Differences between Heat and Temperature | Understand |
| 4 (b) | When heat is supplied to a body its temperature rises, and when heat is taken from it the temperature falls; for the same substance, the greater the heat supplied the greater the rise in temperature, although the rise also depends on the mass of the body. | The Relationship between Heat and Temperature | Understand |
| 4 (c) | From the body at the higher temperature to the body at the lower temperature. | The Relationship between Heat and Temperature | Remember |
| 4 (d) | 27 + 273 = 300 K. | The Relationship between Heat and Temperature | Apply |
| 5 (a) | Cup A (90 °C). | Differences between Heat and Temperature | Understand |
| 5 (b) | Bucket B; although its temperature is lower, it contains a far greater mass of water (2 000 cm3 against 100 cm3), and the heat energy in a body depends on its mass as well as on its temperature, so the total heat in B is greater. | The Relationship between Heat and Temperature | Analyse |
| 5 (c) | Temperature measures only the degree of hotness of the water and does not depend on how much there is, while heat is the total energy in the water and depends on the quantity as well; so the hotter water is not always the one with more heat. | Differences between Heat and Temperature | Analyse |
| 5 (d) | Its temperature falls until it is the same as that of the room; this is because the water is hotter than its surroundings, so heat flows from the water to the cup and the surrounding air until both are at the same temperature. | The Relationship between Heat and Temperature | Analyse |
| 6 (a) | A beaker (or small saucepan) with water, a thermometer, a source of heat such as a Bunsen burner or a stove, a tripod stand and wire gauze, and a clock or stop-watch. | The Relationship between Heat and Temperature | Remember |
| 6 (b) | Pour a measured volume of water into the beaker and stand it on the gauze; place the thermometer in the water, with its bulb well below the surface but not touching the bottom, and read the starting temperature; light the burner and start the stop-watch; read and record the temperature every one minute, stirring gently, until the water boils; switch off the heat and plot or compare the readings. | The Relationship between Heat and Temperature | Apply |
| 6 (c) | A ruled two-column table headed 'Time (minutes)' and 'Temperature of water (°C)', with rows left blank for the readings. | The Relationship between Heat and Temperature | Create |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) In the tables, award the marks entry by entry; a candidate who writes the answers as a list instead of a table still earns the content marks. (4) Insist on the distinction between heat (energy, in joules) and temperature (degree of hotness, in kelvin or degrees Celsius). (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) A **renewable source of energy is one that is replaced by nature as fast as it is used, so it does not run out** (1 mark); examples are **solar, wind, hydro and biogas** (1 mark).
- (ii) A **non-renewable source took millions of years to form and is being used up far faster than it can be replaced** (1 mark); examples are **coal, crude oil and natural gas** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 4 marks: 1 mark for each definition and 1 mark for at least one correct example in each case.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Renewable sources:** wind, hydro, biogas
- **Non-renewable sources:** coal, crude oil, natural gas
  - *Marking note: 3 marks: award 1 mark for each pair of correct entries (6 correct entries = 3 marks; 4 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark). A candidate who writes the answers as two lists instead of a table still earns the marks. The list of sources is taken from the curriculum exemplar.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- They are **replaced by nature and will not run out**, while fossil fuels will one day be finished.
- They **do not pollute the air with smoke and harmful gases**, and the source itself is **free**, so the running cost is low (accept: they can serve villages far from the national grid).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO (2 marks).*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) P - the **inlet (mixing) tank**, through which the dung and water are fed into the plant (1 mark)
- (ii) Q - the **digester (digestion tank)**, in which the dung and water are broken down (1 mark)
- (iii) R - the **gas outlet pipe**, which carries the gas to the kitchen (1 mark)
- (iv) S - the **outlet (slurry outlet pipe and pit)**, through which the used slurry leaves the plant (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). Accept any wording that shows the correct function - for example 'feeding tank' for P and 'gas pipe' for R.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Biogas** (mainly **methane**) (1 mark)
- Use: it is **burnt in the school kitchen for cooking** (accept: for lighting the lamps) (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Animal dung is mixed with water and fed in through the inlet tank** (1 mark).
- The mixture is held in the **closed digester, from which air is kept out** (1 mark).
- **Bacteria break down the dung**, and the **gas formed collects above the slurry and is piped off** through R (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. The exclusion of air or the action of bacteria must appear for the second or third mark; an answer that says only 'the dung rots' earns 1 mark.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- The **slurry is used as manure on the school farm** (accept: the compound is kept clean and flies are reduced; the school saves the money spent on firewood, charcoal or LPG; fewer trees are cut for firewood).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one correct benefit other than the gas itself.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- The **dung and organic waste are produced every day** for as long as the animals are kept and the farm is worked (1 mark).
- The source is therefore **replaced as fast as it is used and cannot be used up**, which is what makes a source renewable (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The idea of continuous replacement must appear.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Solar:** there is **no sunshine at night and less on cloudy days**, so storage is needed; the **panels and batteries are costly to buy and to replace**, and **dust on the panels reduces the output** (2 marks).
- (ii) **Hydro:** the **water level in the reservoir falls during a long drought**, so less electricity is produced; the **reservoir silts up with eroded soil**, the dam is **very costly to build**, and **people have to be resettled** (2 marks).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO challenges under each source (4 marks). This answers the curriculum exemplar that asks pupils to create a table of the challenges; a table is acceptable here too.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Plant trees to replace those cut for firewood, and protect the forests along the rivers that feed the dam.**
- **Maintain the equipment** - clean the solar panels, service the turbines and replace worn-out batteries - and **train local people to carry out repairs**.
- **Use energy sparingly**, fit energy-saving appliances, and **check erosion so that the reservoir does not silt up**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE workable steps (3 marks).*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Fossil fuels are **non-renewable and will one day be used up**, so a country that depends on them alone will be left without power (1 mark).
- **Burning them pollutes the air** with smoke and harmful gases and adds to climate change (1 mark).
- Their **prices rise and fall on the world market**, so electricity becomes costly and uncertain, and money must be spent on importing them (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each for any three sound reasons.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [6 marks]

- **What it is** - Heat: a **form of energy that flows from a hotter body to a cooler one**; Temperature: the **degree of hotness or coldness of a body** (2 marks).
- **SI unit** - Heat: the **joule (J)**; Temperature: the **kelvin (K)** (commonly measured in degrees Celsius) (2 marks).
- **How it is measured** - Heat: with a **calorimeter** (or found from the mass and the temperature change); Temperature: with a **thermometer** (2 marks).
  - *Marking note: 6 marks, 1 mark for each correct entry in the table. Accept 'degree Celsius' for the unit of temperature, but the kelvin is the SI unit. This table answers the curriculum exemplar on the distinguishing features of heat and temperature.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **When heat is supplied to a body its temperature rises; when heat is taken away the temperature falls** (1 mark).
- For the same substance, the **greater the heat supplied the greater the rise in temperature**, though the rise also depends on the **mass of the body** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- From the **body at the higher temperature to the body at the lower temperature** (from hotter to cooler)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- **27 + 273 = 300 K**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for 300 K. Accept the working 27 + 273 shown with the correct answer; the unit K should be written.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- **Cup A**, whose thermometer reads 90 °C
  - *Marking note: 1 mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Bucket B** (1 mark).
- Although its **temperature is lower**, it holds a **far greater mass of water - 2 000 cm³ against 100 cm³** (1 mark).
- The **heat energy in a body depends on its mass as well as on its temperature**, so the total heat energy stored in B is greater (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks: 1 mark for naming B and 2 marks for the reason. Naming B with no reason earns 1 mark only.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Temperature measures only the degree of hotness** of the water and **does not depend on how much water there is** (1 mark).
- **Heat is the total energy in the water and depends on the mass as well as on the temperature**, so the hotter container is not necessarily the one with more heat energy (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. This is the key distinction in the standard.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- Its **temperature falls** (1 mark),
- because the water is **hotter than its surroundings, so heat flows out of it into the cup and the surrounding air** (1 mark),
- and it goes on losing heat **until the water and the surroundings are at the same temperature**, that is room temperature (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. A candidate who writes that 'coldness enters the water' loses the second mark; heat flows out, cold does not flow in.*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- A **beaker (or small saucepan) containing water**
- A **thermometer**
- A **source of heat** (Bunsen burner, spirit lamp or stove), with a **tripod stand and wire gauze**, and a **clock or stop-watch**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE suitable items (3 marks). The thermometer and the heat source should appear.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Pour a measured volume of water into the beaker** and stand it on the gauze on the tripod.
- **Place the thermometer in the water** with its bulb well under the surface but **not touching the bottom**, and **read the starting temperature**.
- **Light the burner and start the stop-watch at the same moment.**
- **Read and record the temperature every one minute**, stirring gently, until the water boils; then **switch off the heat and compare the readings**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR correct steps in a workable order (4 marks). The correct placing of the thermometer bulb and the regular timed readings should appear for full marks.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- A **ruled table with the headings 'Time (minutes)' and 'Temperature of the water (°C)'** (1 mark).
- **Units shown in the headings and blank rows provided** for the readings (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks as shown. A table without units in the headings scores 1 mark.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- **Handle the hot beaker with a cloth or tongs and keep away from the flame and the boiling water** (accept: do not stir with the thermometer; tie back loose clothing; stand clear of the steam).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one sound precaution. 'Be careful' on its own earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 1: Energy | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.4.1.2** - Show an understanding of the sources of renewable energy and how to manage these sources in a sustainable manner. **B8/JHS2.4.1.3** - Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between heat and temperature.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 1: Energy, Basic 8, pages 70 and 71. Content standard B8/JHS2.4.1.2 with indicators B8/JHS2.4.1.2.1 and B8/JHS2.4.1.2.2, and content standard B8/JHS2.4.1.3 with indicator B8/JHS2.4.1.3.1. The exemplars quoted are: explain renewable and non-renewable sources of energy; identify the various sources and classify them, e.g. wind, coal, hydro, crude oil, natural gas, solar and biogas; describe how to produce energy from a renewable source; research the stages involved in managing renewable energy sources; create a table to describe the challenges associated with the management of different sources of renewable energy; create a table to show the distinguishing features of temperature and heat; and discuss the relationship between temperature and heat.

> Note: Sub-Strand 1 (Energy) carries three content standards at Basic 8. B8/JHS2.4.1.1 (conversion of energy) was examined in the companion paper; this paper examines the remaining two standards, B8/JHS2.4.1.2 (Section A items 1 to 24 and Questions 1, 2 and 3) and B8/JHS2.4.1.3 (Section A items 25 to 40 and Questions 4, 5 and 6). The classification list in Question 1(b) is taken word for word from the curriculum exemplar, and the tables in Question 1(b) and Question 4(a) answer the exemplars that ask pupils to create tables.

B8/JHS2.4.1.2 (renewable energy and its sustainable management) is examined in Section A items 1 to 24 and in Questions 1, 2 and 3, including the classification exemplar (wind, coal, hydro, crude oil, natural gas, solar, biogas) and the exemplar on producing energy from a renewable source. B8/JHS2.4.1.3 (heat and temperature) is examined in items 25 to 40 and in Questions 4, 5 and 6, including the exemplar that asks for a table of the distinguishing features. |
| Appropriate for the class | Yes - B8 level; pupils classify sources, read a section through a biogas plant, compare heat with temperature and plan a simple heating experiment. The only calculation is the conversion of degrees Celsius to kelvin; the specific heat capacity formula is NOT used, as it lies beyond this indicator. |
| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, two figure-based questions, two table-completion tasks taken from the curriculum exemplars, and a practical planning question. |
| Sufficient application and reasoning | Yes - 36 of 100 marks (36%) at Apply level or above (Apply 9, Analyse 15, Evaluate 10, Create 2). The reasoning load sits in explaining why biogas is renewable, why a country should not depend on fossil fuels alone, and why the cooler bucket holds more heat energy than the hotter cup. |
| Plausible MCQ distractors | Yes - mixed lists in which one member spoils the set (for example 'coal, solar, wind'), the swapping of the definitions of heat and temperature, and the units joule, kelvin, degree Celsius and newton set against one another. |
| Single best answer per MCQ | Yes - reviewed item by item; special care with A8 and A9 (only one list is wholly renewable or wholly non-renewable), A13 (firewood is renewable only if the trees are replaced), A27 and A28 (the joule is the unit of heat, the kelvin the SI unit of temperature) and A40, where the match-and-bucket statement is correct. |
| Marks internally consistent | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40; Section B 9 + 12 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 10 = 60; every sub-question total matches the marking scheme. |
| Total adds up correctly | Yes - 40 + 60 = 100. |
| Answer key correct | Yes - all 40 keys verified item by item against the paper and against Fig. 1 and Fig. 2; the physics re-checked: heat is energy measured in joules and flows from hot to cold, temperature is the degree of hotness measured in kelvin or degrees Celsius, and the heat in a body depends on its mass as well as on its temperature. 30 °C = 303 K and 27 °C = 300 K. |
| Marking scheme matches questions | Yes - expected answers plus marking notes covering partial credit, the marking of the two tables entry by entry, accepted alternatives (degree Celsius for the unit of temperature), and the common errors, including writing that 'coldness enters the water' in Question 5(d). |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - the list of sources to be classified is printed in the question; Fig. 1 letters four parts P to S and shows where the dung enters and the gas goes; Fig. 2 prints the volume of water and the thermometer reading for each container. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - a biogas plant on a school farm, the hydroelectric station at Akosombo, the Tema oil refinery, solar lamps in a village, a clinic thermometer and the school kitchen. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - renewable and non-renewable sources, their sustainable management and the distinction between heat and temperature are exactly what the three indicators set out. Specific heat capacity, latent heat and the modes of heat transfer (conduction, convection and radiation) are NOT examined; the simple statement that heat flows from a hotter to a cooler body is used only because the indicator speaks of the relationship between heat and temperature in the environment. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - defining and classifying energy sources, labelling and explaining a biogas plant, listing management challenges, completing a comparison table, interpreting two containers of water, converting a temperature to kelvin, and planning and recording a heating experiment. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper completes Sub-Strand 1 (Energy). Content standard B8/JHS2.4.1.1 (energy conversion) is examined in the companion paper; the two standards examined here are B8/JHS2.4.1.2 and B8/JHS2.4.1.3. The blueprint shows which indicator each item serves.
- Question 1(b) and Question 4(a) answer the curriculum exemplars that ask pupils to create tables. Mark them entry by entry, and do not withhold content marks from a candidate who writes the entries as lists.
- The heart of the heat-and-temperature standard is Question 5(b) and 5(c): the cooler bucket holds more heat energy than the hotter cup because heat depends on mass as well as on temperature. Expect many candidates to answer 'Cup A' to both parts; mark the reasoning carefully.
- Insist on the correct units: heat in joules, temperature in kelvin (or degrees Celsius in everyday use). A candidate who gives the unit of heat as 'degrees' earns no mark.
- In Question 4(d), 27 °C = 300 K. Accept the answer with or without the working, but the unit K must be written.
- In Question 2(a), accept any wording that shows the correct function of the part; the exact textbook names (inlet, digester, gas outlet pipe, slurry outlet) are not required.
- Question 6 is a practical plan. If your class carried out the heating activity, accept their own tables of readings, and ask them to describe how the temperature rose and then stayed steady while the water boiled.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) In the flow chart, award marks for the correct stages in the correct order; the shape of the boxes does not matter. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- Electricity transmission is the **carrying of electrical energy from the power station where it is generated** (1 mark)
- **through cables, pylons, transformers and substations to the places where it is used** - homes, schools and factories (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Step-up transformer** - it **raises the voltage** of the electricity leaving the power station (1 mark) **before it is sent along the transmission lines**, so that less energy is lost on the way (1 mark).
- (ii) **Pylon** - the **tall steel tower that carries the high-voltage cables high above the ground**, out of reach (1 mark).
- (iii) **Insulator** - it **holds the cable away from the metal pylon** so that the current cannot pass into the tower and down to earth (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 4 marks as shown. In (i), 'it changes the voltage' earns 1 mark only; the direction of the change must be stated.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- The cables have **resistance**, so some electrical energy is always **turned into heat in them** as the current flows (1 mark).
- For the same amount of power, a **higher voltage means a smaller current** flowing in the cables (1 mark).
- The heat lost depends on the size of the current, so the **smaller current wastes far less energy** over the long distance (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. No formula is required; award full marks for the reasoning 'higher voltage - smaller current - less heat lost'.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) J - the **step-up transformer** at the power station (1 mark)
- (ii) K - the **step-down transformer at the substation** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). The side notes in Fig. 1 say that the voltage is raised at J and lowered at K; accept 'substation' for K only where the lowering of the voltage is also mentioned.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Its **voltage is raised at the power station and lowered again at the substation**.
- It **travels long distances along cables carried on pylons and is then shared out along the distribution lines** (accept: some of the energy is lost as heat in the cables).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct points (2 marks).*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The transmission voltage is **far too high for use in houses**: it would be **extremely dangerous and would destroy the appliances** (1 mark).
- It must be **brought down to the value that lamps, fans and other appliances are made to work on** (about 230 V in Ghana) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept the safety point or the appliance point for either mark.*

**(d)** [4 marks]

- **Four boxes drawn and joined by arrows pointing in one direction** (1 mark).
- **Box 1: the power station**, where the electricity is generated (1 mark).
- **Box 2 and Box 3: the step-up transformer with the transmission lines, and the substation with its step-down transformer** (1 mark).
- **Box 4: the school (the consumer)**, where the electricity is used (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 4 marks as shown. This is the curriculum exemplar that asks for a flow chart from the point of generation to the point of consumption. A chart whose arrows run the wrong way, or whose stages are out of order, loses the first mark.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- **Never touch or go near a fallen cable; keep others away and report it at once to the electricity company.**
- **Do not fly kites, climb trees or raise ladders and long metal objects near the lines**, and **do not build or tamper with transformers and substations** under the wires.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sound rules (2 marks).*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [6 marks]

- (i) **Resistor** - it **limits or controls the size of the current** flowing in the circuit (1 mark), and so **protects the other components from too large a current** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Diode** - it **allows current to pass through it in one direction only** (1 mark) and **blocks the current in the opposite direction** (1 mark).
- (iii) **LED (light emitting diode)** - it is a diode that **gives out light when current passes through it** (1 mark) **in the correct (forward) direction** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 6 marks, 2 marks for each component as shown.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- (i) Resistance - the **ohm** (1 mark)
- (ii) Capacitance - the **farad** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (2 marks). Accept the symbols, and accept the microfarad as a practical unit of capacitance.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- An LED has **very little resistance of its own**, so if it were connected alone **too large a current would flow through it and destroy it** (1 mark).
- The resistor **limits the current to a safe value**, so the LED lights properly and is not damaged (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) W - the **cell (battery)** (1 mark)
- (ii) X - the **switch** (shown open) (1 mark)
- (iii) Y - the **resistor** (1 mark)
- (iv) Z - the **capacitor** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). Accept 'dry cell' or 'battery' for W.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- The **circuit is completed and a current flows** from the cell through the resistor, so **charge begins to collect on the plates of the capacitor** (1 mark).
- The **LED flashes (glows briefly)** while this charging current is flowing (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(c)** [1 marks]

- The current **falls steadily to zero**, so **no further current flows** in that branch of the circuit
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. 'The current stops' is acceptable.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- The **LED glows brightly for a moment and then fades out** (1 mark).
- The **charged capacitor now acts as the source** and **drives a current through the LED as it discharges** (1 mark).
- As the **stored charge is used up the current falls**, so the light grows dimmer and finally goes out (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. This answers the curriculum exemplar on the discharging action of a capacitor. A candidate who says the LED stays on permanently earns no mark.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Two metal plates placed close together but not touching** (1 mark),
- **separated by an insulating material (air, waxed paper, mica or plastic)**, with a connecting lead joined to each plate (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The insulator between the plates must be mentioned for the second mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- When the switch is closed, **charge flows on to one plate and away from the other**, so one plate becomes **negatively charged and the other positively charged** (1 mark).
- The **current is large at first and falls steadily as the charge builds up** on the plates (1 mark).
- Charging stops when the **voltage across the capacitor is equal to the voltage of the supply**; the current then falls to zero (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. No charge actually crosses the insulator between the plates; do not penalise a candidate who does not mention this, but credit it as an alternative point.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- When the supply is removed and the plates are **joined through a conducting path, the stored charge flows back round the circuit** (in the opposite direction) (1 mark).
- This **gives a current that is large at first and falls to zero** as the capacitor empties, lighting an LED briefly if one is in the path (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Storing charge to give the flash in a camera**, and **smoothing the supply in a radio, television or phone charger**.
- **Keeping the clock or memory of a device running briefly when the power goes off**, **starting the motor of a fan or refrigerator**, or **timing the flashing of a lamp** (accept any two).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct uses (2 marks).*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Collect the components** - cell, switch, resistor, capacitor, LED and connecting wires - and **check that the cell is good**.
- **Connect the cell, the switch, the resistor and the capacitor in a loop**, joining the capacitor the correct way round (positive lead to the positive side).
- **Connect the LED across the capacitor**, with its longer leg towards the positive side, and **check every joint**.
- **Close the switch and observe the LED; then open the switch and observe it again**, recording what is seen each time.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR workable steps in a sensible order (4 marks). The correct way round of the LED or the capacitor, and the testing, should appear for full marks.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **On closing the switch**: the LED **flashes briefly and then goes out** as the capacitor charges up (1 mark).
- **On opening the switch**: the LED **glows again for a moment and fades away** as the capacitor discharges through it (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Use only the low-voltage cell provided - never the mains supply** - and **do not short-circuit the cell**.
- **Connect the capacitor and the LED the correct way round**, **discharge the capacitor before handling the leads**, and switch off when the work is finished.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sound precautions (2 marks). 'Be careful' on its own earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The **LED is connected the wrong way round**, so it cannot conduct (accept: the LED is damaged).
- The **cell is flat or wrongly connected, or a joint is loose so that the circuit is not complete** (accept: the resistor used is far too large).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sensible faults (2 marks).*

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 2: Electricity and Electronics | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.4.2.1** - Demonstrate knowledge of electricity transmission. **B8/JHS2.4.2.2** - Demonstrate understanding of the functions of capacitors in relation to LEDs, diodes and resistors in electronic circuits.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 2: Electricity and Electronics, Basic 8, page 72. The exemplars quoted are: identify different stages of electricity transmission; draw a flow chart to show the stages of electricity transmission from the point of generation to the point of consumption; research information about capacitors in electronic circuits and explain their functions when connected with direct current (DC); and describe the charging and discharging actions of a capacitor and explain the role of LEDs, diodes and resistors in an electronic circuit.

> Note: This paper covers the whole of Sub-Strand 2 at Basic 8: both content standards and both of their indicators. Section A items 1 to 20 and Questions 1 and 2 serve B8/JHS2.4.2.1.1 (transmission); items 21 to 40 and Questions 3, 4, 5 and 6 serve B8/JHS2.4.2.2.1 (capacitors with LEDs, diodes and resistors). The flow-chart exemplar is examined directly in Question 2(d), and the charging-and-discharging exemplar in Questions 4 and 5. | Every question within supplied curriculum scope | Yes - the paper covers the whole of Strand 4, Sub-Strand 2 at Basic 8. B8/JHS2.4.2.1.1 (explain how electricity transmission occurs) is examined in Section A items 1 to 20 and in Questions 1 and 2, including the exemplars on identifying the stages and drawing a flow chart from generation to consumption. B8/JHS2.4.2.2.1 (the charging and discharging action of a capacitor in a DC circuit) is examined in items 21 to 40 and in Questions 3, 4, 5 and 6, including the exemplar on the role of LEDs, diodes and resistors. |
| Appropriate for the class | Yes - B8 level; pupils name the stages of transmission, read a circuit diagram, explain charging and discharging in words and build a simple circuit. No calculations with Ohm's law, no time constants and no capacitor formulae are required, since the indicator asks pupils to demonstrate and describe the action, not to compute it. |
| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, two figure-based questions, a flow-chart drawing task, a fault-finding question and a practical circuit-building task. |
| Sufficient application and reasoning | Yes - 36 of 100 marks (36%) at Apply level or above (Apply 8, Analyse 15, Evaluate 9, Create 4). The reasoning load sits in explaining why transmission uses a high voltage, why the voltage must be lowered again, why a resistor protects an LED, and what is seen at the LED while a capacitor charges and discharges. |
| Plausible MCQ distractors | Yes - the neighbouring component (resistor against capacitor against diode), the neighbouring unit (ohm, farad, volt, ampere), the step-up transformer against the step-down transformer, and the reversed description of the charging current. |
| Single best answer per MCQ | Yes - reviewed item by item; special care with A5 and A8 (step-up at the station, step-down at the substation), A31 and A32 (the charging current is large at first and falls to zero, and a fully charged capacitor passes no further direct current) and A39, where the comparison of a capacitor with a cell is only partly correct. |
| Marks internally consistent | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40; Section B 9 + 12 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 10 = 60; every sub-question total matches the marking scheme. |
| Total adds up correctly | Yes - 40 + 60 = 100. |
| Answer key correct | Yes - all 40 keys verified item by item against the paper and against Fig. 1 and Fig. 2; the physics re-checked: raising the voltage lowers the current and so the heat lost in the cables; a diode conducts one way only; an LED needs a series resistor; a capacitor stores charge on two plates separated by an insulator, and in a steady DC circuit it blocks the current once it is fully charged. |
| Marking scheme matches questions | Yes - expected answers plus marking notes covering partial credit, the marking of the flow chart by stages and arrow direction, and the common errors, including saying only that a transformer 'changes the voltage' without the direction, and saying that the LED stays alight after the capacitor is fully charged. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - Fig. 1 names four of the six stages and letters only the two that are asked for, with side notes stating that the voltage is raised at J and lowered at K; Fig. 2 letters four components and names the LED, and the question says plainly that the switch is closed and later that the cell is removed. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - a power station, pylons and substations on the national grid, the household meter and fuse box, the 230 V supply used in Ghana, a fallen cable in the community, and a school workshop activity with cells and LEDs. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the stages of transmission and the action of capacitors with LEDs, diodes and resistors are exactly what the two indicators set out. Ohm's law calculations, the structure of the transformer core, semiconductor theory and alternating-current theory are NOT examined; alternating current is named only once, as the kind of supply used in homes. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - defining transmission, stating the function of transformers, pylons and insulators, reading a flow chart and drawing one, naming circuit components, describing charging and discharging, listing uses of capacitors, building and testing a circuit, and finding faults in a circuit that does not work. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper covers both content standards of Sub-Strand 2, so it completes Electricity and Electronics at Basic 8. The blueprint shows the indicator against every item.
- In Question 1(b)(i) and in the objective items on transformers, insist on the direction of the change: a step-up transformer RAISES the voltage; 'it changes the voltage' is worth half the marks at most.
- Question 2(d) is the curriculum exemplar that asks for a flow chart from the point of generation to the point of consumption. Mark the stages and the direction of the arrows; the shape and neatness of the boxes do not matter.
- Questions 4 and 5 are the heart of the capacitor standard. The expected sequence is: switch closed - charging current large at first - LED flashes - current falls to zero as the capacitor becomes fully charged - cell removed - capacitor discharges through the LED, which glows and fades.
- A common error is to write that the capacitor 'produces' electricity like a cell. Credit only answers that make clear that a capacitor stores charge given to it, while a cell produces electrical energy from chemicals.
- In Question 6, if your class actually built the circuit, mark their own observations. A large capacitor (1000 microfarads or more) and a resistor of about 1 kilohm with a 1.5 V or 3 V supply give a flash that is easy to see.
- Safety: pupils must use only low-voltage cells for this work. Never allow mains voltage in a classroom circuit activity.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In calculations, award a method mark for correct working even where the final answer is wrong, and insist on the unit in the final answer. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Energy can neither be created nor destroyed** (1 mark);
- it can only be **changed from one form into another**, so the **total energy before a change equals the total energy after it** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The first mark needs both 'not created' and 'not destroyed'; the second needs the change of form or the equality of the totals.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Energy conservation means **using energy carefully and avoiding waste** in the home, the school and the workplace (1 mark);
- so that **less fuel and electricity are used, costs are lower and the supply lasts longer** for the future (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Do NOT accept the law of conservation of energy as the answer here; the question asks for the everyday meaning.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Energy conversion** is the **changing of energy from one form into another**, for example electrical energy into light in a lamp (1 mark).
- **Energy conservation** is **using energy carefully so that none is wasted**, for example switching the lamp off when it is not needed (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark for each side of the difference. A candidate who explains only one of the two terms scores 1 mark.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- It **puts energy into the form we actually need** - light for reading, heat for cooking, movement for transport and machines (1 mark).
- It makes the **free natural energy of the Sun, the wind and flowing water useful** to people (1 mark).
- It **powers industry, hospitals, schools and communication**, so it supports work, education, health and the economy (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE sound points (3 marks). This answers the curriculum exemplar on classifying the importance of energy conversion in daily life.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- The **air conditioner**, which used **120 kWh**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **120 + 90 + 45 + 30 + 15** (1 mark)
- **= 300 kWh** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the correct addition of all five values and 1 mark for the answer with the unit kWh.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **(120 ÷ 300) × 100** (1 mark)
- **= 40%** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the correct method and 1 mark for the answer. Follow through from a wrong total in (b) - award the method mark.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- **90 − 15 = 75 kWh**
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. The unit must be given.*

**(e)** [3 marks]

- **Use the air conditioner for fewer hours, or use a fan instead**, and keep the doors and windows closed while it works.
- **Fit energy-saving (LED) bulbs and switch off lights that are not needed**, using daylight where possible.
- **Iron many clothes at one time**, **avoid opening the refrigerator too often**, and **switch off the television when nobody is watching**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE practical ways (3 marks). The answer should relate to the appliances shown in Fig. 1.*

**(f)** [2 marks]

- Lighting used **45 kWh**, so the cost is **45 × GH¢1.50** (1 mark)
- **= GH¢67.50** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for reading 45 kWh from the chart and multiplying, 1 mark for the answer in cedis. A candidate who uses the wrong bar but multiplies correctly earns the method mark only.*

**(g)** [1 marks]

- **Less electricity used means less fuel has to be burnt at the power station**, so **fewer harmful gases are released into the air** and fewer natural resources are used up.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for the link between using less electricity and less fuel burnt or less pollution.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Electrical energy** is changed into **light energy** (1 mark)
- **and heat energy** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. A candidate who gives only 'electrical to light' scores 1 mark, since Fig. 2 shows that heat is also produced.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Useful form: **light energy (10 J)** (1 mark)
- Wasted form: **heat energy (90 J)**, which escapes to the surroundings (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **10 J + 90 J = 100 J**, which is **exactly the energy supplied** to the lamp (1 mark).
- This shows that **no energy has been created or destroyed**: all of it has simply been **changed into other forms**, as the law of conservation of energy states (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The second mark needs the idea of conservation; simply writing '100 J' earns 1 mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **(10 ÷ 100) × 100** (1 mark)
- **= 10%** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the method and 1 mark for the answer with the per cent sign.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- An LED lamp **turns a much greater part of the electrical energy into light and wastes far less as heat** (1 mark).
- The family therefore gets the **same brightness for much less electricity**, so the **bill is lower and less fuel is burnt at the power station** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Burning fuels releases smoke and harmful gases** that pollute the air and cause coughs and chest diseases (1 mark).
- The **carbon dioxide released adds to global warming and changes the climate** (1 mark).
- **Cutting trees for firewood and charcoal destroys forests and causes soil erosion** (accept: dams flood farmland and displace people; oil spills pollute rivers and kill fish; generators make noise) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE sound points (3 marks).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Burning coal, petrol, diesel and gas **releases large amounts of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere** (1 mark).
- The carbon dioxide **traps heat that the Earth would otherwise send back into space** (1 mark).
- As more of the gas collects, the **Earth becomes warmer and the climate changes** - unreliable rains, floods and droughts (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. Candidates need not use the term 'greenhouse effect', but the trapping of heat must be described for the second mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The **forest cover is lost, so the soil is exposed and washed away by the rain (erosion)**, and **animals lose their habitats**.
- There are **fewer trees to take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen**, and the **rainfall of the area may fall, so streams dry up**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO effects (2 marks).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Less fuel is burnt**, so there is **less air pollution and less carbon dioxide** released.
- **Fewer trees are cut for firewood and charcoal**, and **the fuels and other resources last longer for future generations** (accept: fewer new power stations and dams are needed).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO benefits (2 marks).*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Switch off lights, fans and computers when the classroom or office is empty**, and at the close of school.
- **Use daylight in the classrooms** instead of switching on lamps during the day.
- **Fit energy-saving (LED) bulbs** and repair faulty switches and appliances.
- **Cook for the whole school at one time in covered pots**, and use an improved stove that needs less firewood.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR practical ways (4 marks).*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Less electricity, gas and charcoal are used, so the bills and the fuel bought each month cost less** (1 mark).
- **Appliances that are switched off and well maintained last longer**, so less money is spent on repairs and replacements (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **The habit:** leaving the **television, fan or security lights on when nobody needs them** (1 mark).
- **Why it wastes energy:** the appliance goes on **changing electrical energy into light, sound and heat that nobody uses**, and the bill rises (1 mark).
- **The correction:** **switch it off at the socket when it is not in use**, or fit a timer or sensor so that the lights come on only at night (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks as shown: 1 mark for naming a genuine habit, 1 mark for explaining the waste and 1 mark for a workable correction.*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A **clear title** and a short statement of **what energy conversion and energy conservation mean**.
- **Examples of energy changes in the school** (lamps, fans, the kitchen stove, the solar panel).
- **Practical tips for saving energy**, such as switching off lights and fans, and using daylight.
- **The effects of wasting energy** on the school's bills and on the environment, with a **simple diagram or chart and a short slogan**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR suitable items (4 marks). This answers the curriculum exemplar that asks pupils to make a poster presentation on their findings.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- A **rectangle representing the poster, divided into separate areas** (1 mark).
- **The title across the top and a diagram or chart in the middle** (1 mark).
- **A list of tips at the side and a slogan at the bottom**, with every area clearly named (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks as shown. Award the marks for a sensible, well-planned layout; artistic quality is not being marked. A plan with no labels scores a maximum of 1 mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Two sources: **science textbooks and the school library**, and the **internet** (accept newspapers, radio and television, the school's own electricity bills, or an officer from the electricity company) (1 mark for any two).
- Checking: **compare the information with a second source or a textbook, check how recent it is, and check that it comes from a known body** such as the Energy Commission or the electricity company (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for naming two sources and 1 mark for a sound way of checking reliability. This answers the exemplar on searching multimedia sources for information.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- **Display the poster on the notice board and explain it at the school assembly** (accept: talk to each class in turn, or present it at a science club meeting, an open day or a PTA meeting).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one workable way of presenting the findings.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 3: Conversion and Conservation of Energy | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.4.3.1** - Evaluate the impact of conversion of energy and energy conservation on the environment.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 3: Conversion and Conservation of Energy, Basic 8, page 73, content standard B8/JHS2.4.3.1 with the single indicator B8/JHS2.4.3.1.1. The exemplars quoted are: classify the importance of energy conversion and energy conservation in daily life; search from multimedia sources, books and the internet for information on the impact of energy conversion and conservation in their environment; and make a poster presentation on their findings.

> Note: This sub-strand carries one content standard and one indicator, so the blueprint separates the items by exemplar and by topic: the importance of conversion and conservation in daily life (Questions 1, 2, 3 and 5), the impact on the environment, which the content standard asks pupils to evaluate (Question 4), and the research-and-poster exemplar (Question 6). The formal law of conservation of energy belongs here rather than in the paper on B8/JHS2.4.1.1, where it was deliberately held back. The school's sheets use the shorter coded form (B8.4.3.1); both forms are given in the blueprint.

The three exemplars are examined: classifying the importance of energy conversion and conservation in daily life (Questions 1, 2, 3 and 5); gathering information on the impact of energy conversion and conservation in the environment (Question 4 and Question 6(c)); and making a poster presentation on the findings (Question 6). |

The arithmetic is limited to addition, subtraction, a percentage and one multiplication by a unit price. |
| Genuinely BECE-style | Yes - 40 four-option objectives plus structured theory with printed mark allocations, a data-handling question on a bar chart, an energy-flow diagram with a percentage calculation, an evaluative question on the environment, and a poster design task. |
| Sufficient application and reasoning | Yes - 37 of 100 marks (37%) at Apply level or above (Apply 11, Analyse 9, Evaluate 10, Create 7). The reasoning load sits in distinguishing conversion from conservation, showing that 10 J + 90 J = 100 J proves the law, explaining how burning fuels warms the Earth, and judging which measures would save the most energy. |
| Plausible MCQ distractors | Yes - conversion set against conservation, 'energy is destroyed' and 'energy is created' set against the correct statement of the law, and energy-saving actions set against actions that merely look sensible. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper is where the formal law of conservation of energy is examined. It was deliberately kept out of the paper on energy conversion (B8/JHS2.4.1.1), where it was referred to only in words.
- Keep the two senses of the word 'conservation' apart. Question 1(a) asks for the scientific law; Question 1(b) asks for the everyday meaning, which is the careful use of energy. Many candidates will give the law twice - mark 1(b) strictly.
- Question 3(c) is the key link between the two senses: the 10 J of light plus the 90 J of heat make exactly the 100 J supplied, which is the law in action.
- Award method marks generously in the calculations, but insist on the unit in the final answer: kWh in 2(b) and 2(d), cedis in 2(f), and the per cent sign in 2(c) and 3(d).
- Allow follow-through in Question 2(c): a candidate who found a wrong total in 2(b) but divided correctly still earns the method mark.
- Question 6 is the curriculum's poster exemplar. If your class actually produced posters, mark their own work against part (a), display the best of them, and let the groups present at assembly.
- Question 6(c) is about digital literacy as much as science: candidates must say how they would check that information found online is reliable.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In calculations, award a method mark for correct working even where the final answer is wrong, and insist on the unit in the final answer. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Magnetic materials (any two):** **iron, steel, nickel, cobalt** (1 mark for two).
- **Non-magnetic materials (any two):** **copper, aluminium, wood, rubber, plastic, glass** (1 mark for two).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for two correct magnetic materials and 1 mark for two correct non-magnetic materials. One correct material in a pair scores nothing for that pair.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **North near north: the magnets repel** - they push each other apart, because **like poles repel** (1 mark).
- **North near south: the magnets attract** - they pull together, because **unlike poles attract** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept the general rule as the explanation.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- A **permanent magnet keeps its magnetism for a long time**, while a **temporary magnet loses its magnetism as soon as the current or the magnetising force is removed**.
- A permanent magnet is usually made of **steel and is harder to magnetise**, while a temporary magnet is usually made of **soft iron and is magnetised easily** (accept: an electromagnet is a temporary magnet).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO valid differences (2 marks).*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **Place the knitting needle flat on a table and hold it firmly**, then take a bar magnet and place **one pole at one end of the needle** (1 mark).
- **Stroke the needle from one end to the other in one direction only**, lifting the magnet well clear of the needle at the end of each stroke and returning to the same starting end; repeat **many times (about 30 to 50) with the same pole** (1 mark).
- **Test the needle** by seeing whether it can pick up pins or iron filings, or by suspending it freely to see whether it comes to rest pointing north and south (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks as shown. The second mark depends on 'in one direction only' with the same pole; a candidate who strokes to and fro scores 0 for that mark. This is the curriculum exemplar on producing magnets using a bar magnet.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **P - coil of insulated copper wire** wound round the nail (1 mark).
- **Q - soft iron nail**, the core (1 mark).
- **R - dry cells / battery in a cell holder** (1 mark).
- **S - switch** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). Accept 'solenoid' for P, 'iron core' for Q and 'battery' for R. Do not accept 'wire' alone for P.*

**(b)** [1 marks]

- **An electromagnet** (a temporary magnet made by electricity).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Accept 'temporary magnet' only if 'electromagnet' is given.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The paper clips fall off the nail** (1 mark).
- Opening the switch **stops the current, so the magnetic field dies away and the soft iron loses its magnetism immediately** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the observation and 1 mark for the reason. The reason mark needs the current stopping AND the loss of magnetism.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Increase the number of turns of wire** wound round the nail.
- **Use more dry cells (a larger current)** in the circuit (accept: use a thicker soft iron core).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct ways (2 marks).*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- **Soft iron becomes a strong magnet as soon as the current flows and loses its magnetism as soon as the switch is opened** (1 mark).
- So the clips can be **picked up and released whenever the pupils wish**; **steel would stay magnetised** and would not let the clips go (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. A candidate who says only 'soft iron is a temporary magnet' scores 1 mark; the second mark needs the use made of that property.*

**(f)** [1 marks]

- **Lifting and dropping scrap iron and steel with a crane in a scrap yard or steel works** (accept: separating iron from other waste, electric bells, loudspeakers, electric motors).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one correct industrial use.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- The **acceleration of a body is directly proportional to the force applied to it** and takes place **in the direction of the force** (1 mark).
- and is **inversely proportional to the mass of the body**; in symbols **F = ma** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Award the second mark for the symbol form F = ma with the symbols explained.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **The larger the force applied, the larger the acceleration** - the two rise in the same ratio, so the **acceleration is directly proportional to the force** (1 mark).
- This is because the **mass of the trolley (2 kg) stays the same throughout**; in every row, force ÷ acceleration = 2 kg (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. The first mark needs 'directly proportional' or a clear statement that doubling the force doubles the acceleration; the second needs the constant mass.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **F = ma, so a = F ÷ m** (1 mark)
- **a = 20 ÷ 4** (1 mark)
- **a = 5 m/s²** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 3 marks: 1 mark for the correct formula, 1 mark for the correct substitution and 1 mark for the answer with the unit m/s². A correct answer with no working scores 2 marks.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **The loaded truck has a much larger mass than the empty one** (1 mark).
- From **F = ma, a = F ÷ m**, so with the **same force the larger mass gives a smaller acceleration** (1 mark).
- So the loaded truck **picks up speed slowly**, and a **larger force - a stronger push or a more powerful engine - is needed** to start it as quickly as the empty truck (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks as shown. Accept any sound daily-life example, such as pushing a loaded truck at Kaneshie market, a loaded wheelbarrow of sand, or a trotro full of passengers.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Showing direction** - the **magnetic compass** used by travellers and surveyors.
- **Producing sound** - the **loudspeaker** of a radio, a television or a mobile phone.
- **Giving a warning** - the **electric bell or the security alarm** on a door.
- **Lifting and separating scrap iron** - the **electromagnetic crane in a scrap yard**, or the separation of iron from other waste at a recycling plant (accept: magnetic door catch of a cupboard or refrigerator; electric motor in a fan, blender or corn mill; the bicycle dynamo).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR applications (4 marks). The mark needs both the use and the device or place; a bare list of devices with no use scores a maximum of 2 marks. This is the curriculum exemplar on demonstrating applications of magnetic force.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- The crane carries a **large electromagnet**; when the **current is switched on it becomes strongly magnetised and attracts the pieces of iron and steel**, which stick to it (1 mark).
- The crane **lifts and swings the load** across to the lorry or the heap where it is wanted (1 mark).
- The **current is then switched off**, the electromagnet **loses its magnetism and the scrap drops** at the right place, without anyone touching it (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks as shown. Candidates who describe a permanent magnet lifting the scrap score a maximum of 1 mark, since the load could not be released.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Set-up:** place a **trolley carrying a steel bar on a smooth, level bench**, mark a start line and a finish line, and arrange to pull the trolley with a **strong magnet** (1 mark).
- **Method:** pull the trolley with **one magnet and time how long it takes to reach the finish line**; then repeat with **two or three magnets held together, keeping the same trolley and the same distance**, so that only the force is changed (1 mark).
- **Result:** the trolley reaches the finish line in a **shorter time when the larger magnetic force is used**, which shows that the **larger the force, the larger the acceleration** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks as shown. Insist that only the force is changed: the same trolley, the same mass and the same distance. This is the curriculum exemplar on performing an experiment to show the relationship between force and motion using magnetic force.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- A **simple machine** is a device with **few or no moving parts that makes work easier by changing the size or the direction of the force applied** (1 mark).
- A **complex (compound) machine** is a machine **made up of two or more simple machines working together** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Lever** - a crowbar, a pair of scissors or the handles of a wheelbarrow.
- **Pulley** - the pulley used to draw water from a well or to lift blocks on a building site.
- **Inclined plane** - a ramp used to roll drums onto a lorry (accept: **wedge** - an axe or a knife; **screw** - a bolt or a bottle top; **wheel and axle** - a door knob or a steering wheel).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE simple machines, each with a correct example (3 marks). A name with no example scores half of nothing - award the mark only when both are given. This is the curriculum exemplar that recaps simple machines from B7/JHS1.4.4.2.1.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- A **simple machine is one device with few or no moving parts**, while a **complex machine is built from two or more simple machines working together**.
- A simple machine is usually **worked by the effort of a person and is cheap and easy to repair**, while a complex machine often **needs fuel or electricity, does much more work in a shorter time, and costs more to buy and maintain**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO valid differences (2 marks).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Corn mill** - grinds maize into dough for banku and kenkey (accept **blender** - grinds pepper, tomatoes and onions).
- **Tractor** - ploughs and harrows the land on a farm (accept **sewing machine** - sews cloth into garments; **bicycle or motorcycle** - carries people and loads; **water pump** - lifts water for irrigation).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO complex machines, each with its correct use (2 marks). Do not award a mark for a simple machine such as a cutlass, a ramp or a single pulley.*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **J - the brake lever** on the handlebar (1 mark).
- **K - the chain**, running over the toothed wheels (sprockets) (1 mark).
- **L - the pedal and crank** (1 mark).
- **M - the front wheel** (accept: wheel and tyre) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks).*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **J - a lever**: the brake lever turns about a pivot so that a small effort of the fingers gives a large pull on the brake cable (1 mark).
- **M - a wheel and axle**: the large wheel turns on the small axle at the hub (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. The example need not be explained; the correct name of the simple machine earns the mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- It is **made up of several simple machines working together** - levers (brake levers), wheels and axles (the wheels, the pedals and cranks), the chain and toothed wheels, and screws (the nuts and bolts) (1 mark).
- These parts **all act together to change the push of the rider's legs into the turning of the wheels**, which no single simple machine could do (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. A candidate who simply says 'it has many parts' scores 0; the simple machines must be identified for the first mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The pupil **travels to school, to the farm and to the market far more quickly and with less effort**, so he or she **arrives on time and less tired**, and **saves the money that would be spent on transport fares**.
- **Loads such as water, firewood and farm produce can be carried**, and the family can **reach the clinic quickly in an emergency**; the bicycle also **uses no fuel, so it does not pollute the air**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sound benefits (2 marks). This answers the curriculum exemplar on how the functions of a complex machine can improve the quality of life.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 4: Force and Motion | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.4.4.1** - Demonstrate the production of magnet, domestic and industrial application of magnetic force and its relationship with Newton's Second Law of motion and in everyday life. **B8/JHS2.4.4.2** - Demonstrate understanding of complex machines and how they work.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 4: Force and Motion, Basic 8, pages 74-75. Content standard B8/JHS2.4.4.1 with indicators B8/JHS2.4.4.1.1 (exemplars: produce magnets using magnetic materials such as pieces of iron and a bar magnet, and using electricity; demonstrate some applications of magnetic force in domestic and industrial activities, e.g. compass, alarms, loudspeakers; explore other industrial and domestic applications of magnetic force and present findings) and B8/JHS2.4.4.1.2 (exemplars: explain Newton's Second Law of motion with examples from daily life; perform an experiment to show the relationship between force and motion using magnetic force and the principle of Newton's Second Law of Motion); and content standard B8/JHS2.4.4.2 with indicator B8/JHS2.4.4.2.1 (exemplars: recap simple machines from B7/JHS1.4.4.2.1; explain what complex machines are and how they differ from simple machines; identify simple machines in complex machines; explain how the functions of a complex machine can improve the quality of life).

> Note: The paper carries two content standards and three indicators. Questions 1 and 2 cover the making of magnets (B8/JHS2.4.4.1.1, exemplar 1), Question 4 covers the domestic and industrial applications of magnetic force (B8/JHS2.4.4.1.1, exemplars 2 and 3), Question 3 covers Newton's Second Law and the force-and-motion experiment (B8/JHS2.4.4.1.2), and Questions 5 and 6 cover simple and complex machines (B8/JHS2.4.4.2.1). The school's sheets use the shorter coded form (B8.4.4.1 and B8.4.4.2); both forms are given in the blueprint.
