## QUALITY-CONTROL SUMMARY

| Check | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Items traceable to the curriculum | Yes - every Section A item and every Section B part is mapped in the blueprint to B8/JHS2.4.4.1.1, B8/JHS2.4.4.1.2 or B8/JHS2.4.4.2.1 and to one of the five topics drawn from the exemplars. |
| Key balance in Section A | Yes - the correct answers are evenly spread over A, B, C and D (10 each), with no letter repeated more than twice in a row and no cyclic pattern. |
| One defensible answer per item | Yes - each item has a single correct option; the distractors are common classroom errors, such as confusing mass with force, confusing the direction of the stroking in the single-touch method, and calling a single pulley or a ramp a complex machine. |
| Marks add up | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40 marks; Section B 9 + 12 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 10 = 60 marks; total 100 marks. |
| Cognitive spread | Yes - the paper runs from recall of magnetic materials, the law and the names of simple machines, through understanding and application (making a magnet, calculating an acceleration, designing an experiment), to analysis and evaluation (why soft iron is used, why a loaded truck is harder to start, how a bicycle improves life). |
| Difficulty mix close to 30 / 50 / 20 | Yes - the mix is reported in the Cognitive-Level Distribution section below and is within the tolerance set for a mock paper. |
| Figures readable in black and white | Yes - both figures are hand-drawn pencil sketches with handwriting-style labels, and they print clearly in black and white on a photocopier. |
| Figure labels do not give the answers away | Yes - the parts of the electromagnet in Fig. 1 and the parts of the bicycle in Fig. 2 carry only the letters P, Q, R, S, T and J, K, L, M; the names the candidates must supply are nowhere printed on the figures, and neither caption names the method or the simple machines. |
| Calculations checked | Yes - in Question 3(c), a = F / m = 20 / 4 = 5 m/s²; the table in Question 3 is consistent with F = ma for a 2 kg trolley (4 N with 2 m/s², 6 N with 3 m/s², 10 N with 5 m/s²); Section A items 25 and 26 give 12 / 3 = 4 m/s² and 5 x 3 = 15 N. |
| Marking scheme usable by any teacher | Yes - every part carries its mark allocation, the expected points are listed, and the italic marking notes state what is compulsory for each mark, what alternatives are acceptable, and the common errors to watch for. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - Fig. 1 shows the complete circuit with the switch and the clips; the table in Question 3 gives the mass of the trolley and the unit of each row; every calculation states the quantities needed. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - pupils of Nsuta M/A Basic School building an electromagnet, a bicycle used by a pupil in Tamale, a loaded truck at Kaneshie market, a corn mill grinding maize for banku and kenkey, and a scrap yard sorting iron and steel. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - magnetic fields are named but no field-line theory is examined; Newton's Second Law is kept to F = ma with whole numbers, as the indicator intends; momentum, friction coefficients, mechanical advantage and velocity ratio are not introduced. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - naming materials and poles, describing a practical method of making a magnet, reading a labelled circuit sketch, explaining the behaviour of soft iron, reading a table of results, stating a law, performing a calculation, designing an experiment, listing applications of magnetic force, and identifying the simple machines inside a bicycle. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- Question 1(d) and Question 2 together cover the first exemplar of B8/JHS2.4.4.1.1: making a magnet with a bar magnet and making one with electricity. If your class actually carried out the two methods, mark their own records against these answers.
- In Question 1(d) the stroking must be in one direction only and with the same pole. Candidates who stroke to and fro lose that mark, because the needle would not become a magnet.
- Question 2(e) is the discriminating item of the paper: the candidate must connect the property of soft iron to the use made of it. Award 1 mark for the property alone.
- Newton's Second Law is examined at the level the indicator sets: the acceleration rises with the force and falls with the mass, with F = ma used on whole numbers. Do not penalise a candidate who writes a = F/m instead of F = ma.
- Award the method marks in Question 3(c) even where the arithmetic is wrong, but insist on the unit m/s² in the final answer.
- In Question 4(c) the control of the experiment matters: the same trolley, the same mass and the same distance, with only the magnetic force changed. Refuse the third mark to a candidate who changes the load as well as the force.
- Question 5(b) asks for a name AND an example in each case. A list of three names with no examples scores nothing; tell your class this before the next mock.
- In Question 6(b), accept 'wheel and axle' for M and 'lever' for J only. 'Pulley' for the chain drive in 6(c) is accepted because the chain and sprockets act in the same way as a belt and pulleys.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Accept the common Ghanaian names of the tools, for example 'machete' for cutlass and 'shears' for secateurs. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- An agricultural tool is a **simple implement, usually worked by hand, used to carry out activities on a farm or in a garden** (1 mark).
- Farmers use tools because they **make the work easier, faster, neater and safer than using the bare hands** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Cutlass** - for **clearing weeds and grass** from the plot.
- **Hoe** - for **tilling the soil and making ridges or mounds**.
- **Watering can** - for **watering seedlings and vegetable beds**.
- **Wheelbarrow** - for **carrying manure, soil and farm produce** (accept rake, garden fork, trowel, secateurs, knapsack sprayer, sickle, axe, pickaxe, head pan or dibber with a correct use).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR tools, each with a correct use (4 marks). A tool named with no use, or with a wrong use, scores nothing for that item. This is the curriculum exemplar on collecting and listing the different types of agricultural tools.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **The activity to be done** - clearing, tilling, planting, watering, pruning or carrying.
- **The condition of the land or the crop** - how hard the soil is, how tall the weeds are, how delicate the seedlings are.
- **The size, weight and strength of the pupil** who will use it, and whether the tool is **sharp, sound and safe to use** (accept: whether it is available in the store).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE sound points (3 marks).*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [6 marks]

- **A - cutlass** (machete) (1 mark).
- **B - hoe** (1 mark).
- **C - rake** (1 mark).
- **D - watering can** (1 mark).
- **E - garden fork** (1 mark).
- **F - wheelbarrow** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (6 marks). Accept 'machete' for A and 'digging fork' for E. Do not accept 'knife' for A or 'spade' for E.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **A (cutlass)** - **clearing weeds, grass and shrubs** from the plot (1 mark).
- **D (watering can)** - **watering seedlings and vegetable beds** (1 mark).
- **F (wheelbarrow)** - **carrying manure, soil, refuse and harvested produce** about the garden (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for a correct activity (3 marks).*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **B - the hoe**, which **breaks up and tills the soil** into small lumps (accept **E, the garden fork**, which loosens and turns the soil) (1 mark).
- **C - the rake**, which **levels the bed, makes the soil fine and gathers off the stones and dry leaves** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for each tool correctly named WITH what it does. The rake must be one of the two tools given.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- **F - the wheelbarrow**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark. Accept the letter alone or the name alone.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Hold the handle firmly with both hands, stand with the feet apart** and **swing the hoe so that the blade enters the soil** (1 mark).
- **Pull the loosened soil towards you, turn it over and break the lumps**, removing roots and stones (1 mark).
- **Work backwards in strips across the plot** until the whole bed is dug, then **draw the soil together into a level bed or into ridges** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks as shown. Accept any sound, well-ordered description of the digging, the turning of the soil and the shaping of the bed. This is the curriculum exemplar on explaining how the tools are used to perform specific activities.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Fill the can with clean water, fit the rose and hold the can by the handle** (1 mark).
- **Walk slowly along the bed, tilting the can so that the water falls over the seedlings**, moving it to and fro so that every plant is reached and the soil is wetted evenly (1 mark).
- **The rose breaks the water into many fine drops**, so it **does not wash away the soil or beat down and damage the young seedlings** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks: 2 marks for the method and 1 mark for the reason. The reason mark needs the gentle, fine drops and the protection of the seedlings or the soil.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The work is **done more quickly and with less effort**, and the job is **done neatly and properly**.
- The **crops, the soil and the tool itself are not damaged**, and there is **less risk of injury** to the user.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sound reasons (2 marks).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The injury:** a **cut on the hand or the foot from a cutlass or a hoe** (accept a blister, a wound from a tool left blade upwards, or poisoning from a sprayer) (1 mark).
- **The prevention:** **keep a safe working distance from other pupils, carry the cutlass with the blade pointing down and away from the body, wear boots and gloves, pass a tool handle first and never play with tools** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for a genuine injury and 1 mark for a prevention that matches it.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **W - cutlass** (machete) (1 mark).
- **X - hoe** (1 mark).
- **Y - watering can** (1 mark).
- **Z - secateurs (pruning shears)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (4 marks). Accept 'sickle' for W and 'pruning knife' for Z. Do not accept the hoe for W, since the weeds must first be cut down.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **W:** the weeds are **tall and woody**, and a **sharp cutlass cuts them down quickly at ground level with a swinging stroke** (1 mark); a small hand tool such as a trowel could not do this work, and the plot must be cleared before it can be tilled (1 mark).
- **Z:** the hedge must be **cut evenly on the top and the sides** (1 mark); **secateurs or shears cut the small branches cleanly without tearing them** or damaging the rest of the hedge (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks for each reason (4 marks). Award the second mark of each pair only where the candidate goes beyond repeating the name of the tool - a comparison with an unsuitable tool, or the quality of the cut, earns it.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The wheelbarrow** (accept the rake or the watering can) (1 mark).
- It would be needed in **more than one area**: for example, to **cart away the cut weeds from W, bring manure to the ridges in X and carry off the trimmings from Z** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the tool and 1 mark for a reason that covers at least two of the four areas. A tool named with only one use scores 1 mark.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Wash or scrape off the soil after use and dry the tool well.**
- **Rub the metal parts with oil or grease** so that they do not rust.
- **Sharpen the cutting edges regularly with a file**, and **tighten or replace loose or broken handles**.
- **Store the tools in a dry store or shed**, hung up or arranged neatly, and never leave them lying in the field.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR correct ways (4 marks).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **They last longer**, so the school **saves the money it would spend replacing them**.
- **They work well**, so the work is **easier, faster and neater**.
- **They are safe to use** - blunt blades and loose handles slip and cause injuries - and they are **always ready for the next lesson**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE sound reasons (3 marks).*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Carry a cutlass or any sharp tool with the blade pointing downwards and away from the body**, and **pass a sharp tool handle first**.
- **Keep a safe distance from other pupils when swinging a tool**, never play with or run while carrying one, and **never leave a tool lying with its blade or prongs facing upwards** (accept: wear boots and gloves).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO genuine safety rules (2 marks).*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Visit the garden store, the school farm and nearby farms and list all the tools found** (1 mark).
- **Collect a picture of each tool** - draw it, photograph it or cut one from a catalogue or a magazine (1 mark).
- **Paste each picture on its own page and write the name, the use and the care of the tool beside it** (1 mark).
- **Arrange the pages in groups** - cutting tools, digging tools, carrying tools, watering tools - and add a **cover, a title page and a list of contents** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR sensible steps in a reasonable order (4 marks). This is the curriculum exemplar on matching each tool with its activity and creating an album of the tools.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Name of the tool** (with its local name).
- **The farm activity it is used for**, and **how it is used**.
- **How it is cared for and stored** (accept: the parts of the tool, or the safety rules for using it).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE suitable headings (3 marks).*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Two sources: **the agricultural science textbook and the school library**, and **the internet** (accept farm catalogues, newspapers, the garden store itself, a farmer, a hardware seller or the agricultural extension officer) (1 mark for any two).
- Checking: **compare the information with a second source or the textbook**, or **show it to the teacher, an experienced farmer or the agricultural extension officer** for confirmation (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for naming two sources and 1 mark for a sound way of checking. This part also carries the digital-literacy competency.*

**(d)** [1 marks]

- **Display it in the garden store, the library or at the school open day, and present it to the class or at assembly**, so that it serves as a guide for the pupils who use the tools.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark for any one sensible way of presenting the album.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 5: Agricultural Tools | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.4.5.1** - Demonstrate knowledge and skills in the use of basic and simple agricultural tools for basic on-farm activities.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 5: Agricultural Tools, Basic 8, page 76. Content standard B8/JHS2.4.5.1 with indicator B8/JHS2.4.5.1.1 (exemplars: collect and list different types of agricultural tools used for on-farm activities; match each tool with the familiar type of agricultural activity it is used for and create an album of the tools) and indicator B8/JHS2.4.5.1.2 (exemplars: explain how the different agricultural tools are used on a farm or school garden to perform specific agricultural activities; practise the use of different agricultural tools for specific activities on a farm or school garden; select appropriate tools for specific agriculture tasks).

> Note: The paper carries one content standard and two indicators. Questions 1 and 2 cover the listing and naming of tools and the matching of each tool to its activity (B8/JHS2.4.5.1.1); Question 6 covers the album exemplar of the same indicator. Question 3 covers the correct use of tools and Question 4 the selection of the appropriate tool for a task (B8/JHS2.4.5.1.2); Question 5 covers the care, maintenance and safe use that the practical exemplar of that indicator demands. The school's sheets use the shorter coded form (B8.4.5.1); both forms are given in the blueprint.

| Key balance in Section A | Yes - the correct answers are evenly spread over A, B, C and D (10 each), with no letter repeated more than twice in a row and no cyclic pattern. |
| One defensible answer per item | Yes - each item has a single correct option. The distractors are tools that pupils genuinely confuse - rake and garden fork, trowel and dibber, sickle and secateurs - and common wrong practices, such as carrying a cutlass blade upwards. |
| Marks add up | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40 marks; Section B 9 + 12 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 10 = 60 marks; total 100 marks. |
| Cognitive spread | Yes - the paper runs from naming tools, through matching each tool to its activity and describing correct use, to selecting the right tool for a given plot, justifying the choice and planning an album. |
| Difficulty mix close to 30 / 50 / 20 | Yes - the mix is reported in the Cognitive-Level Distribution section below and is within the tolerance set for a mock paper. |
| Figures readable in black and white | Yes - both figures are hand-drawn pencil sketches with handwriting-style labels, and they print clearly in black and white on a photocopier. |
| Figure labels do not give the answers away | Yes - the six tools in Fig. 1 carry only the letters A to F, and no tool is named anywhere on the figure or in its caption. The four areas in Fig. 2 state the work waiting in each - tall weeds, ridges to be made, seedlings on dry soil, an uneven hedge - but name no tool, so the candidate must still choose one. |
| Practical content is genuinely practical | Yes - Questions 3 and 4 ask how the hoe and the watering can are actually handled and which tool suits each plot of a real school garden, which is what indicator B8/JHS2.4.5.1.2 requires the pupils to practise. |
| Marking scheme usable by any teacher | Yes - every part carries its mark allocation, the expected points are listed, and the italic marking notes state what is compulsory for each mark, which local names are acceptable, and the common errors to watch for. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - Fig. 1 shows each tool separately with its own letter; Fig. 2 states the work waiting in each area; and where more than one tool would serve, the marking scheme lists the acceptable alternatives. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - a Basic 8 school garden, the garden store, the cutlass and hoe of the Ghanaian farm, a compost heap, the school open day, and the agricultural extension officer. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the paper keeps to basic and simple hand tools as the indicator states. Tractors and other farm machinery are not examined; the knapsack sprayer appears only as a tool that applies liquid chemicals, with no chemistry of weedicides. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - defining and listing, naming tools from a sketch, matching tools to activities, describing how a tool is handled, choosing tools for four different plots and justifying the choice, stating care and safety rules, and planning an album. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper closes Strand 4. It is practical by nature: if your class worked in the school garden this term, mark their own records and tool-handling against Questions 3, 4 and 5 as well.
- Accept the local and common names of the tools. 'Machete' for cutlass, 'shears' for secateurs and 'digging fork' for garden fork all earn the mark; a vague 'knife' or 'spade' does not.
- In Question 2(a) the candidate must read the sketches. Tell the class beforehand that the rake has teeth on a bar while the garden fork has long prongs at the end of a handle - this is the commonest confusion in the paper.
- Question 4(b) is the discriminating part: a candidate who only repeats the name of the tool scores half the marks. The second mark of each pair needs a real reason - the nature of the weeds or the quality of the cut.
- Do not accept the hoe as the first tool for area W. Tall weeds must be cut down with a cutlass before the plot can be tilled.
- In Question 3(a) and 3(b), the method marks are for a clear, ordered description. A candidate who writes only 'use the hoe to dig' scores 1 mark at most.
- Question 5 carries the safety teaching of the sub-strand. Read the answers to 5(c) aloud in class; these are the rules that prevent accidents during practical lessons.
- Question 6 is the curriculum's album exemplar. If your groups actually produced albums, mark their work against part (a), display the best of them in the garden store, and let the groups present at assembly.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

Water the heap lightly, cover it with leaves or a sack, and turn it every two weeks. After about two to three months the compost is dark, crumbly and sweet-smelling, and is ready to be spread on the beds. | Sustainable Approaches to Waste Management | Apply |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In calculations, award a method mark for correct working even where the final answer is wrong, and insist on the per cent sign where a percentage is asked for. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Waste** is **any material that is no longer wanted or useful to the person or place that produced it** (1 mark).
- **Waste management** is the **collection, sorting, treatment and safe disposal of waste**, including reducing, reusing and recycling it (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Solid waste** - plastic bottles, sachet-water bags, broken bottles, sweepings.
- **Liquid waste** - bath water, water from the kitchen sink, waste water from a factory.
- **Gaseous waste** - smoke from a chimney, exhaust fumes from a vehicle.
- **Medical waste** - used syringes, bandages and expired drugs (accept domestic, agricultural, industrial or electronic waste with a correct example).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR types, each with a correct example (4 marks). A type named with no example, or with a wrong example, scores nothing for that item. Candidates may use either classification - by state (solid, liquid, gaseous) or by source (domestic, industrial, agricultural, medical, electronic) - or a mixture of the two.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- To **keep the community clean and free from offensive smells**, and to **prevent diseases** such as cholera, typhoid and malaria.
- To **stop gutters from choking and causing floods**, and to **protect the soil, the streams and the air from pollution**.
- To **recover useful materials and manure** from the waste, and to keep the community attractive to visitors and to business.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE sound reasons (3 marks).*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [5 marks]

- **A - reduce** (prevention: avoid producing the waste in the first place) (1 mark).
- **B - reuse** (1 mark).
- **C - recycle** (1 mark).
- **D - recover** - composting, or recovering energy from the waste (1 mark).
- **E - disposal** - landfill or incineration (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (5 marks). The order must be as shown. Accept 'refuse' or 'prevent' for A, 'composting' for D and 'dumping in a sanitary landfill' for E.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Waste that is never produced does not have to be collected, treated or disposed of at all**, so no land, fuel or money is spent on it and it cannot pollute the environment (1 mark).
- It also **saves the raw materials and the energy** that would have been used to make the goods in the first place (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. A candidate who merely writes 'because it is at the top' scores 0.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **A (reduce):** **carry a basket to the market instead of collecting plastic bags**, or write and photocopy on both sides of the paper (1 mark).
- **B (reuse):** **wash a glass bottle and use it again to store drinking water**, or use empty tins as pots for seedlings in the school garden (1 mark).
- **C (recycle):** **collect plastic bottles and sachet bags and send them to a recycling factory** to be made into new plastic items (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each (3 marks). The example must match the level: a candidate who gives recycling as an example of reuse scores 0 for that mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Nothing useful is recovered** - the materials, the plant nutrients and the energy in the waste are all lost (1 mark).
- It **takes up land**, and dumps and open burning **pollute the soil, the water and the air and breed flies, rats and mosquitoes** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sound reasons (2 marks).*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Diseases such as cholera, typhoid and dysentery spread**, because flies settle on the refuse and then on food, and dirty water enters the wells and streams.
- **Mosquitoes breed in the stagnant water** held in discarded tins and containers and spread **malaria**; rats and cockroaches also multiply.
- **Gutters choke with plastics and the town floods** when it rains.
- **The air, the soil and the streams are polluted** by smoke, bad smells and the liquid that drains from the dump; **animals swallow plastics and die**, and the community looks dirty.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR correct effects (4 marks).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Plastics do not rot**, so they **collect in the gutters and block them** (1 mark).
- When it rains the **water cannot flow away, so it overflows and floods the streets and houses** (1 mark).
- The **flood water carries rubbish and human waste into homes and wells, spreading cholera and typhoid**, and the **pools left behind breed mosquitoes that spread malaria** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks as shown - blocking, flooding and the spread of disease. A candidate who stops at the flooding scores 2 marks.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Open burning gives off **thick smoke, soot, carbon dioxide and poisonous gases**, especially when **plastics and rubber** are burnt (1 mark).
- The smoke **pollutes the air**, so the air is dirty to breathe and visibility is poor (1 mark).
- People living nearby suffer **coughing, catarrh, sore eyes and chest diseases such as asthma and bronchitis**, and the fire may spread and destroy property (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks as shown; 1 mark each for the gases, the pollution and the effect on health.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- **Taking the waste to a public container**, used by **80 households**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **36 + 24** (1 mark)
- **= 60 households** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for adding the two correct values and 1 mark for the answer.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **20 ÷ 200 × 100** (1 mark)
- **= 10%** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the correct method and 1 mark for the answer with the per cent sign.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Burning** - it gives off **smoke and poisonous gases that pollute the air** and cause chest diseases (1 mark).
- **Dumping in a gutter or the bush** - it **chokes the gutters and causes floods**, breeds flies and mosquitoes and litters the land (1 mark). (Accept **burying** in an unprepared pit, since plastics do not rot and the drainage can pollute the groundwater.)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for each harmful method correctly named WITH its reason. A method with no reason scores nothing.*

**(e)** [3 marks]

- **Provide more public containers and have them emptied regularly**, and extend the collection service to more houses.
- **Teach households to separate their waste** and to **compost the biodegradable part** for the farms and gardens, while plastics and metals are collected for recycling.
- **Stop open burning and dumping in gutters** through education and the enforcement of the sanitation bye-laws, supported by a regular community clean-up day.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE workable recommendations (3 marks). The recommendation must follow from the survey results; a general statement such as 'the people should be serious' scores 0. This is the curriculum exemplar on presenting a report on a community survey.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Find out what waste the school produces and where it comes from**, then **agree on the aim and plan the activity with the head teacher** (1 mark).
- **Provide and clearly label separate bins** for food waste, paper, plastics and metals, and **place them at the classrooms, the kitchen and the canteen** (1 mark).
- **Educate the pupils at assembly** on which waste goes into which bin, and **appoint a sanitation prefect or duty group** for each week (1 mark).
- **Empty the bins regularly - compost the food waste in the school garden and hand the plastics and metals to the recyclers** - and keep records of what is collected (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR sensible steps in a workable order (4 marks). This is the curriculum exemplar that asks pupils to carry out a waste management activity using the knowledge they have gained.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Compare the compound before and after** - count the heaps of litter or photograph the same spots each week.
- **Measure the waste**: see whether the **number of bags sent to the dump each week has fallen**, and how much **compost and how many sacks of plastics have been recovered**.
- **Check whether the bins are being used correctly** and **ask the pupils, teachers and cleaners for their views**; look also at whether the cost of waste collection has fallen.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE genuine ways of evaluating (3 marks). The way must allow a comparison or a measurement; 'the school will be clean' alone scores 0. This part carries the evaluation exemplar of indicator B8/JHS2.5.1.1.2.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Talk about the project at assembly and at the P.T.A. meeting, and put up posters and slogans** on the notice board; form a **sanitation club** and reward the cleanest class each month.
- **Invite the chief, the assembly member and the environmental health officer**, hold a **community clean-up day**, and spread the message through the information centre, the local radio station or social media.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO practical ways (2 marks).*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Choose a shaded corner of the garden and clear a space or dig a shallow pit** (1 mark).
- **Collect biodegradable waste** - kitchen peelings, vegetable remains, grass, leaves and animal droppings - and **build the heap in layers**: plant waste, then droppings or old manure, then a thin layer of topsoil, until it is about a metre high (1 mark).
- **Water the heap lightly and cover it** with leaves, grass or an old sack to keep in the moisture and the heat (1 mark).
- **Turn the heap every two weeks** to let in air; after about **two to three months** the compost is **dark, crumbly and sweet-smelling** and is ready to be spread on the beds (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR correct steps in a workable order (4 marks). The layering and the turning are the two steps examiners should look for.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Composting **turns the waste into free manure that adds nutrients and humus to the soil** and saves the money spent on fertiliser, while burning destroys it all.
- Composting **produces no smoke**, so it **does not pollute the air or harm health**, and it keeps the waste out of the gutters and off the dump.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO advantages (2 marks).*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Plastics, glass, tins and other metals** - they are **non-biodegradable, so they do not rot** and would remain in the compost and in the soil (1 mark).
- **Medical waste, batteries and other chemical waste** (accept diseased plants or meat scraps) - they are **dangerous, poison the soil, and attract rats and flies** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for each kind of waste correctly named WITH a reason.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Wash and reuse the bottles and containers** to store water, kerosene or seeds, or cut them open to serve as **pots for seedlings in the school garden**.
- **Collect and sell the sachet bags and bottles to a recycling company**, where they are made into new bottles, buckets, chairs, roofing sheets or paving blocks (accept: make bags, mats and craft items from clean sachet bags).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO practical uses (2 marks).*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 5: Humans and the Environment | **Sub-strand:** 1: Waste Management | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.5.1.1** - Demonstrate knowledge of waste management systems and apply it in an environment.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 5: Humans and the Environment, Sub-Strand 1: Waste Management, Basic 8, page 77. Content standard B8/JHS2.5.1.1 with indicator B8/JHS2.5.1.1.1 (exemplars: outline approaches to waste management in promoting sustainable management; conduct a survey in a community's waste management practices and present a report) and indicator B8/JHS2.5.1.1.2 (exemplars: carry out an activity to manage waste using the knowledge acquired in indicator B8/JHS2.5.1.1.1 in their communities; evaluate the waste management practices carried out in a community and present a report).

> Note: The paper carries one content standard and two indicators. Questions 1, 2 and 3 cover the explanation of sustainable waste management practices and the approaches of the waste hierarchy (B8/JHS2.5.1.1.1, exemplar 1); Question 4 carries the survey-and-report exemplar of the same indicator (exemplar 2). Questions 5 and 6 cover the application indicator B8/JHS2.5.1.1.2: carrying out a waste management activity in the school and community, evaluating it, and turning biodegradable waste into compost. The school's sheets use the shorter coded form (B8.5.1.1); both forms are given in the blueprint.

## QUALITY-CONTROL SUMMARY

| Check | Status |

| Items traceable to the curriculum | Yes - every Section A item and every Section B part is mapped in the blueprint to B8/JHS2.5.1.1.1 or B8/JHS2.5.1.1.2 and to one of the five topics drawn from the exemplars. |
| Key balance in Section A | Yes - the correct answers are evenly spread over A, B, C and D (10 each), with no letter repeated more than twice in a row and no cyclic pattern. |
| One defensible answer per item | Yes - each item has a single correct option. The distractors are the real misconceptions of the sub-strand: that reuse and recycling are the same thing, that burning rubbish disposes of it safely, and that waste has no value. |
| Marks add up | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40 marks; Section B 9 + 12 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 10 = 60 marks; total 100 marks. |
| Cognitive spread | Yes - the paper runs from recall of the types of waste, through understanding the waste hierarchy and the effects of poor sanitation, to reading a survey chart, calculating percentages, planning a school waste project and evaluating whether it has worked. |
| Difficulty mix close to 30 / 50 / 20 | Yes - the mix is reported in the Cognitive-Level Distribution section below and is within the tolerance set for a mock paper. |
| Figures readable in black and white | Yes - both figures are hand-drawn pencil sketches with handwriting-style labels, and they print clearly in black and white on a photocopier. |
| Figure labels do not give the answers away | Yes - the five levels in Fig. 1 carry only the letters A to E, with an arrow showing that A is the most preferred and E the least, so the candidate must still supply every name. Fig. 2 prints the value above each bar, which is the data the candidate needs, but states no conclusion. |
| Calculations checked | Yes - in Question 4(b), 36 + 24 = 60 households; in Question 4(c), 20 / 200 x 100 = 10%; the five bars of Fig. 2 add up to 80 + 40 + 36 + 24 + 20 = 200 households, which is the number surveyed. Section A item 33 gives the same 10%. |
| Marking scheme usable by any teacher | Yes - every part carries its mark allocation, the expected points are listed, and the italic marking notes state what is compulsory for each mark, what alternatives are acceptable, and the common errors to watch for. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - Fig. 1 states the order of preference; Fig. 2 gives the total surveyed and the value of every bar; and where either classification of waste is acceptable, the marking scheme says so. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - sachet-water bags, public waste containers, choked gutters and flooding, the district assembly and its sanitation bye-laws, the environmental health officer, a school compost heap, and a household survey in Asokwa. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the paper keeps to waste management practices and their effects. Sewage treatment plants, the chemistry of leachate and climate modelling are not examined; the percentage calculation in Question 4 uses figures printed on the chart. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - defining and classifying, naming and applying the levels of the waste hierarchy, explaining the effects of poor sanitation, reading a survey bar chart and calculating from it, writing recommendations, planning and evaluating a school project, and describing how to make compost. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper opens Strand 5. It is a practical sub-strand: if your class carried out the community survey or a clean-up activity this term, mark their own reports against Questions 4(e) and 5 as well.
- In Question 2(a) the five names must be in the right order. A candidate who gives the right five names in the wrong order scores a maximum of 2 marks; say so when you return the scripts.
- Watch for the commonest confusion in the sub-strand: reuse (using the same item again as it is) against recycling (sending the material to a factory to be made into something new). Question 2(c) is where it shows.
- Question 4 is arithmetic on a chart, not a mathematics question. Award the method mark in 4(c) even where the arithmetic is wrong, but insist on the per cent sign in the final answer.
- In Question 4(d) and 6(c), a method or a material named without a reason scores nothing. The reason carries the thinking.
- Question 5(b) is the discriminating part of the paper. Candidates must give a way of evaluating that can actually be measured or compared - counting bags of waste, weighing compost, photographing the same spots - not a general hope that the school will be clean.
- Question 6(a) is best marked against what your class actually did. A heap built in layers and turned regularly is the answer being looked for.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In calculations, award a method mark for correct working even where the final answer is wrong, and insist on the per cent sign where a percentage is asked for. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed; medical terms spelt as they sound, such as 'jondis' for jaundice, earn the mark.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- A **communicable disease is caused by a germ and can be passed from one person to another**, directly or through food, water, air or a vector (1 mark).
- A **non-communicable disease cannot be passed from person to person**; it comes from the person's own body, diet or way of life, for example diabetes, hypertension or sickle-cell disease (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept 'infectious disease' for communicable.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Through the air, in droplets from coughing and sneezing** - **measles** (accept tuberculosis, influenza) (1 mark).
- **Through contaminated food and water** - **cholera** (accept typhoid fever, dysentery) (1 mark).
- **Through infected blood and body fluids, including shared blades and needles** - **hepatitis B** (accept HIV) (1 mark).
- **Through the bite of a vector** - **malaria**, carried by the female Anopheles mosquito (accept mother-to-child transmission, or direct skin contact with ringworm or scabies) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR routes, each with a correct disease (4 marks). A route with no disease, or with a disease that does not travel that way, scores nothing for that item.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Wash the hands with soap under running water** before eating and after using the toilet, and **keep the toilets, the canteen and the compound clean with safe drinking water**.
- **Cover the mouth and the nose when coughing or sneezing**, keep the classrooms well aired, and **do not share cups, blades, needles or toothbrushes**.
- **Immunise the pupils, keep a sick pupil away from the others until he or she is well, and teach the pupils about the diseases** at assembly.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE sound measures (3 marks).*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- **Hepatitis B**, with 40 cases in all.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **24 + 16** (1 mark)
- **= 40 cases** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the addition of the male and female values and 1 mark for the answer.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **40 ÷ 100 × 100** (1 mark)
- **= 40%** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the method and 1 mark for the answer with the per cent sign. Allow follow-through from a wrong total in (b).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **24 − 16** (1 mark)
- **= 8 more males than females** (1 mark)
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the subtraction and 1 mark for the answer.*

**(e)** [3 marks]

- **More men share razor blades, clippers and other sharp instruments** at barbering shops and during shaving, tattooing or tribal marking.
- **More men work where they meet blood or sharp instruments**, or may **have more sexual partners**, so they are exposed more often.
- **Women attend antenatal and child welfare clinics, where they are screened, treated and advised earlier**, so fewer of them come to be recorded as cases (accept: men report late to hospital, so their cases are recorded as full disease).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE reasonable suggestions (3 marks). These are suggestions, not facts about this community; accept any answer that is scientifically sensible and respectful. Do NOT accept answers that insult or blame either sex. This is the curriculum exemplar on determining the possible causes from compiled data.*

**(f)** [2 marks]

- To **see which diseases are commonest and which group is most at risk**, and so **plan health education, screening and immunisation** for them.
- To **order the right drugs, vaccines and test kits**, to **compare one year with the next to see whether the measures are working**, and to report to the district health directorate for support.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sound uses (2 marks).*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- The germ is the **hepatitis B virus** (1 mark).
- It attacks the **liver** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. 'A virus' alone earns the first mark; 'bacterium' earns nothing.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Through **contact with the blood or body fluids of an infected person**, including **shared razor blades, needles, syringes, clippers and toothbrushes**.
- Through **transfusion with unscreened infected blood**, or the use of unsterilised instruments for injections, tattooing or tribal marks.
- Through **unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected person**, and **from an infected mother to her baby during pregnancy or at birth**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct routes (3 marks). Do not award a mark for routes that do not spread hepatitis B, such as sharing a desk, shaking hands or mosquito bites.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Yellowing of the eyes and the skin (jaundice)** and **dark, cola-coloured urine**.
- **Tiredness and general weakness**, with **loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting**.
- **Fever** and **pain in the abdomen**, especially on the right side below the ribs.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct symptoms (3 marks). Note that many people carry the virus with no symptoms at all; a candidate who says so in addition is not penalised.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **On the patient:** the **liver is damaged, which may lead to cirrhosis, liver cancer and even death**; the patient becomes weak, misses school or work, and may remain a carrier for life.
- **On the family:** **money is spent on treatment and the family loses the patient's work and income**; other members of the household may be infected, and the family suffers worry and sometimes stigma.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO effects (2 marks).*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [1 marks]

- **The liver**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- The condition is **jaundice** (1 mark).
- The **damaged liver can no longer remove the yellow bile pigment from the blood**, so it **collects in the blood and stains the eyes and the skin yellow** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for the name and 1 mark for the explanation. Accept 'the liver is not working properly, so the yellow colouring stays in the blood'.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Immunisation with the hepatitis B vaccine** - the surest protection.
- **Never sharing razor blades, needles, syringes, clippers or toothbrushes**, and insisting on **sterile instruments** for injections, tattooing and tribal marks.
- **Using only screened blood for transfusion**, **avoiding unprotected sexual intercourse**, and **screening pregnant women so that their babies are protected at birth**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct preventive measures (3 marks).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The vaccine makes the **body produce antibodies, so the person is protected before ever meeting the virus**, and it is **far cheaper and safer than treating the disease**.
- It **prevents the liver damage, cirrhosis and liver cancer** that can follow, and when **many people are vaccinated there are fewer carriers**, so the disease spreads less in the community.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sound reasons (2 marks).*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- **Treat the classmate with kindness and respect, keep the matter confidential and continue to study, play and eat together**, since hepatitis B is not spread by ordinary contact (1 mark).
- **Encourage him or her to attend the clinic and take the treatment prescribed**, make sure **nobody shares blades, needles or toothbrushes**, and get themselves **vaccinated and tested** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Any answer that suggests sending the classmate away, announcing the result publicly or refusing to sit with the pupil scores 0 for that point. Stigma is a learning outcome of this sub-strand.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **HIV - human immunodeficiency virus** (1 mark).
- **AIDS - acquired immune deficiency syndrome** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 mark each. Accept 'immuno-deficiency' written as one or two words.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Through **unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected person**.
- Through **transfusion with unscreened infected blood**, or by **sharing needles, syringes, razor blades and other skin-piercing instruments**.
- From an **infected mother to her child during pregnancy, at birth or through breast milk**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct routes (3 marks).*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- By **shaking hands, hugging, playing together or sharing a desk, clothes, books or a toilet**.
- By **eating food prepared or shared with an infected person**, by **coughing, sneezing or breathing the same air**, or by **mosquito and other insect bites**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO correct answers (2 marks). This part is included to correct the fear and stigma that surround HIV.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The child suffers **high fever, a rash over the body, red watery eyes, a runny nose and a cough**, and becomes **weak and off food**.
- Measles may lead to **blindness, ear infection, severe diarrhoea, pneumonia, malnutrition and even death**, and the child misses school for a long time.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO effects (2 marks).*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Find out how common the disease is** from the records of the health centre, and set a clear target for the plan (1 mark).
- **Organise health education** at assembly, in the churches and mosques, at the market and on the information centre or local radio, using posters, drama and the class presentation (1 mark).
- **Arrange a screening and vaccination day with the health centre** for pupils and community members, and encourage pregnant women to attend antenatal clinic (1 mark).
- **Campaign against the sharing of blades, needles, clippers and toothbrushes**, and teach the barbers and hairdressers to sterilise their tools and use a new blade for each customer (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR workable activities (4 marks). This is the curriculum exemplar that asks pupils to search for information on hepatitis and develop a plan to minimise the disease.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **The nurse or community health officer at the health centre** - to **screen, vaccinate, treat and give correct information** (1 mark).
- **The chief, the assembly member, religious leaders or the P.T.A.** - to **call the community together and support the message** (accept the barbers and hairdressers, who must change their practice) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO people or groups, each with how they would help (2 marks). A name with no role scores nothing.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Two sources: **the health centre and its nurses**, and **the Ghana Health Service, the textbook, the school library or the internet** (1 mark for any two).
- Checking: **compare the information with a second source, show it to the nurse or the teacher, and use only material from known health bodies, checking how recent it is** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 mark for naming two sources and 1 mark for a sound way of checking. This part carries the digital-literacy competency.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Compare the number of hepatitis B cases recorded at the health centre before the plan and after six months or a year**, and **count how many people were screened and vaccinated** (1 mark).
- **Check whether the barbers and hairdressers now use a new blade for each customer**, and **test what people know with a short questionnaire before and after the education** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO ways that can actually be measured or compared (2 marks). A general hope that 'people will be healthy' scores 0.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 5: Humans and the Environment | **Sub-strand:** 2: Human Health | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.5.2.1** - Demonstrate knowledge of common communicable diseases, such as hepatitis, of humans, causes, symptoms, effects and their prevention.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 5: Humans and the Environment, Sub-Strand 2: Human Health, Basic 8, page 78. Content standard B8/JHS2.5.2.1 with the single indicator B8/JHS2.5.2.1.1. The exemplars quoted are: compile data on the number of males and females who suffer from common communicable diseases such as hepatitis, from a medical centre, and determine the possible causes of these diseases; identify the causes, symptoms, effects and prevention of hepatitis, HIV, measles and others and make a presentation; and search for the causes, symptoms and prevention of hepatitis and develop a plan to minimise the disease.

> Note: This sub-strand carries one content standard and one indicator, so the blueprint separates the items by exemplar and by topic: the data-compilation exemplar, with males and females taken from the records of a health centre (Question 2); the causes, symptoms, effects and prevention of hepatitis, HIV and measles (Questions 1, 3, 4 and 5); and the exemplar that asks pupils to search for information on hepatitis and develop a plan to minimise the disease (Question 6). The school's sheets use the shorter coded form (B8.5.2.1); both forms are given in the blueprint.

## QUALITY-CONTROL SUMMARY

| Check | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Items traceable to the curriculum | Yes - every Section A item and every Section B part is mapped in the blueprint to indicator B8/JHS2.5.2.1.1 and to one of the five topics drawn from the three exemplars. The diseases examined - hepatitis, HIV and measles - are the three named in the curriculum, with cholera, typhoid, tuberculosis and malaria as the 'others' the exemplar allows. |
| Key balance in Section A | Yes - the correct answers are evenly spread over A, B, C and D (10 each), with no letter repeated more than twice in a row and no cyclic pattern. |
| One defensible answer per item | Yes - each item has a single correct option. The distractors are the real misconceptions of the sub-strand: that HIV is spread by touch or by mosquitoes, that hepatitis is caused by a bacterium, and that a sick classmate should be sent away. |
| Marks add up | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40 marks; Section B 9 + 12 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 10 = 60 marks; total 100 marks. |
| Cognitive spread | Yes - the paper runs from recall of causes and symptoms, through understanding of the routes of transmission and the reasons for prevention, to reading a health-centre chart, calculating from it, suggesting why one sex is more affected, and designing and evaluating a community plan. |
| Difficulty mix close to 30 / 50 / 20 | Yes - the mix is reported in the Cognitive-Level Distribution section below and is within the tolerance set for a mock paper. |
| Figures readable in black and white | Yes - both figures are hand-drawn pencil sketches with handwriting-style labels. Fig. 1 separates the sexes by a plain bar and a hatched bar with a key, so it does not depend on colour. |
| Figure labels do not give the answers away | Yes - Fig. 1 prints the value above each bar, which is the data the candidate needs, but draws no conclusion. In Fig. 2 the organ is lettered Q and the sign lettered R; the caption states only what is seen - that the whites of the eyes and the skin have turned yellow - and names neither the organ, the sign nor the disease. |
| Calculations checked | Yes - in Question 2(b), 24 + 16 = 40 cases; in 2(c), 40 / 100 x 100 = 40%; in 2(d), 24 - 16 = 8. The four diseases in Fig. 1 total 40 + 30 + 20 + 10 = 100 cases, which is the figure given in 2(c). Section A item 38 gives the same 40%. |
| Sensitive content handled properly | Yes - HIV and hepatitis are treated factually and without blame. Question 4(e) and Question 5(c) are written specifically to correct stigma, and the marking scheme refuses marks for any answer that would exclude or expose a patient. Question 2(e) warns examiners not to accept answers that insult either sex, and item 37 of Section A requires the confidentiality of patients' names. |
| Marking scheme usable by any teacher | Yes - every part carries its mark allocation, the expected points are listed, and the italic marking notes state what is compulsory for each mark, what alternatives are acceptable, and the common errors to watch for. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - Fig. 1 gives the value of every bar and a key for the sexes; Question 2(c) supplies the total of 100 cases that the percentage needs; and Question 2(e) says plainly that suggestions, not facts, are being asked for. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - a health centre at Nkawkaw and its records, barbering shops and shared clippers, antenatal clinic and child welfare, the district health directorate, the information centre and local radio, and the chief and assembly member in a community campaign. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the paper keeps to the causes, symptoms, effects and prevention of common communicable diseases. The structure of viruses, the antibody-antigen reaction, the stages of HIV infection and the names of antiretroviral drugs are not examined; immunisation is explained only as the body being made to produce its own protection. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - defining and distinguishing, matching routes of spread to diseases, reading and calculating from a health-centre bar chart, suggesting reasons for a pattern in data, naming an organ and a sign from a sketch, explaining why a sign appears, listing preventive measures, correcting stigma, and designing and evaluating a community plan. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper completes the Basic 8 Integrated Science course: Strand 5, Sub-Strand 2 is the last sub-strand of the year.
- Handle this paper with care in class. Several candidates will have hepatitis B, HIV or another condition in their own families. Mark the work privately and never read a candidate's answer about illness aloud.
- Question 4(e) and Question 5(c) are the heart of the sub-strand. Refuse marks for any answer that would send a patient away, announce a test result publicly or refuse to sit with a classmate; discuss the correct answers with the class afterwards.
- In Question 2(e) candidates are asked to SUGGEST reasons. Accept any sensible, respectful suggestion; the mark is for the reasoning, not for a single right answer.
- Award the method marks in Question 2 even where the arithmetic is wrong, but insist on the per cent sign in 2(c).
- In Question 3(b) and 5(b), watch for candidates who list routes that do not apply - mosquito bites, sharing a desk, shaking hands. These earn nothing, and they are the misconceptions this sub-strand exists to remove.
- Question 6 is the curriculum's planning exemplar. If your class actually prepared a plan or made a presentation this term, mark their own work against parts (a), (b) and (d), and invite the community health nurse to hear it.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In calculations, award a method mark for correct working even where the final answer is wrong, and insist on the per cent sign where a percentage is asked for. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed; medical terms spelt as they sound, such as 'gonoria' for gonorrhoea or 'meningitas' for meningitis, earn the mark.)*

### Question 1 (9 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **P - rod-shaped**, like short sticks (accept *bacillus*, rod-like, cylindrical) (1 mark).
- **Q - round or spherical, joined together in pairs** (accept *coccus*, *cocci*, ball-shaped, in pairs) (1 mark).
- **R - spiral, coiled or wavy** (accept *spirillum*, corkscrew-shaped, curved) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. Accept the everyday description or the scientific name; the candidate does not need both. Do not award a mark for naming a disease here - the question asks for shape.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Food poisoning** (from *Salmonella*, *Staphylococcus* or *Escherichia coli*).
- **Gonorrhoea.**
- **Meningitis.**
- Also accept: **cholera, typhoid fever, tuberculosis, tetanus, whooping cough, syphilis, leprosy**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE correct bacterial diseases (3 marks). Refuse the mark for diseases that are not bacterial - malaria, measles, hepatitis B, HIV and AIDS, ringworm and athlete's foot are caused by protozoa, viruses or fungi.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Warmth** - the food is kept at room temperature, which is warm enough for the bacteria to grow.
- **Moisture** - cooked food such as rice, stew or kenkey holds water, which the bacteria need.
- **Food (nutrients)** - the bacteria feed on the starch and the protein in the meal.
- Also accept: **enough time** for the numbers to double again and again, and the **food left uncovered** so that bacteria from the air, from dust and from flies settle on it.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE conditions (3 marks). 'Dirtiness' alone is too vague; it must be linked to germs reaching the food.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Food poisoning is an illness that follows the eating of food or the drinking of water that contains harmful bacteria or the poisons (toxins) that the bacteria have produced** (1 mark).
- **Salmonella** (1 mark).
- **Staphylococcus** (accept *Escherichia coli*, *Clostridium*, *Shigella*, *Campylobacter*) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks: 1 for the explanation, 1 for each of TWO named bacteria. The explanation must mention the germ or its poison in the food; 'food that is bad' alone earns nothing.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Vomiting.**
- **Diarrhoea - frequent, watery stools.**
- **Stomach (abdominal) pain or cramps.**
- **Fever**, with chills.
- Also accept: **nausea, headache, weakness and tiredness, dry mouth and great thirst**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR symptoms (4 marks). Mark only the first four given. 'Sickness' on its own is too vague.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The food was cooked in the morning and served in the afternoon**, so it stood for several hours in a warm, moist state in which any surviving bacteria multiplied many times over.
- **The pan was left open**, so dust, flies and unwashed hands could carry bacteria onto the food.
- Also accept: **the food was not reheated thoroughly before it was served**, and **there was no cold store or refrigerator** to keep it safe.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sound reasons (2 marks). The reason must explain how the bacteria got in or how they multiplied.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **Wash the hands with soap under running water** before handling food, after using the toilet and after taking money, and keep the fingernails short.
- **Cook the food thoroughly and serve it hot**, and reheat any left-over food until it is steaming before it is sold again.
- **Keep the food covered** with a clean net or lid so that dust and flies cannot reach it.
- Also accept: **use clean water and clean, well-washed utensils**; **do not sell food that was prepared the day before**; **go for the medical examination and hold a valid health certificate from the Environmental Health Unit**; **wear a clean apron and cover the hair**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE practical measures (3 marks). The measure must be something the vendor herself can do; 'the government should build a market' earns nothing here.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **March** (1 mark).
- **32 cases** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 each. The number must match the month named; a correct number read against the wrong month earns only the number mark if the month is wrong.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **8 + 20 + 32 + 24 + 10 + 6** (1 mark for the correct working).
- **= 100 cases** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. Award the method mark for a correct addition statement even where the arithmetic slips.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **32 / 100 x 100** (1 mark for the working).
- **= 32%** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. Insist on the per cent sign. A candidate who used a wrong total in (b) but divides correctly here keeps the method mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **January to March is the height of the dry, dusty Harmattan season.** The hot, dry, dusty air **dries and injures the lining of the nose and the throat**, so the bacteria pass into the body far more easily (1 mark).
- **People also spend the nights in crowded, poorly aired rooms**, where droplets from coughing, sneezing and talking are easily breathed in by others (accept: more gatherings and travelling in the dry season) (1 mark).
- **From April the rains begin**, the dust settles and the air becomes moist, so fewer people are infected and the number of cases falls.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks for any TWO sound points. The answer must link the season to the way the germ enters or spreads. 'It is hot' alone earns nothing. Do not accept mosquitoes - meningitis has no vector.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- **They show at once when the number of cases is rising**, so an outbreak is detected early and can be reported and controlled before it spreads.
- **They show the time of year and the places at greatest risk**, so the directorate can time its vaccination campaign and its health education and can send drugs, beds and staff where they are needed.
- Also accept: **they allow this year to be compared with past years**, and they are evidence when asking the assembly or the Ministry for support.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO uses (2 marks). The use must be a decision the health service can take; 'to know the disease' is too vague.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Meningitis is the inflammation, or swelling, of the meninges - the thin coverings of the brain and the spinal cord** (1 mark).
- It is commonly caused by a **bacterium** (accept *Neisseria meningitidis*, the meningococcus; accept the note that some forms are viral) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 each. The first mark needs the brain or spinal cord covering; 'a disease of the head' is not enough.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **A sudden high fever.**
- **A severe headache.**
- **Vomiting.**
- **A dislike of bright light** - the patient turns away from the window.
- Also accept: **confusion or drowsiness, convulsions (fits), a rash, and in a baby a bulging soft spot on the head with refusal to feed**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE symptoms (3 marks). Do not award the stiff neck, which the question excludes.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Deafness, or damage to the hearing** - the commonest lasting effect.
- **Damage to the brain**, leading to difficulty in learning, loss of memory, epilepsy or paralysis.
- Also accept: **blindness**, **long absence from school**, and **death**, for meningitis can kill within a day or two.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO effects (2 marks). Accept effects on the family, such as the cost of treatment, only as the second answer.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **Vaccination of the people at risk**, especially in the meningitis belt before the dry season.
- **Avoid overcrowded sleeping rooms and keep rooms and halls well aired**, with windows open.
- **Cover the mouth and the nose when coughing or sneezing**, and avoid sharing cups, bottles and spoons.
- Also accept: **report every suspected case to a health facility at once so that the patient is treated and close contacts are given preventive drugs**, and **health education through schools, radio and the information centre**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE measures (3 marks). Measures that belong to other diseases - sleeping under a treated net, boiling drinking water - earn nothing here, because meningitis is spread by droplets.*

### Question 5 (9 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- It is caused by a **bacterium** (accept *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, the gonococcus) (1 mark).
- **Through unprotected sexual contact with a person who has the infection** (1 mark).
- **From an infected mother to her baby during birth**, when the baby passes through the birth canal (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks: 1 for the bacterium and 1 for each of TWO routes. Refuse the mark for shaking hands, sharing a toilet seat, mosquito bites or eating together - these do NOT spread gonorrhoea, and they are the beliefs this lesson exists to correct.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Pain or a burning feeling when passing urine**, often with the need to pass urine more often.
- **An unusual discharge** from the sexual organs.
- Also accept: **pain in the lower abdomen**, and the important point that **many infected women, and some men, show no symptoms at all** while still able to pass the infection on.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO symptoms (2 marks). Mark this part privately and do not read answers aloud.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **It can damage the reproductive organs and leave the person unable to have children** (infertility).
- **A baby born to an untreated mother may develop a severe infection of the eyes and become blind.**
- Also accept: **lasting pain in the lower abdomen**, **the spread of the infection to the joints and the blood**, and **a greater risk of catching other infections, including HIV**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO effects (2 marks).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **He stopped the drug as soon as he felt better**, so the bacteria that survive are not killed; they multiply, become **resistant to the antibiotic**, and the illness returns in a form that is much harder to treat.
- **He was never examined or tested**, so the illness may not be gonorrhoea at all, and the drug the hawker sold may be the wrong one, the wrong dose, expired or fake.
- **His partner has not been treated**, so the two will keep passing the infection back to each other and on to others, and untreated gonorrhoea can leave him unable to have children.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO sound reasons (2 marks). The best answers mention resistance or the untreated partner. 'It is bad' earns nothing. Treat this item factually in class and name no one.*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **The individual** - washes the hands with soap, keeps food and the body clean, avoids crowded, airless rooms, goes early to a health facility when ill and **finishes the full course of the medicine** (1 mark).
- **The community** - organises communal labour to clear gutters and clean the market and the toilets, supports vaccination and education campaigns through the chief, the Assembly member and the information centre, and cares for patients without shaming them (1 mark).
- **The government** - supplies vaccines, drugs, clinics and trained health workers, provides safe water and sanitation, makes and enforces food-safety laws through the Food and Drugs Authority and the Environmental Health Unit, and runs public education (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 for each level. The role must belong to the level named; a candidate who gives 'build hospitals' for the individual earns nothing for that mark.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **(i) A short title of a few words** that can be read from a distance, for example *Cook it well, cover it, eat it hot*; *Wash your hands - save your stomach*; *Stop food poisoning today* (1 mark).
- **(ii) Two short, practical messages** (1 mark each), for example: *Wash your hands with soap before you eat*; *Cover your food against flies and dust*; *Do not eat food kept overnight without reheating*; *Buy from vendors with a health certificate*; *Drink only safe water*.
- **(iii) One non-word feature** (1 mark): **a large, clear picture or drawing** - a covered pan, a hand being washed, a fly on open food; also accept **bright, contrasting colours**, **very large bold letters**, a **tick-and-cross comparison**, or the **message repeated in the local language**.
  - *Marking note: 4 marks in all: 1 + 2 + 1. In (i) and (ii) reward brevity - a long paragraph copied from the notes is not a poster message and earns nothing. Any correct message is acceptable; do not insist on the examples given here. No marks are lost for drawing or handwriting quality.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Ask a health worker** - the nurse at the health centre, the community health officer or the Environmental Health Officer - and write down what is said.
- **Use reliable written sources** - the science textbook, a pamphlet from the health centre, or the website of the Ghana Health Service, the Food and Drugs Authority or the World Health Organization.
- **Compare at least two different sources** and keep only the facts on which they agree; reject what somebody merely heard in the street or saw forwarded on social media.
- Also accept: **show the draft poster to the science teacher or the nurse for checking before it is printed**, and **write the source of the information at the bottom of the poster**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE steps (3 marks). At least one step should involve checking or comparing, not merely collecting; but do not withhold marks if three sound collecting steps are given.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 5: Humans and the Environment | **Sub-strand:** 2: Human Health | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.5.2.2** - Demonstrate knowledge of the nature of selected bacterial diseases of humans, their causes, symptoms, effects and prevention.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 5: Humans and the Environment, Sub-Strand 2: Human Health, Basic 8, page 80. Content standard B8/JHS2.5.2.2 with the single indicator B8/JHS2.5.2.2.1. The exemplars quoted are: discuss the nature of bacterial diseases; search for information and make presentations on food poisoning, gonorrhoea and meningitis and their mode of transmission from person to person, community to community and country to country; describe the symptoms, effects and prevention of food poisoning, gonorrhoea and meningitis; describe the role of individuals, community members and government in managing these diseases; and design and produce a poster to educate community members on the incidence and control of named bacterial diseases.

> Note: This sub-strand carries one content standard and one indicator, so the blueprint separates the items by exemplar and by topic: the nature of bacteria and of bacterial disease (Question 1); food poisoning (Question 2); meningitis, including the health-centre records that the transmission exemplar calls for (Questions 3 and 4); gonorrhoea (Question 5); and the exemplars on the roles of the individual, the community and government and on producing a poster (Question 6). This paper is the partner of Paper 19, which covered the communicable-disease standard B8/JHS2.5.2.1; together the two papers complete Sub-Strand 2. The school's sheets use the shorter coded form (B8.5.2.2); both forms are given in the blueprint.
