| Only one defensible answer per objective item | Yes - every stem was re-read against its four options. The distractors are the beliefs pupils actually hold: that gonorrhoea can be caught from a toilet seat or a handshake, that meningitis is carried by mosquitoes, that food poisoning comes from too much salt, and that a course of antibiotics may be stopped as soon as the pain goes. |
| Correct answers spread evenly | Yes - A = 10, B = 10, C = 10, D = 10, and no letter is repeated more than twice in a row. |
| Marks add up | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40 marks; Section B 9 + 12 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 10 = 60 marks; total 100 marks. |
| Cognitive spread | Yes - the paper runs from recall of causes and symptoms, through understanding of how each germ travels, to reading a health-centre bar chart, calculating a percentage from it, explaining a seasonal pattern, judging the danger of an unfinished course of antibiotics, and designing a poster. |
| Difficulty mix close to 30 / 50 / 20 | Yes - the mix is reported in the Cognitive-Level Distribution section below and is within the tolerance set for a mock paper. |
| Figures readable in black and white | Yes - both figures are hand-drawn pencil sketches with handwriting-style labels. Fig. 1 relies on outline shape alone and Fig. 2 prints the value above each bar, so neither depends on colour. |
| Figure labels do not give the answers away | Yes - in Fig. 1 the three fields are lettered P, Q and R and the caption says only that all three are germs seen under a microscope; it names no shape and no disease. Fig. 2 is headed 'suspected cases' and gives the month and the number, but draws no conclusion about the season. |
| Calculations checked | Yes - in Question 3(b), 8 + 20 + 32 + 24 + 10 + 6 = 100 cases; in 3(c), 32 / 100 x 100 = 32%. The highest bar, March, carries 32 cases, which matches both answers. |
| Sensitive content handled properly | Yes - gonorrhoea is named in the syllabus and is treated here factually and without blame. The questions ask about the germ, the symptoms, the effects and the proper treatment; no candidate is asked about his or her own conduct, no moral judgement is invited, and the marking scheme refuses marks for answers based on gossip or on the false routes of spread. The examiner notes require private marking. |
| Marking scheme usable by any teacher | Yes - every part carries its mark allocation, the expected points are listed, and the italic marking notes state what is compulsory for each mark, what alternatives are acceptable, and the common errors to watch for. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - Question 1(a) asks for the SHAPE and the marking note refuses a disease name; Question 4(b) excludes the stiff neck in the stem; Question 6(b) states exactly how many messages are wanted and awards marks part by part. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - a funeral at Nsawam where rice and stew stood in an open pan, a food vendor in front of the school and her health certificate from the Environmental Health Unit, the health centre at Bawku in the Upper East Region, the Harmattan season in the north, communal labour, the chief, the Assembly member and the information centre. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the paper keeps to the nature, causes, symptoms, effects and prevention of the three named bacterial diseases. The structure of the bacterial cell, Gram staining, the naming of antibiotic families and the stages of infection are not examined, and the scientific names of the bacteria are accepted but never required. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - describing shapes from a microscope sketch, naming diseases, explaining the conditions for bacterial growth, diagnosing an outbreak after a funeral, advising a food vendor, reading and calculating from a bar chart, explaining a seasonal pattern, listing symptoms and preventive measures, judging a case of self-medication, and designing and fact-checking a community poster. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper is the partner of Paper 19. Paper 19 covered the communicable-disease standard B8/JHS2.5.2.1; this paper covers B8/JHS2.5.2.2, the bacterial diseases. Use the two together to complete Sub-Strand 2.
- Question 5 deals with gonorrhoea, which the syllabus names. Teach and mark it as a matter of health, not of morals. Mark the work privately, never read a candidate's answer aloud, and do not ask pupils to share personal experience.
- Question 5(d) and Section A item 39 both attack self-medication and the unfinished course of antibiotics. Discuss the correct answers with the class; this is the single most useful lesson in the sub-strand.
- Watch for candidates who import the prevention of other diseases - sleeping under a treated net, boiling drinking water - into the meningitis question. These earn nothing, because meningitis travels in droplets.
- Award the method marks in Question 3 even where the arithmetic is wrong, but insist on the per cent sign in 3(c).
- Question 6(b) is the curriculum's poster exemplar. If your class actually produced posters this term, mark their own work against the three sub-parts and display the best of them at the school assembly or the clinic.
- In Question 6(c), reward any candidate who thinks of checking a fact against a second source, or of asking the nurse before printing. That is the digital-literacy competency the indicator carries.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (3) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (4) In the design question, mark the reasoning and not the drawing; a labelled sketch and a clear explanation earn full marks. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (6) Where a candidate names a real Ghanaian example that the scheme does not list, award the mark if it fits the point being made.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **P - science** (the careful, orderly study of nature to find out how and why things happen) (1 mark).
- **Q - technology** (the use of that knowledge to make tools, machines and methods) (1 mark).
- **R - innovation** (a new or improved product, method or idea that is actually put to use) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. The single word is enough; the explanation in brackets is not required. Do not accept 'invention' for P or Q.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Science supplies the knowledge, and technology puts that knowledge to work** to meet a human need (1 mark).
- **Technology in turn supplies science with instruments** - the microscope, the thermometer, the computer - so that scientists can observe and measure what they could not reach before, and so discover more (1 mark).
- **A correct example** (1 mark), for example: the scientific finding that an electric current produces a magnetic field was used to build the electric motor and the fan; the study of germs led to vaccines and to the refrigerator used to store them; the study of light led to the solar panel.
  - *Marking note: 3 marks: 1 for science feeding technology, 1 for technology feeding science back, 1 for a correct example. A candidate who gives only one direction of the relationship, however well explained, earns at most 2 marks with the example.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The needs and the problems of the people decide what is studied and what is made.** Where malaria is common, scientists work on malaria; where there is no mains electricity, inventors work on solar lamps (1 mark).
- **So the relationship works in both directions**: science and technology change the way people live, and the way people live, their needs, their money and their government's choices, decide what science and technology do next (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. The first mark is for society setting the agenda; the second for recognising that the relationship is two-way. An answer that merely repeats 'it goes back to P' earns nothing.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Mobile money** - people send and receive money, pay school fees and buy goods **without travelling to a bank**, which many villages do not have.
- Also accept: **the solar lantern or solar home system** (light and charging where there is no mains electricity); **the solar-powered vaccine refrigerator** at a rural clinic; **the cassava or palm-fruit processing machine** (less of the harvest is wasted); **the solar fish dryer** (clean, fast drying, free of flies); **the drone used to deliver blood and medicines**; **plastic waste recycled into pavement blocks**; **the borehole with a hand pump**.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 for a real innovation, 1 for the problem it solves. The two must match. A machine named with no problem stated earns 1 mark only.*

### Question 2 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Agriculture** - the tractor, the irrigation pump, the knapsack sprayer, improved seed.
- **Health care** - the X-ray machine, the solar-powered vaccine refrigerator, the laboratory microscope.
- **Communication** - the mobile telephone, the radio, the internet.
- **Transport** - the lorry, the motor bicycle, the aeroplane.
- Also accept: **industry** (processing and packaging machines); **the home** (the refrigerator, the gas cooker, the electric iron); **education** (the computer, the projector); **banking and trade** (mobile money, the ATM); **water supply** (the borehole and pump).
  - *Marking note: 4 marks: 1 mark for each area that is correctly named AND matched with a suitable example. An area with no example, or an example that does not belong to the area, earns nothing for that item.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Work is done faster and with less effort**, so one person can do in a day what once took a week.
- **More food and more goods are produced**, and less of the harvest is wasted, so there is food to sell as well as to eat.
- **Illness is found and treated earlier**, and vaccines, clean water and light at night have lengthened life.
- Also accept: **messages and money move in seconds**; **new jobs, trades and businesses have been created**; **pupils can learn from sources far beyond the school**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE benefits (3 marks). The benefit must be to people, not merely a description of the machine.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Pollution** - smoke and fumes in the air, waste water and chemicals in the rivers, oil and refuse on the land.
- **Destruction of the natural environment** - forests cleared, farmland dug up and rivers silted by mining and building.
- **Mountains of waste** - plastic sachets and bottles that block the gutters and cause floods, and old phones, televisions and refrigerators that nobody can safely destroy.
- Also accept: **some workers lose their jobs to machines**; **accidents and injuries from machines and vehicles**; **noise from mills, generators and loudspeakers**; **less exercise and more time wasted on screens**; **dependence on imported machines, spare parts and fuel**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE problems (3 marks). The problem must follow from the technology; 'people are lazy' alone is too vague unless it is tied to machines doing the work.*

### Question 3 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **X - smoke, or fumes, rising from the burning cables** (1 mark).
- **Y - the stream, or river, running past the yard** (1 mark).
- **Z - the heap of electronic waste (e-waste)** - old televisions, computers, refrigerators and telephones (accept 'scrap' or 'old electrical appliances') (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. For Z accept any answer that shows the candidate recognises discarded electrical or electronic goods; 'rubbish' alone is too vague.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **It is breathed in.** The smoke carries poisonous gases and very fine particles that irritate the nose, throat and lungs, causing coughing, chest pain, asthma and, over years, lasting damage to the lungs.
- **It carries metal poisons such as lead.** These enter the blood and can damage the brain and the nerves, and they are especially harmful to young children and to unborn babies.
- Also accept: **the smoke settles on food, water and washing** in the nearby houses; **it causes burning eyes and headaches**; **it hides the air pollution that worsens heart disease**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO effects (2 marks). The answer must say what the smoke does to the body, not merely that it is 'bad'.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Rain washes acids, oils and metal poisons out of the broken appliances** and the run-off carries them down into the stream (1 mark).
- **The stream becomes polluted**: the water is no longer safe to drink, cook or bathe in; fish and other water life are killed; and the poisons pass into people who drink the water, eat the fish or eat crops watered from it (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 for the poisons reaching the water, 1 for the consequence to the water life or to the people. 'It makes the water dirty' alone earns 1 mark at most.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The gain is small and private, but the harm is large and shared.** A few workers earn a little, while the smoke, the polluted stream and the poisoned soil damage the health of the whole neighbourhood, including children who earn nothing from the yard.
- **The damage lasts far longer than the income.** Metal poisons stay in the soil and the water for many years and the cost of treating illness falls on the families and on the state.
- **The choice is not between this yard and no work at all.** The same metals can be recovered safely at a proper recycling plant, with tools, gloves, masks and no open burning, so the jobs can be kept while the harm is removed.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks for any TWO sound points (2 marks). The best answers weigh the benefit against the cost rather than simply condemning the workers. An answer that blames the workers alone, with no reasoning, earns nothing.*

**(e)** [3 marks]

- **Provide, or licence, a proper recycling plant** where the metals are recovered by machine instead of by open burning.
- **Ban open burning on the site and enforce the ban**, through the Environmental Protection Authority and the assembly's by-laws.
- **Train the workers and supply protective equipment** - gloves, boots, masks - and register them so that their health is checked.
- Also accept: **move the yard away from houses and from the stream**; **require importers and sellers of electrical goods to take back old appliances**; **provide collection points and public education so that e-waste is separated from ordinary refuse**; **support the workers with other work while the site is cleaned up**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE measures (3 marks). The measure must be within the power of the assembly or the government. 'The workers should stop' is not a measure and earns nothing.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **A single excavator moves in one day what a hundred people with shovels could not move in months**, so a far larger area of forest and farmland is cleared and dug up in a very short time.
- **The machines work in and beside the river itself and use chemicals such as mercury on a large scale**, so the water is muddied and poisoned far faster than the river can clean itself.
- Also accept: **machines reach deep and remote places hand tools never could**, and **the pits and heaps they leave behind are too large for the people to fill in again**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO reasons (2 marks). The answer must compare the scale or the speed with hand mining.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **The rivers become muddy and are poisoned with mercury**, so the water is unsafe and costs far more to treat for town supply.
- **Farmland and forest are destroyed** and left as pits and heaps of sand, so cocoa and food crops are lost and farmers lose their livelihood.
- **People fall ill** - mercury poisoning, skin and stomach disease from dirty water - and the open pits fill with water in which children drown and mosquitoes breed.
- Also accept: **fish and other water life are killed**; **the soil is no longer fertile**; **school attendance falls as children are drawn into the pits**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE effects (3 marks). Mark only the first three. Accept effects on land, water, health or livelihood.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Minerals are produced in quantity** and sold abroad, earning foreign exchange and taxes that pay for roads, schools, clinics and electricity.
- **Jobs and incomes are created** for miners, drivers, mechanics, traders and food sellers, and skills are learnt.
- Also accept: **raw materials for industry**, and **development of roads, power and water in mining districts**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO benefits (2 marks). This part exists to keep the answer balanced; a candidate who refuses to admit any benefit earns nothing here.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **Licence, inspect and police the mines**, so that only registered miners work and the law against mining in river beds and forest reserves is enforced.
- **Require every miner to restore the land** - to refill the pits, replace the topsoil and replant trees or crops when the gold is finished - and to lodge money in advance to pay for it.
- **Treat the waste water in settling ponds and ban the careless use of mercury**, replacing it with safer recovery methods.
- Also accept: **train and equip small-scale miners with cleaner methods**; **monitor the rivers regularly and publish the results**; **keep a buffer of untouched land along every river**; **involve the chiefs and the community in watching over the land**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE workable measures (3 marks). 'Stop all mining' is not a way of using the technology and earns nothing; 'stop illegal mining' does earn a mark, because the law is being enforced.*

### Question 5 (8 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **The problem is stated plainly and is a real one** in a school or a community (1 mark).
- **The goal is stated**: what the device or method must actually do - for example, *it must sound a warning when the tank is full*, or *it must dry fifty kilogrammes of maize in two days without the rain touching it* (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. This part carries the competency CP 6.1, the ability to define a goal towards solving a problem. A candidate who describes a gadget but never says what problem it solves earns nothing here.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **A list of suitable materials that can really be obtained locally** - for example empty bottles, a float, wire, a bell or buzzer, an old dry cell, bamboo, wire mesh, a polythene sheet, scrap wood (1 mark).
- **A simple labelled sketch** showing the main parts and where each material goes (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. Award the sketch mark for any drawing with at least two sensible labels. No marks are taken off for untidy drawing; this is a science paper, not an art paper.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The explanation follows a clear order** - what happens first, next and last (1 mark).
- **It rests on a correct scientific idea** (1 mark): the float rises because it is lighter than water and closes the circuit, so the buzzer sounds; the glass traps heat so the air inside the dryer becomes hotter than the air outside and carries the moisture away; the dark surface absorbs more radiation than a shiny one.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. The science need not be advanced, but it must be correct. A design that could not possibly work as described earns the first mark only, for the orderly explanation.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **One benefit** (1 mark): water, money, time, food or fuel saved; work made safer or easier; health improved; waste reduced.
- **One difficulty** (1 mark): the cost of the materials; parts that wear out or rust and must be replaced; the device may fail in rain or harmattan dust; somebody must be trained to use and repair it; it may be stolen or damaged.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 each. Reward honesty: a candidate who can name a real weakness in his or her own design is thinking like an engineer. A candidate who writes 'there is no difficulty at all' earns nothing for the second mark.*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **The science teacher, a laboratory technician or a qualified engineer or electrician** in the community.
- **The science textbook, an encyclopaedia or the school or public library.**
- **The website or the office of a recognised body** - the Ghana Standards Authority, the Energy Commission, the Food and Drugs Authority, the CSIR, a university or the Ministry of Energy.
- Also accept: **a published scientific article or report**, and **the manufacturer's own documents, read critically alongside an independent source**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE sources (3 marks). 'Social media', 'the internet' on its own, or 'my friends' earn nothing, because they name no responsible author.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Who wrote it, and what do they know?** Is the author a scientist, an institution or an unnamed person forwarding a message?
- **Does any other independent source agree?** A claim that appears in two or three trusted places separately is far stronger than one that appears everywhere in exactly the same forwarded words.
- **Is evidence given?** Are there measurements, a test anyone can repeat, or only promises and pictures?
- Also accept: **how recent the information is**; **whether the writer gains money if you believe it**; **whether the claim contradicts well-established science** - energy cannot be created out of nothing, so a machine that gives out more energy than it takes in is impossible; **whether the language is calm and exact or excited and exaggerated**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE checks (3 marks). Award a mark generously to any candidate who notices that the claim breaks the law of conservation of energy, which was taught in Sub-Strand 4.3.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- **(i) Two helps** (1 mark each): quick contact with parents and friends, especially in an emergency; access to information, dictionaries, past questions and lessons; sending and receiving money for fees and provisions; a torch, a calculator, a clock and a camera in one pocket.
- **(ii) Two harms** (1 mark each): hours lost from study, chores and sleep; false and harmful information believed and passed on; bullying, insults and contact with strangers; the cost of data and the risk of theft; eye strain, poor posture and less exercise and play.
  - *Marking note: 4 marks in all: 2 + 2. Mark only the first two answers in each part. A candidate who writes only that the phone 'is good' or 'is bad' without saying how earns nothing. This part carries CC 8.2 - look for ideas set out in a clear order.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 5: Humans and the Environment | **Sub-strand:** 3: Science and Industry | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.5.3.1** - Demonstrate an understanding of connections among science, technology, innovation, society and the environment.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 5: Humans and the Environment, Sub-Strand 3: Science and Industry, Basic 8, page 81. Content standard B8/JHS2.5.3.1 with the single indicator B8/JHS2.5.3.1.1. The two exemplars quoted are: explain the interrelationship of science, technology and innovation; and discuss technological advancements in the world and their impact on the Ghanaian environment. The named core competencies are CP 6.1 (ability to effectively define goals towards solving a problem), CC 8.2 (explain ideas in a clear order with relevant detail) and DL 5.5 (evaluate the quality and validity of information).

> Note: This sub-strand carries one content standard and one indicator, so the blueprint separates the items by exemplar and by topic. The first exemplar, the interrelationship of science, technology and innovation, is assessed in Question 1 and in Question 5, the design task that carries CP 6.1. The second exemplar, technological advancement and its impact on the Ghanaian environment, is assessed in Questions 2, 3 and 4. Question 6 carries DL 5.5, the evaluation of the quality and validity of information. The school's sheets use the shorter coded form (B8.5.3.1); both forms are given in the blueprint.

| Only one defensible answer per objective item | Yes - every stem was re-read against its four options. Where a judgement is called for, the stem says MAIN, BEST or MOST balanced, so the intended answer is the only defensible one. |
| Correct answers spread evenly | Yes - A = 10, B = 10, C = 10, D = 10, and no letter is repeated more than twice in a row. |
| Marks add up | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40 marks; Section B 10 + 10 + 12 + 10 + 8 + 10 = 60 marks; total 100 marks. |
| Cognitive spread | Yes - the paper runs from the meanings of science, technology and innovation, through matching technologies to the sectors they serve, to reading a scene of electronic waste, weighing jobs against health and pollution, designing a device for a local problem and judging whether a claim circulating on the phones can be trusted. |
| Difficulty mix close to 30 / 50 / 20 | Yes - the mix is reported in the Cognitive-Level Distribution section below and is within the tolerance set for a mock paper. |
| Figures readable in black and white | Yes - both figures are hand-drawn pencil sketches with handwriting-style labels and use outline, shape and position only, so neither depends on colour. |
| Figure labels do not give the answers away | Yes - in Fig. 1 the three stages are lettered P, Q and R and the boxes describe what happens at each stage without ever using the words science, technology or innovation, which are what Question 1(a) asks for. In Fig. 2 the smoke, the stream and the heap are lettered X, Y and Z; the caption calls the place only 'a scrap yard on the edge of a town' and never uses the term electronic waste. |
| Calculations checked | Not applicable - this sub-strand carries no computation. The quantitative demand is met instead by the weighing of benefits against costs in Questions 3(d) and 4(c). |
| Sensitive content handled properly | Yes - the scrap workers and the small-scale miners are treated as people earning a living in difficult conditions, not as criminals. Question 3(d) requires the candidate to weigh their income against the harm, and the marking scheme refuses marks for an answer that merely blames them; Question 4(c) requires the benefits of mining to be admitted. |
| Marking scheme usable by any teacher | Yes - every part carries its mark allocation, the expected points are listed, and the italic marking notes state what is compulsory for each mark, what alternatives are acceptable, and the common errors to watch for. The design question in particular tells the teacher to mark the reasoning and not the drawing. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - Question 2(a) says exactly how many areas and that each needs an example; Question 5 lists four sample problems so that no candidate is left with nothing to design; Question 6(c) is split into (i) and (ii) with the marks shown against each. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - mobile money and the village without a bank, the solar vaccine refrigerator at a rural clinic, the cassava processing machine, the corn mill beside a classroom, plastic sachets in the gutters, the scrap yard on the edge of town, galamsey and the muddied rivers, the Environmental Protection Authority, the Ghana Standards Authority and the District Assembly. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the paper keeps to the relationship among science, technology, innovation and society and to the environmental impact of technological advancement. The chemistry of mercury, the electronics of the appliances and the economics of foreign exchange are mentioned only as context and are never examined. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - naming the stages in a flow diagram, explaining a two-way relationship, matching technologies to sectors, reading a scene and lettering its features, explaining how a pollutant reaches the body and the water, weighing income against harm, proposing measures for an assembly, designing a device with materials and a sketch, and judging the reliability of a claim circulating on social media. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand is about connections, not about new facts. Reward the candidate who can link a scientific idea to the thing it made possible and to the change it brought to people's lives, even where the wording is simple.
- Question 1(c) is the heart of the indicator. Many candidates see only that science changes society; press the class afterwards to see that society also decides what science is done.
- Question 3 is drawn from the scrap yards that exist on the edge of several Ghanaian towns. Teach it as a problem to be solved, not as a scandal; the workers in the sketch are earning a living in conditions nobody should have to work in.
- Question 4(c) deliberately asks for the benefits of mining. Do not let a class fall into the habit of condemning a technology without weighing it; that is not scientific thinking.
- Question 5 is an open design task. Expect wide variation and mark against the four sub-parts rather than against a model answer. If your class actually built something this term, mark their own project here and display the best designs.
- Question 6 carries the digital-literacy competency DL 5.5. The water-into-fuel claim is invented for this paper, but claims of that kind circulate constantly; a candidate who spots that it breaks the conservation of energy has understood two sub-strands at once.
- Section A items 34, 35 and 40 also test judgement rather than recall. Discuss them with the class after marking.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In calculations, award a method mark for correct working even where the final answer is wrong, and insist on the unit where one is asked for. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (6) Accept any real Ghanaian example that fits the point being made, even where the scheme does not list it.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **P - energy, that is heat and light, travelling from the sun to the surface of the earth** (1 mark).
- **Q - heat given off by the warmed earth, escaping through the layer into space** (1 mark).
- **R - heat that the layer of gases sends back down to the surface of the earth** (accept 'heat trapped and returned by the gases') (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 mark each. For P accept 'sunlight', 'solar energy' or 'radiation from the sun'. For R the answer must show the heat coming BACK to the earth; 'heat in the air' is not enough.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Carbon dioxide** (1 mark).
- **Methane** (1 mark).
- Also accept: **water vapour**, **nitrous oxide**, **chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO (2 marks). Do not accept oxygen or nitrogen; they are the commonest gases in the air but they do not trap heat in this way.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **The average temperature of the earth rises** - the earth becomes warmer. This is called global warming (1 mark).
- **The thicker layer absorbs more of the heat that is leaving the earth**, so less heat escapes into space along arrow Q (1 mark).
- **More of that heat is sent back down to the surface along arrow R**, so heat builds up at the surface and in the lower air (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks. The first mark is for the rise in temperature; the other two for the mechanism - less heat escaping and more heat returned. An answer that says only 'the earth becomes hot' earns 1 mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Burning fuels** - firewood, charcoal, petrol, diesel and gas - in kitchens, vehicles, generators and factories.
- **Cutting down and burning forests**, which both releases carbon dioxide and removes the trees that would have absorbed it.
- Also accept: **bush burning before the planting season**; **heaps of refuse left to rot, and landfill sites, which give off methane**; **keeping large herds of cattle**; **flooded rice fields**; **industry and mining**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO activities (2 marks). The activity must be one that people do; a volcano is natural and earns nothing.*

### Question 2 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **1980 - 27.0 °C** (1 mark).
- **2020 - 28.4 °C** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 each. The unit °C must appear at least once in the answer; do not take the mark off twice for the same omission.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **28.4 − 27.0** (1 mark for the correct working).
- **= 1.4 °C** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. Award the method mark for the correct subtraction even where the arithmetic slips. Insist on the unit in the final answer.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The temperature rises steadily from one reading to the next**, by about 0.3 to 0.4 °C every ten years, and at no point does it fall (1 mark).
- **This suggests that the climate of the area is becoming warmer** - it is a sign of climate change, not merely a hot year (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 for describing the steady rise, 1 for the conclusion. 'The line goes up' alone earns the first mark only.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The rains no longer begin and end when they used to**, and the rainy season has become shorter or less reliable.
- **Longer and hotter dry spells**, with streams, dams and wells drying up.
- Also accept: **heavier storms and more flooding when the rain does come**; **harvests failing, or crops that once grew well no longer doing so**; **grass and trees drying earlier**; **more dust and a longer Harmattan**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO signs (2 marks). The sign must be a long-term change, not a single storm or one hot afternoon.*

**(e)** [2 marks]

- **One station describes one place only**, and its reading can be affected by local changes - buildings, tarred roads or cleared trees round the station - rather than by the climate of the whole country (1 mark).
- **Collect and compare records from several stations and over as many years as possible**, set them beside the figures published by the Ghana Meteorological Agency or a world body, and add what the farmers and fishers of the area report about the seasons (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 for the weakness of a single record, 1 for a sensible way of strengthening the evidence. This part carries CP 5.1, combining information from several sources to reach a conclusion.*

### Question 3 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Climate change is a long-term change in the average pattern of temperature, rainfall and the seasons** of a place, or of the earth as a whole, observed over many years (2 marks).
- **Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at one place at one moment** - today's sunshine, this afternoon's storm - **while climate is the average of that weather taken over many years**, usually thirty or more (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks: 2 for the definition, which must contain the idea of a LONG-TERM change in the average, and 1 for the distinction. A candidate who says only 'the weather is changing' earns 1 mark.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Burning petrol, diesel, charcoal and firewood** in vehicles, generators and kitchens - releases **carbon dioxide**.
- **Cutting down forests (deforestation)** - the carbon stored in the wood is released, and the **absorption of carbon dioxide by the trees is lost**.
- **Bush burning before planting** - releases **carbon dioxide** and destroys the grass and young trees that would absorb it.
- **Heaping refuse in dumps where it rots** - releases **methane**.
- Also accept: **keeping large herds of cattle** (methane); **industry, mining and cement works** (carbon dioxide and other gases); **flooded rice fields** (methane).
  - *Marking note: 4 marks: 1 mark for each activity correctly paired with its gas or process. An activity with no gas named earns the mark only if the process, such as 'the trees that absorb carbon dioxide are lost', is clearly given.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **The rains no longer come when expected**, so seed planted at the usual time dies, or ripening crops are caught by an early dry spell, and harvests fail.
- **Longer and hotter dry seasons** dry up the streams, the dams and the pasture, so there is too little water for crops and animals.
- **Heavier storms and floods** wash away crops, seedlings and the topsoil itself.
- Also accept: **more pests and crop diseases** in the warmer conditions; **cocoa and other tree crops suffering where the dry season is longer and hotter**; **lower yields, so food prices rise and farmers earn less**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE effects (3 marks). The effect must be explained, not merely named: 'poor harvest' earns the mark only if the candidate says why.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The rising sea floods the town and washes the land away**, destroying houses, roads and coconut farms, so that families have to move inland.
- **Salt water enters the wells, the lagoons and the farmland**, so the water is no longer fit to drink and crops will not grow.
- Also accept: **fish catches fall** as the warmer sea changes where the fish are found, so fishers earn less; **storms are stronger and the sea rougher**, so fishing is more dangerous.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO effects (2 marks).*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Adaptation is changing the way we live and work so that we can cope with the changes that are already happening** (1 mark).
- **Example of adaptation**: planting early-maturing or drought-resistant maize; building a sea defence wall at Keta; harvesting rain water; changing the planting calendar; storing part of the harvest (1 mark).
- **Mitigation is reducing the amount of greenhouse gas we release, or taking it back out of the air, so that the warming itself is slowed** (1 mark).
- **Example of mitigation**: using solar panels instead of a diesel generator; planting trees; cooking on an improved stove or on gas instead of an open wood fire; recycling instead of burning refuse (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 4 marks: 1 for each definition and 1 for each matching example. The commonest error is to give a mitigation example for adaptation; the test is simple - adaptation deals with the EFFECTS, mitigation deals with the CAUSE.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Plant early-maturing and drought-resistant varieties** of maize, millet or cowpea, so that the crop ripens before the rains stop.
- **Change the planting calendar and follow the weather forecast** from the Meteorological Agency and the agricultural extension officer instead of the old fixed dates.
- **Build small dams and dugouts, harvest rain water and irrigate** so that there is water in the dry months.
- Also accept: **improved storage so that part of the harvest is kept against a bad season**; **mixed cropping and keeping livestock as well as crops, so that one failure does not ruin the family**; **planting trees as windbreaks and for shade**; **joining a savings group or a crop insurance scheme**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE measures (3 marks). The measure must help the community COPE; 'stop using generators' is mitigation and earns nothing here.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Plant trees and protect those already standing**, so that carbon dioxide is taken out of the air and stored in the wood.
- **Stop bush burning** and use cleared weeds as compost or mulch instead of setting fire to them.
- **Change the way energy is used** - improved fuel-saving stoves, gas or solar instead of the open wood fire and the diesel generator.
- Also accept: **separate and compost organic waste instead of dumping or burning it**; **recycle plastic, metal and glass**; **walk, cycle or share transport**; **protect the forest reserve and the trees along the riverbank**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE actions (3 marks). The action must reduce the gases released or take them out of the air.*

### Question 5 (8 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **A green economy is one in which people earn a living and the country develops without destroying the environment** (1 mark).
- **It releases little pollution and few greenhouse gases, uses natural resources carefully so that they are not used up, and still provides jobs and incomes** for the people (1 mark).
- Accept the short form: *growth that does not cost us the land, the water and the air.*
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. An answer about the colour green, or about growing vegetables only, earns nothing.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Installing and repairing solar panels and solar lanterns** - supplies electricity without burning fuel, so no greenhouse gas is released.
- **Raising seedlings in a nursery and planting trees** - the growing trees take carbon dioxide out of the air, hold the soil and bring back the forest.
- **Collecting and recycling plastic, metal and electronic waste** - keeps the waste out of the gutters, the land and the sea, and saves the energy that making new material would cost.
- Also accept: **organic farming and composting**; **making and selling improved fuel-saving stoves**; **beekeeping**; **eco-tourism and work in a forest reserve**; **repairing goods instead of replacing them**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE (3 marks). The mark is given only where the work AND its benefit to the environment are both stated.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Plant trees on the compound and care for them** - shade, cleaner air and carbon dioxide absorbed.
- **Separate the waste and compost the food and garden waste** - the compost feeds the school garden and the refuse that would rot in a dump and release methane is kept out of it.
- **Stop burning refuse on the compound** - no poisonous smoke for the pupils to breathe and no carbon dioxide released.
- Also accept: **switch off lights and fans when rooms are empty, and fit solar panels or solar lamps**; **harvest rain water from the roof**; **a walking, cycling or transport-sharing day**; **a science or environment club that teaches the community**; **use both sides of every sheet of paper**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE (3 marks), and the benefit must be stated. Reward a candidate who names something the school could really do tomorrow over one who names an expensive project.*

### Question 6 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Growing trees take carbon dioxide out of the air and store the carbon in their wood**, so less of the gas is left to trap heat.
- **Trees cool and shade the land, hold the soil against erosion, slow run-off and flooding, and help to keep rainfall steady**; they also restore the habitats of plants and animals.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO reasons (2 marks). The first reason is the central one; award the second mark for any genuine environmental benefit.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Plan**: decide where on the compound the trees will stand and how many are needed, and obtain the permission of the head teacher (1 mark).
- **Obtain the right seedlings**: choose species suited to the place - shade, fruit or timber - and collect them from the Forestry Commission, the agricultural office or a local nursery (1 mark).
- **Plant and care for them**: dig the holes, plant early in the rainy season, water, mulch and fence or stake each tree, and **assign a named pupil or class to each tree** so that it is watered and protected after the ceremony (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE steps (3 marks), provided they are in a sensible order. Give particular credit to any candidate who provides for the trees to be CARED FOR after planting; that is where most campaigns fail.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **One real difficulty** (1 mark): the seedlings die for want of water in the dry season; goats, cattle or careless people break them; there is no money for seedlings or tools; nobody cares for them during the long holidays.
- **A matching solution** (1 mark): a written watering rota with mulching round each tree; a stake and a wire or palm-frond guard; free seedlings requested from the Forestry Commission or the assembly; the caretaker, or families living near the school, asked to water during the holidays.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 for the difficulty, 1 for a solution that actually answers it. A solution that does not match the difficulty earns nothing.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **Why the law is needed** (1 mark): bush fires destroy trees, grass, crops and wildlife, burn out the humus and leave the soil bare to erosion, and they release large amounts of carbon dioxide while killing the very plants that would have absorbed it; one careless fire can burn a whole district's farms.
- **Form a fire volunteer squad and cut fire belts** round the farms and the woodlot before the dry season, and agree with the chief on when, if ever, burning is allowed (1 mark).
- **Educate and warn those most likely to start fires** - hunters, herders, charcoal burners, children and farmers clearing land - and **report offenders to the chief, the assembly or the Fire Service** so that the law is actually applied (1 mark).
- Also accept: **use the cleared weeds as compost or mulch instead of burning them**, and **agree on by-laws and fines through the assembly**.
  - *Marking note: 3 marks: 1 for the reason, 1 each for TWO practical community actions. 'The government should arrest them' is not a community action; 'we report offenders so that they are arrested' is.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 5: Humans and the Environment | **Sub-strand:** 4: Climate Change and Green Economy | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.5.4.1** - Demonstrate an understanding of the effects of climate change in the world and greening of other tropical countries including Ghana.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 5: Humans and the Environment, Sub-Strand 4: Climate Change and Green Economy, Basic 8, pages 82 and 83. Content standard B8/JHS2.5.4.1 with two indicators. Under B8/JHS2.5.4.1.1 the exemplars are: describe the signs of climate change; search for the causes and effects of climate change and present a report; and explain how countries in the continents are adapting to climate change, for example tree planting and legislation on bush burning. Under B8/JHS2.5.4.1.2 the exemplars are: describe climate change adaptation measures that can be applied in the community; and discuss mitigation strategies that the community can adopt to reduce the effects of climate change.

> Note: The two indicators are examined separately in the blueprint. Indicator 1, the concept of climate change and its effect on the environment, carries topics 23.1, 23.2 and 23.3 and Questions 1, 2 and 3. Indicator 2, climate change and green economy actions, carries topics 23.4 and 23.5 and Questions 4, 5 and 6; the adaptation exemplar of Indicator 1, which names tree planting and legislation on bush burning, is examined in Question 6 and is credited there to Indicator 2 because the question asks the candidate to plan the action rather than to describe another country. The school's sheets use the shorter coded form (B8.5.4.1); both forms are given in the blueprint.

## QUALITY-CONTROL SUMMARY

| Check | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Every item traceable to the curriculum | Yes - all 40 objective items and all 6 theory questions sit under content standard B8/JHS2.5.4.1 and are matched in the blueprint to one of its two indicators: B8/JHS2.5.4.1.1 for the concept, the signs, the causes and the effects, and B8/JHS2.5.4.1.2 for adaptation, mitigation and green economy actions. |
| Only one defensible answer per objective item | Yes - every stem was re-read against its four options. The distractors are the confusions pupils actually make: weather mistaken for climate, a single hot day mistaken for a sign of climate change, adaptation mistaken for mitigation, and the belief that the earth has moved nearer to the sun. |
| Correct answers spread evenly | Yes - A = 10, B = 10, C = 10, D = 10, and no letter is repeated more than twice in a row. |
| Marks add up | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40 marks; Section B 10 + 10 + 12 + 10 + 8 + 10 = 60 marks; total 100 marks. |
| Cognitive spread | Yes - the paper runs from the meanings of climate, climate change, adaptation and mitigation, through the mechanism by which the layer of gases warms the earth, to reading a forty-year temperature record, calculating the rise, judging whether one station is enough evidence, planning a tree-planting exercise and explaining why a law against bush burning is needed. |
| Difficulty mix close to 30 / 50 / 20 | Yes - the mix is reported in the Cognitive-Level Distribution section below and is within the tolerance set for a mock paper. |
| Figures readable in black and white | Yes - both figures are hand-drawn pencil sketches with handwriting-style labels. Fig. 1 uses arrows and outline only, and Fig. 2 prints the value beside every point, so neither depends on colour. |
| Figure labels do not give the answers away | Yes - in Fig. 1 the three arrows are lettered P, Q and R and the band is called only 'layer of gases round the earth'; the words greenhouse, carbon dioxide and global warming do not appear, and they are what Question 1 asks for. Fig. 2 is titled only as a record of average yearly temperature and draws no conclusion. |
| Calculations checked | Yes - in Question 2(a) the graph is read as 27.0 °C in 1980 and 28.4 °C in 2020; in 2(b), 28.4 − 27.0 = 1.4 °C. The five plotted values rise by 0.3, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.4 °C, which is the steady pattern Question 2(c) asks the candidate to describe. |
| Sensitive content handled properly | Yes - the paper names no country or group as being to blame. Section A item 25 makes the fair point that the countries producing least greenhouse gas often suffer most, and the questions put the emphasis on what Ghanaian communities and pupils can themselves do. |
| Marking scheme usable by any teacher | Yes - every part carries its mark allocation, the expected points are listed, and the italic marking notes state what is compulsory for each mark, what alternatives are acceptable, and the common errors to watch for - in particular the adaptation and mitigation mix-up in Question 4(a). |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - Question 3(b) says that each activity must be paired with its gas or process; Question 4 states plainly which of the two kinds of action each part wants; Question 5(b) and 5(c) say that the benefit must be given as well as the activity. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - a weather station in the north, the farmer whose rains once came in March, cocoa in a longer dry season, the sea at Keta and Ada, a hydroelectric dam, small dams and dugouts, the Ghana Meteorological Agency, the Forestry Commission, the Fire Service, the chief and the assembly, and the national tree-planting day. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the paper keeps to the concept, signs, causes and effects of climate change and to adaptation, mitigation and green economy actions. The chemistry of the infra-red absorption, the carbon budget, ozone depletion and international treaties are not examined; the mechanism is described only as heat being held in and sent back by the layer of gases. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - interpreting arrows on a diagram, naming gases, explaining a mechanism, reading and calculating from a line graph, judging the strength of evidence, defining and distinguishing two kinds of action, listing community measures, describing green jobs and school actions, planning a tree-planting exercise and arguing for a law. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper covers both indicators of the sub-strand, so it may be used as an end-of-topic test for the whole of Climate Change and Green Economy.
- Question 4(a) is the item that separates the class. Most candidates can define climate change; far fewer can keep adaptation and mitigation apart. Teach the simple test - adaptation deals with the effects, mitigation deals with the cause - and mark strictly against it.
- In Question 2(e) reward any candidate who sees that one station is not enough. That is the competency CP 5.1, combining information from several sources, and it is worth more than another list of signs.
- Award the method marks in Question 2(b) even where the arithmetic is wrong, but insist on the unit °C in the final answer.
- Questions 5(c) and 6 are practical. If your school actually planted trees or started separating its waste this term, mark the class's own work against these parts and send the best plan to the head teacher.
- In Question 6(b), give particular credit for providing that the trees be cared for AFTER the planting day. A tree planted and abandoned is not a mitigation measure.
- Section A items 25, 39 and 40 call for judgement rather than recall. Discuss them with the class after marking.
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In calculations, award a method mark for correct working even where the final answer is wrong, and insist on the unit cm³ where a volume is asked for. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (6) Where a candidate names a rock or a soil found in his or her own district that the scheme does not list, award the mark if the description fits.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Aim: to find out how much water each of the three soils holds back, or lets through** (1 mark).
- **The property compared is the water-retaining ability (water retention) of the soils**, which is the other side of how freely they drain (1 mark).
- Accept also: *to compare the drainage of the three soils*.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 each. 'To test the soils' is too vague. Accept either retention or drainage for the second mark, since each implies the other.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Soil A: 100 − 42 = 58 cm³** (1 mark).
- **Soil B: 100 − 25 = 75 cm³** (1 mark).
- **Soil C: 100 − 8 = 92 cm³** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 each. The working 100 minus the volume collected must be seen or implied. Insist on cm³ at least once; do not penalise the missing unit three times over.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **A is the sandy soil**: it let the most water through (42 cm³), because its particles are large and the spaces between them are wide, so water drains freely (1 mark).
- **C is the clay soil**: it let only 8 cm³ through and held back 92 cm³, because its particles are very fine and tightly packed, so the water is held in the tiny spaces (1 mark).
- It follows that **B is the loamy soil**, which lies between the two.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 for each soil correctly identified WITH a reason drawn from the particle size or the spaces. A bare letter with no reason earns nothing.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **The same mass (or volume) of soil in each funnel.**
- **The same volume of water poured into each funnel** - here 100 cm³.
- **The same funnels, and the same filter paper or cotton wool** at the neck of each.
- Also accept: **all three soils dried in the same way before the test**; **the water poured at the same rate**; **the same time allowed for the water to drain before reading**; **the soils packed to the same tightness**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE controlled variables (3 marks). The answer must be something that is KEPT THE SAME; naming the soil type, which is the thing being changed, earns nothing.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Texture** - how coarse or fine the soil feels, which depends on the size of its particles.
- **Colour** - dark brown or black soils are usually rich in humus, while pale or red soils are usually poorer in it.
- **Water-retaining ability and drainage** - how much water the soil holds and how fast the rest passes through.
- Also accept: **air content (porosity)**; **structure, that is the way the particles cling together into crumbs**; **the amount of humus**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE physical properties (3 marks). The fertility or the pH of a soil is not a physical property and earns nothing.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Size of the particles** - sandy: **large (coarse)**; clay: **very small (fine)** (1 mark for the row).
- **Drainage of water** - sandy: **very fast, free drainage**; clay: **very slow, often waterlogged** (1 mark).
- **Amount of water retained** - sandy: **little**; clay: **a great deal** (1 mark).
- **Ease of working with a hoe** - sandy: **light and easy to work**; clay: **heavy and hard to work - sticky when wet, hard and cracked when dry** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 4 marks, 1 for each complete row. Both cells of a row must be correct for the mark; a row with one cell right and one wrong scores nothing.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **It holds enough water for the crop but allows the surplus to drain**, so the plant is neither thirsty nor waterlogged.
- **It keeps air in its spaces**, so the roots and the soil organisms can respire.
- **It is usually rich in humus and plant nutrients**, and it holds those nutrients instead of letting them wash away.
- Also accept: **it is easy to work and the roots spread through it freely**; **it does not cake or crack like clay, nor dry out like sand**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any THREE reasons (3 marks). 'It is the best soil' repeats the question and earns nothing.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The light, gritty (sandy) field**: dig in **organic manure, compost, poultry droppings or green manure**, and mulch the surface, so that the soil holds more water and more nutrients (1 mark).
- **The heavy, sticky (clay) field**: work in **sand and well-rotted manure or compost** to open the soil, and **make ridges, mounds or drains** so that the surplus water can run off (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 each. The treatment must match the field; a candidate who adds sand to the sandy field earns nothing for that mark.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **W - the topsoil** (1 mark).
- **X - the subsoil** (1 mark).
- **Y - the weathered or broken rock**, the layer of loose, angular fragments (accept 'partly weathered rock') (1 mark).
- **Z - the parent rock, or bedrock**, the solid unbroken rock (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 4 marks, 1 each. Accept 'horizon A', 'horizon B', 'horizon C' and 'horizon D' only where the matching ordinary name is also given. The whole set of layers is called the soil profile.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **W is darker, because it is rich in humus; X is paler and contains little humus.**
- **W is loose and crumbly and holds most of the plant roots, earthworms and other soil organisms**, while **X is more compact and stony, and few roots and organisms reach it**.
- Also accept: **X receives the minerals washed down from W by rain water**, and **W is the thinner of the two layers in this cut**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO differences (2 marks). A difference must compare the two layers; a statement about W alone earns nothing.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **It is the layer in which the crop is planted and in which almost all the feeding roots grow** (1 mark).
- **It holds the humus, the plant nutrients, most of the soil water and air, and the earthworms, bacteria and fungi that keep the soil alive**, so the yield of the farm depends on it (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. An answer that says only 'it is on top' earns nothing.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Clearing and burning the vegetation and leaving the land bare**, so that the rain washes the topsoil away and the sun burns out the humus - prevent it by **keeping a cover crop, mulching, or planting trees as a windbreak** (1 mark).
- **Ploughing or making ridges straight up and down a slope**, which lets the run-off carry the soil downhill - prevent it by **ploughing and ridging along the contour, or by terracing the slope** (1 mark).
- Also accept: **sand winning, mining and road building that strip the topsoil** - require that the topsoil be set aside and replaced afterwards; **overgrazing by too many animals** - control the number of animals and move them from place to place; **continuous cropping without manure or fallow** - rotate crops and return organic matter.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 for each activity that is correctly paired with a remedy that actually answers it. An activity with no remedy, or a remedy that does not fit, earns nothing for that item.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Igneous rock** - formed when **molten rock material (magma or lava) cools and becomes solid** (1 mark).
- **Sedimentary rock** - formed when **layers of sand, mud, shell and other sediment are deposited, pressed and cemented together over a very long time** (1 mark).
- **Metamorphic rock** - formed when **an existing rock is changed by great heat and pressure inside the earth**, without melting completely (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 for each type correctly named AND matched with its formation. A name alone, with no formation, earns nothing.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Igneous: granite** (accept basalt, pumice, obsidian) (1 mark).
- **Sedimentary: limestone** (accept sandstone, shale, mudstone, conglomerate) (1 mark).
- **Metamorphic: marble** (accept slate, quartzite, schist, gneiss) (1 mark).
- Note for the teacher: granite is widely quarried in Ghana for building stone and chippings, and limestone is quarried at Nauli and Buipe for cement.
  - *Marking note: 3 marks, 1 each. The example must be matched to the right type; a correct rock named under the wrong heading earns nothing.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Colour**, and whether the colour is even or mixed.
- **Hardness** - whether it can be scratched with a nail or scratches glass; and whether it crumbles in the hand.
- **Texture** - the size of the grains and whether the surface feels rough or smooth, glassy or dull.
- **Whether it shows layers, bands or separate crystals**, which helps to place it as sedimentary, metamorphic or igneous.
- Also accept: **how heavy it feels for its size**; **where and when it was collected**; **a sketch or photograph**.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: award 1 mark for any TWO correct features and 2 marks for FOUR. The name of the rock is not a feature to be observed; it is the conclusion.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The mineral part of every soil comes from rock that has been broken down**: weathering reduces the rock beneath to smaller and smaller pieces, which mix with the humus from decayed plants and animals to make soil (1 mark).
- **The kind of rock therefore decides the kind of soil formed** - its particles, its colour and the minerals it contains. This is why the rock under a soil is called its parent material (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. The first mark is for the breaking down of rock into the soil particles; the second for the link between the type of rock and the type of soil.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Weathering is the breaking down of rock into smaller and smaller pieces where the rock lies**, by heat and cold, water, chemicals or living things (1 mark).
- **In weathering the pieces are not carried away; in erosion the broken material or the soil IS carried away** by running water, wind, ice or gravity (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. The distinction is the one examiners look for: weathering breaks down in place, erosion transports.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Heating and cooling**: the sun heats the rock by day and it cools at night, so the rock expands and contracts again and again until it cracks and pieces flake off the surface.
- **The action of water**: rain water seeps into the cracks and, being slightly acidic, slowly dissolves some of the minerals, weakening the rock; running water also wears the surface away.
- **The roots of the tree and other plants**: as a root grows in a crack it widens it and forces the pieces of rock apart; lichens and mosses also attack the surface chemically.
- **Wind-blown sand and grit** wear and scratch the exposed surface; **burrowing animals, and people quarrying or farming**, break the rock further.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any FOUR ways (4 marks), provided each is described and not merely named. The candidate need not use the words physical, chemical and biological, but give credit where they are used correctly.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- **Stage 1** - the **solid rock is attacked by heat, cold, water and plant roots and begins to crack** (1 mark).
- **Stage 2** - the **cracks widen and the rock breaks into boulders, stones and gravel** (1 mark).
- **Stage 3** - **continued weathering grinds these pieces into fine particles - sand, silt and clay** (1 mark).
- **Stage 4** - **lichens, mosses and small plants grow in the particles, die and decay; their remains and those of animals add humus**, and the mixture of mineral particles, humus, water and air forms a soil deep enough for crops (1 mark).
- Teachers should note that this takes **hundreds of years**, which is why topsoil once lost cannot quickly be replaced.
  - *Marking note: 4 marks, 1 for each stage, and the stages must be in the correct order. A candidate who gives all four points out of order earns at most 3 marks. The humus stage is essential for the fourth mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **The soil water round the root hair is a very weak solution, while the cell sap inside the root hair is a stronger, more concentrated solution** (1 mark).
- **Water therefore passes through the thin wall and membrane of the root hair into the cell by osmosis**, from the weaker to the stronger solution; the many long, thin root hairs give a very large surface for this to happen (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks. The word osmosis alone earns 1 mark; the second mark needs the difference in concentration. Dissolved mineral salts are carried in with the water, but they also enter by other means - do not penalise a candidate who says only that they come in with the water.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **(i) Too dry**: there is too little water in the soil for the roots to replace what the leaves are losing, so the cells lose their firmness and the plant droops (1 mark).
- **(ii) Waterlogged**: the water fills the air spaces in the soil, so **the roots cannot get the oxygen they need to respire**; they begin to rot and can no longer take in water, so the plant wilts even though it is standing in water (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 2 marks, 1 each. Part (ii) is the discriminating one; the mark requires the lack of oxygen at the roots.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Set-up** (1 mark): take three identical tins or pots with drainage holes, label them sandy, loamy and clay, fill each with the same volume of its soil, and plant the same number of seeds of the same crop - maize or beans - at the same depth in each.
- **Fair test and measurement** (1 mark): give each pot the same volume of water at the same times, keep all three in the same place with the same sunlight, and then **measure the height of the seedlings and count the leaves every three days for two or three weeks**, recording the results in a table before comparing them.
  - *Marking note: 2 marks: 1 for a workable set-up, 1 for controlling the other conditions AND taking measurements. A candidate who merely says 'plant in three soils and see' earns the first mark only.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Mulch the surface** with grass, straw, leaves or crop residues, so that less water evaporates from the soil.
- **Dig in compost or organic manure**, which helps the soil to hold water like a sponge.
- Also accept: **plant a cover crop**; **plant trees as shade or as a windbreak**; **weed the field, since weeds take up the water**; **make ridges or tied ridges to trap the rain where it falls**; **irrigate from a dugout or small dam**; **stop burning the crop residues**.
  - *Marking note: 1 mark each for any TWO measures (2 marks).*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 5: Humans and the Environment | **Sub-strand:** 5: Understanding the Environment | **Class:** Basic 8 (JHS 2)

**Content Standard:** **B8/JHS2.5.5.1** - Demonstrate understanding of the differences among soils, plant roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits of plants in the different environments. **B8/JHS2.5.6.1** - Recognise the different types of rocks as origin of different types of soils.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 5: Humans and the Environment, Sub-Strand 5: Understanding the Environment, Basic 8, pages 84 and 85. Two content standards are examined. Under B8/JHS2.5.5.1 the indicators are B8/JHS2.5.5.1.1 (exemplars: collect and describe different samples of soils from the school garden and the community; discuss how each soil type retains water and supports the root system of plants; conduct an experiment to demonstrate how different soil types retain water) and B8/JHS2.5.5.1.2 (exemplars: examine and discuss the physical properties of each soil type and how they support crop production; observe and describe the growth of different plants on different soil types; demonstrate how plants absorb water and nutrients from the soil by osmosis). Under B8/JHS2.5.6.1 the indicator is B8/JHS2.5.6.1.1 (exemplars: identify different labelled samples of rocks; describe the visible characteristics of each rock; collect samples from the community and compare them with the laboratory samples using a rock identification guide; research and report the stages of weathering of rocks to form soil).

> Note: This paper is the only one in the series to examine two content standards, because the syllabus places the rocks standard, B8/JHS2.5.6.1, inside the same sub-strand as the soils standard and treats rocks as the origin of soils. The blueprint separates the three indicators: I1 (B8/JHS2.5.5.1.1) carries topics 24.1 and 24.2 and Questions 1 and 2; I2 (B8/JHS2.5.5.1.2) carries topic 24.3 and Question 6; I3 (B8/JHS2.5.6.1.1) carries topics 24.4 and 24.5 and Questions 3, 4 and 5. The parts of the soils standard that deal with roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits in different environments are NOT examined here, because the two indicators written under that standard in the syllabus deal only with soils; the school's sheets use the shorter coded forms (B8.5.5.1 and B8.5.6.1), and both forms are given in the blueprint.

| Check | Status |

| Every item traceable to the curriculum | Yes - all 40 objective items and all 6 theory questions sit under the two content standards of this sub-strand, B8/JHS2.5.5.1 and B8/JHS2.5.6.1, and each is matched in the blueprint to one of their three indicators. |
| Only one defensible answer per objective item | Yes - every stem was re-read against its four options. The distractors are the mistakes pupils actually make: that clay holds little water, that waterlogging drowns a plant by washing off its leaves, that weathering and erosion are the same thing, and that marble is a sedimentary rock. |
| Correct answers spread evenly | Yes - A = 10, B = 10, C = 10, D = 10, and no letter is repeated more than twice in a row. |
| Marks add up | Yes - Section A 40 x 1 = 40 marks; Section B 10 + 12 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 8 = 60 marks; total 100 marks. |
| Cognitive spread | Yes - the paper runs from the constituents and properties of soil, through reading an experiment and calculating from it, identifying soils from their behaviour, naming the layers of a soil profile, classifying rocks and judging what should be recorded in an identification guide, to setting the stages of weathering in order and designing a pot experiment. |
| Difficulty mix close to 30 / 50 / 20 | Yes - the mix is reported in the Cognitive-Level Distribution section below and is within the tolerance set for a mock paper. |
| Figures readable in black and white | Yes - both figures are hand-drawn pencil sketches with handwriting-style labels. Fig. 1 prints the volume collected under each funnel and Fig. 2 distinguishes its layers by stipple, outline and the shape of the fragments, so neither depends on colour. |
| Figure labels do not give the answers away | Yes - in Fig. 1 the soils are lettered A, B and C and are never called sandy, loamy or clay, which is what Question 1(c) asks the candidate to work out from the volumes. In Fig. 2 the four layers are lettered W, X, Y and Z; the caption calls the drawing only 'a cut through the ground at the edge of a new road' and names no layer. |
| Calculations checked | Yes - in Question 1(b), 100 − 42 = 58 cm³, 100 − 25 = 75 cm³ and 100 − 8 = 92 cm³. The three volumes drawn in Fig. 1 are 42, 25 and 8 cm³ out of the 100 cm³ poured, and they fall in the order sandy, loamy, clay that Question 1(c) requires. |
| Sensitive content handled properly | Not applicable in the usual sense; the content carries no personal or health sensitivity. Question 3(d) does touch on sand winning and mining, and it is framed as damage to be prevented rather than as blame on any group. |
| Marking scheme usable by any teacher | Yes - every part carries its mark allocation, the expected points are listed, and the italic marking notes state what is compulsory for each mark, what alternatives are acceptable, and the common errors to watch for - in particular that both cells of a table row in Question 2(b) must be right for the mark, and that the four stages in Question 5(c) must be in order. |
| Free from unnecessary ambiguity | Yes - Question 1(b) states that the water HELD BACK is wanted, not the water collected; Question 2(b) supplies the table so that every candidate compares the same four properties; Question 5(c) says plainly that the stages must be given in order. |
| Ghanaian contexts natural and accurate | Yes - the school garden and the community samples that the syllabus calls for, a farmer at Techiman with a light field and a heavy field, a cut at the edge of a new road, a granite boulder in a field near the school, and the note that granite is quarried for chippings and limestone at Nauli and Buipe for cement. |
| No content beyond the curriculum | No - the paper keeps to the physical properties of soils, soil water and its importance in crop production, and the types of rock and the weathering that turns them into soil. Soil chemistry and pH, the mineralogy of the rocks, the rock cycle in full and the quantitative treatment of osmosis are not examined; osmosis is described only as water passing from the weaker to the stronger solution. |
| Questions sufficiently varied | Yes - reading and calculating from an experiment, identifying soils from their behaviour, listing properties, completing a comparison table, naming the layers of a profile, pairing an activity with its remedy, classifying and exemplifying rocks, deciding what to record in an identification guide, setting weathering stages in order, explaining osmosis and wilting, and designing a pot experiment. |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper completes the Basic 8 syllabus. It is also the only paper in the series that examines two content standards, because the syllabus places the rocks standard, B8/JHS2.5.6.1, in the same sub-strand as the soils standard.
- Question 1 is the curriculum's own experiment. If your class actually set up the three funnels this term, mark their own results and figures against this question; their volumes will differ from those in Fig. 1, and that is as it should be.
- In Question 1(d), insist on variables that are KEPT THE SAME. A large number of candidates name the soil type, which is the one thing that must differ.
- Question 2(b) is marked row by row and both cells must be right. Show the class the completed table afterwards; a clear comparison table is worth more to them than a page of prose.
- In Question 5(c) the stages must be in order, and the humus stage is the one most often forgotten. Stress that soil is mineral particles AND humus; rock dust alone is not soil.
- Question 6(b)(ii) separates the class: many candidates can say why a dry plant wilts, far fewer that a waterlogged plant wilts because its roots cannot get oxygen.
- Question 4 asks for a rock identification guide, which is exemplar 3 of the rocks indicator. If your class made one, display it in the laboratory and mark their own entries against part (c).
- The two figures are hand-drawn sketches, in the style pupils are expected to produce in their own answers; redraw them on the chalkboard if you wish.
- Edit the school name, academic year and examination title on page 1 before printing.
- This is an original, teacher-made mock. It is not a reproduction of any WAEC or NaCCA examination paper.
